entry.title: Spark 4.x features by release: what shipped from 4.0 to 4.3 and what it costs

link.title: Spark 4.x features by release: what shipped from 4.0 to 4.3 and what it costs

entry.content:
• Index: every feature, newest release first
  • Three shifts behind the features
    • SQL becomes the main surface again
    • Batch and streaming converge on one declarative layer
    • Python and Connect move off the JVM path
  • The features, release by release
    • Spark 4.3: stateful real-time mode, semi-structured SQL, and history tracking
    • Spark 4.2: new types, new joins, and a clearer SQL surface
    • Spark 4.1: pipelines, procedural SQL, and real-time mode
    • Spark 4.0: the break, and a far more expressive SQL
  • Run the examples yourself
  • When these features bite
  • Release cadence, support and connectors
  • Which upgrades are worth it
    • Upgrade by upgrade
    • Before you upgrade
  • References
  • Trademarks

TL;DR

  • Four minor releases in about seventeen months, each with its own centre of gravity: a break with the past and a far more expressive SQL (4.0), pipelines and procedural SQL (4.1), new data types and joins (4.2), stateful low-latency streaming and history tracking (4.3).
  • Newest release first. This post is the overview: one picture and a one-line-per-feature table for each release. Every release has a deep-dive post with the syntax, a real run and a visual for each feature, and every row below links to its section.
  • Several headline features are off by default or need a connector. The text names the exact setting rather than implying they work out of the box.
  • Removals, default changes and upgrade risks are in the release history post.

Index: every feature, newest release first

Each release has one picture of everything in it here, a table of its features, and a deep-dive post. Every feature below links to its section in that post.

Spark 4.3 (30 Oct 2026), the release with no previews. Deep dive

  • SQL: JSON_TABLE, ASOF JOIN, UNNEST, BIN BY
  • Types: VARIANT editing, TIME(p) and nanosecond timestamps
  • Streaming and pipelines: stateful real-time mode, Auto CDC with SCD Type 2
  • DataFrame API: DataFrame.zip, single-task execution

Spark 4.2 (14 Jul 2026). Deep dive

  • Types and joins: GEOMETRY and GEOGRAPHY, NEAREST BY, vector functions
  • SQL: QUALIFY, SET PATH, metric views, time_bucket
  • Change data capture: the CHANGES clause
  • Procedural SQL: cursors

Spark 4.1 (16 Dec 2025). Deep dive

  • Pipelines and streaming: Declarative Pipelines, real-time mode
  • SQL: SQL scripting, recursive CTEs, VARIANT GA, parameter markers, sketches
  • Python: Arrow UDFs and UDTFs

Spark 4.0 (23 May 2025), the break with the past. Deep dive

  • SQL: ANSI mode, VARIANT, pipe syntax, SQL UDFs, session variables, collation
  • Data and Python: XML source, Python Data Source API, GROUP BY on maps
  • Streaming and Python: transformWithState, polymorphic UDTFs, parameter markers

A Spark release note lists hundreds of tickets, and most of them have nothing to do with the job you run on Monday. This post picks the features a data engineer meets in daily work across 4.0 to 4.3, gives each one line, and points to a deep-dive post for the syntax and what it printed when run.

Release Date Tickets resolved What the release note leads with
4.0.0 23 May 2025 over 5,100 Scala 2.13 and Java 17 as the baseline, ANSI mode on by default, VARIANT, SQL user-defined functions, session variables, pipe syntax, collations, a built-in XML source, a Python data source API, a lightweight Spark Connect client
4.1.0 16 Dec 2025 over 1,800 Spark Declarative Pipelines, Structured Streaming real-time mode, SQL scripting and VARIANT generally available, Arrow-native Python UDFs, recursive CTEs
4.2.0 14 Jul 2026 over 1,700 Geospatial types, change data capture, Arrow-optimized Python UDFs on by default, NEAREST BY joins, SQL path resolution, metric views
4.3.0 30 Oct 2026 over 1,100 Stateful real-time mode, SCD Type 2 in Auto CDC, JSON_TABLE, ASOF JOIN, VARIANT editing functions, faster queries on small data

The last gap is half the size of the first two, and 4.3.0 shipped with no preview builds.

That last point matters when you pick a release. 4.0, 4.1 and 4.2 went through two, four and five preview builds. 4.3.0 had none (no 4.3.0-preview exists on Maven Central or the Apache archive), so it has had the least outside testing, and the patch releases that follow it are where the first corrections will land.

The deep-dive posts hold the examples. Most ran on the release that introduced the feature, on an official Docker image and, for the SQL and Scala examples, on the plain release tarball too; six ran on the 4.3.0 tarball only, and each deep dive says so. The setup is in Run the examples yourself.

Three shifts behind the features

Read the four release notes in order and they look like four unrelated lists. Read them as one line and three decisions run through all of them, which is also why some features arrive in pieces over two or three releases.

Each lane is one shift; each box is what that release added to it.

SQL becomes the main surface again

For a decade the work went into the DataFrame API. The fourth line turns back to SQL and adds constructs that other SQL engines have and Spark did not.

Capability 4.0 4.1 4.2 4.3
New query syntax Pipe syntax (SPARK-49555) Recursive CTEs (SPARK-24497), query parameter markers anywhere (SPARK-53573) QUALIFY (SPARK-31561), NEAREST BY join (SPARK-56395) ASOF JOIN (SPARK-58092), JSON_TABLE (SPARK-58366), UNNEST in FROM (SPARK-58419)
Procedural SQL Session variables (SPARK-42849), SQL user-defined functions (SPARK-46057) SQL scripting, enabled by default (SPARK-54499) Cursors in scripting (SPARK-54759) none in the headlines
Data types VARIANT (SPARK-45827), string collations (SPARK-46830) VARIANT generally available (SPARK-54454) GEOMETRY and GEOGRAPHY (SPARK-51658) VARIANT editing functions (SPARK-57804), nanosecond timestamps in preview (SPARK-56876)
Name resolution none none SET PATH and CURRENT_PATH() (SPARK-54806, behind a flag) none

Teams used to write logic in Python or Scala because SQL could not express it, and paid for it in code analysts could not read and the optimiser could not see through. Putting the constructs into the language fixes that. The cost is that each one is another thing the parser, analyzer and optimiser must keep correct, and several arrive behind a flag first.

Batch and streaming converge on one declarative layer

Streaming and batch meet in one declarative layer, and the streaming side gets a second, lower-latency mode.

Capability 4.0 4.1 4.2 4.3
Pipelines none Spark Declarative Pipelines (SPARK-51727) Auto CDC, SCD Type 1 (SPARK-56249) Auto CDC, SCD Type 2 (SPARK-58321 and others)
Change data none none CHANGES clause and DataFrame APIs for row-level changes (SPARK-55668) consumed by Auto CDC SCD Type 2
Streaming latency Arbitrary state API v2, state data source Real-time mode, stateless (SPARK-53736) none in the headlines Real-time mode with state: aggregation, dropDuplicates, transformWithState (SPARK-58635 and others)
Writes none stored procedures API for catalogs (SPARK-44167) Data Source V2 transaction management (SPARK-55855) dynamic table options for UPDATE, MERGE, DELETE

A pipeline used to need an orchestrator for ordering, a streaming job for freshness and hand-written merge logic for change data, written in different dialects by different teams. Declaring the datasets and letting Spark derive the graph removes that, and the cost is that you hand the execution graph to the framework: when a run behaves oddly, the schedule is not code you wrote. An external orchestrator with micro-batch triggers is still the better fit for pipelines that mix many engines.

Python and Connect move off the JVM path

The client and the language runtime change shape, not just the API.

Capability 4.0 4.1 4.2 4.3
Spark Connect A lightweight Python client, ML over Connect JDBC driver for Connect (SPARK-53484), ML on Connect generally available for Python (SPARK-51236) RDD API compatibility (SPARK-55227) REST endpoints for sessions and operations (SPARK-57941), more complete JDBC driver
Python UDFs Python UDTFs, unified UDF profiling Arrow-native UDF and UDTF decorators (SPARK-52214, SPARK-52979) Arrow-optimized UDFs and Arrow IPC on by default (SPARK-54555) Python performance work
Python data Python Data Source API (SPARK-44076), plotting API (SPARK-49530) filter pushdown for Python data sources grouped-aggregation UDFs in Arrow and pandas none in the headlines
Small data none none none opt-in single-task execution and Arrow-native caching (SPARK-57851, SPARK-57268)

Python was the most used language and the slowest path through Spark, because every row crossed the JVM boundary through pickling, and a client that only talks to a server still needed a full PySpark install. The fix is Arrow end to end, a thin client (4.0 added a 1.5 MB pyspark-client), and a server reachable by JDBC and REST. A default that changes how data crosses the boundary changes behaviour at the edges, in types, nulls and timestamps, which is why 4.2 is the release to test on your own UDFs.

The features, release by release

Each table row gives the feature, what it is and a maturity tag. The deep-dive post for the release has the syntax, the output of a run, and the reasoning.

Tag Meaning
Default Works with no configuration on the release that introduced it
GA, on by default Was experimental earlier and is now enabled and supported
Behind a flag Present, but off until you set a configuration
Preview The release note says so; syntax or behaviour can still change
Needs a connector The engine defines the syntax; a data source has to implement it

The last tag is the one that surprises people. A feature that exists in Spark SQL does not exist for your table until the connector for that table supports it, which is true of change data capture, data source transactions and several INSERT extensions.

Every example is a runnable file in ranga-spark4-examples, organised by release: spark-4.0/, spark-4.1/, spark-4.2/ and spark-4.3/. ./run.sh 4.2 spark-4.2/02_qualify.sql runs one in Docker. Each deep-dive post links the example file for every feature it covers, and Run the examples yourself says how to run them.

Spark 4.3: stateful real-time mode, semi-structured SQL, and history tracking

Everything in Spark 4.3.

Stateful queries move onto the real-time trigger, SQL gains standard answers for JSON, time series and history tracking, and several new types sit behind flags. 4.3.0 shipped without preview builds, so a cautious team waits for the first patch release.

Deep dive: What’s new in Apache Spark 4.3, with the syntax, a real run and a visual for each feature below.

Feature What it is Maturity
Stateful real-time mode Running counts, de-duplication and transformWithState under the real-time trigger, over a pipelined shuffle Default for supported operators; needs a task slot per partition
Auto CDC with SCD Type 2 Keep every version of a record, bounded by __START_AT and __END_AT, inside a pipeline Needs a connector
JSON_TABLE The SQL-standard way to turn a JSON document into typed rows Default, flat form only
UNNEST in FROM ANSI array expansion, in place of explode and LATERAL VIEW Default
ASOF JOIN Match each row to the closest preceding row on the other side Behind a flag
VARIANT editing functions Set, insert, delete and append inside a variant Default
BIN BY Spread a measure over fixed time bins in proportion to the overlap Behind a flag
TIME(p) and nanosecond timestamps Time of day and timestamps with up to nine fractional digits Behind flags; timestamps are a preview
DataFrame.zip Append the columns of a second DataFrame row by row, with no join key Default
Single-task execution Run a small query as one task, with no shuffles (Project Feather) Behind a flag

Also in 4.3, listed in the release notes:

  • Project Feather: opt-in shuffle-free single-task execution and Arrow-native caching for small data (the two flags are in the 4.3 settings table)
  • Items that need a connector: @ time travel on table names (SPARK-57421, SPARK-58012) and dynamic table options for UPDATE, MERGE and DELETE
  • Spark Connect REST endpoints (SPARK-57941), operation IDs for tracing, and a JDBC driver that returns ARRAY, MAP and STRUCT
  • timestamp_nanos and unix_nanos, and VARIANT field-extraction pushdown for aggregate, sort and join queries
  • Default whole-stage code generation for eligible UNIONs, opt-in null join key spreading for outer and anti joins, and pruning of unused fields inside arrays of structs

Spark 4.2: new types, new joins, and a clearer SQL surface

Everything in Spark 4.2.

Spatial types, vector distance functions and a top-K join arrive in the engine, alongside SQL for filtering windows, resolving names and defining metrics once. Three of the headline items, change data capture, INSERT ... WITH SCHEMA EVOLUTION and Data Source V2 transactions, are defined by the engine but implemented by a connector, so built-in sources cannot show them.

Deep dive: What’s new in Apache Spark 4.2, with the syntax, a real run and a visual for each feature below.

Feature What it is Maturity
GEOMETRY and GEOGRAPHY Spatial column types that carry an SRID, with five functions today Default
NEAREST BY join Return the K best rows on the right for each row on the left; brute force today Default
Vector functions Cosine similarity, L2 distance, inner product and norm over ARRAY<FLOAT> Default
QUALIFY Filter on a window function without a subquery Default
SET PATH An ordered schema search path for unqualified names Behind a flag
Metric views Define dimensions and measures once in YAML and query them with MEASURE Default, built-in catalog
time_bucket and IGNORE NULLS Fixed-width time buckets, and explicit null handling in collect_list Default
The CHANGES clause Read what changed between two table versions; the catalog must implement it Needs a connector
Cursors in SQL scripts DECLARE, OPEN, FETCH and CLOSE in a script Behind two internal flags

Also in 4.2, listed in the release notes:

  • Items that need a connector: the CHANGES clause and CDC APIs (SPARK-55668), INSERT ... WITH SCHEMA EVOLUTION and REPLACE ON/USING (SPARK-54971, SPARK-56001), and Data Source V2 transactions (SPARK-55855)
  • Tuple sketches, and broader TIME support across file formats
  • SYSTEM.BUILTIN and SYSTEM.SESSION qualification for built-in functions and temporary views
  • Arrow-optimized Python UDFs on by default (SPARK-54555), so test your own UDFs before trusting it, and zero-copy hand-off of DataFrames to Polars or DuckDB through the Arrow C Data Interface
  • Auto CDC with SCD Type 1 (SPARK-56249), and stateless PySpark queries in real-time mode
  • Spark Connect: RDD API compatibility, YARN cluster mode, and DataFrame inputs to spark.read.*
  • Faster MERGE INTO, operation summaries for UPDATE and DELETE, a web UI rebuilt on Bootstrap 5 with dark mode, heterogeneous Kubernetes executors, Spark History Server scalability, and JDK 25 support

Spark 4.1: pipelines, procedural SQL, and real-time mode

Everything in Spark 4.1.

Pipelines become declarative, SQL gains scripts and recursion, and Structured Streaming gets a real-time trigger for stateless Scala queries on Kafka.

Deep dive: What’s new in Apache Spark 4.1, with the syntax, a real run and a visual for each feature below.

Feature What it is Maturity
Spark Declarative Pipelines Declare datasets; Spark derives the run order from their references Default, via the spark-pipelines CLI
Real-time mode, stateless Long-lived tasks instead of micro-batches, in Scala, with a Kafka source Default, stateless only
SQL scripting BEGIN ... END blocks with variables, loops and error handlers GA, on by default
Recursive CTEs A CTE that refers to itself, for hierarchies and graph walks Default
VARIANT GA and colon paths Read a field with v:path::type GA, on by default
Parameter markers anywhere :name markers in identifiers, limits and scripts Default
Sketch functions Top-k, KLL quantile and Theta sketches that can be stored and merged Default
Arrow-native UDFs and UDTFs @arrow_udf hands the function whole PyArrow arrays Default, needs pyarrow

Also in 4.1, listed in the release notes:

  • CONTINUE HANDLER and multi-variable DECLARE in SQL scripting, and shredding for faster VARIANT reads
  • Spark ML on Connect generally available for Python, zstd compression for protobuf plans, chunked Arrow result streaming, and no 2 GB limit on local relations
  • python_worker_logs() to query Python worker logs, and filter pushdown for Python data sources through pushFilters
  • A JDBC driver for Spark Connect (SPARK-53484)

Spark 4.0: the break, and a far more expressive SQL

Everything in Spark 4.0.

Scala 2.13 and Java 17 become the baseline, ANSI mode turns on by default, and SQL gains a type for JSON, functions, variables, collations and a top-to-bottom syntax.

Deep dive: What’s new in Apache Spark 4.0, with the syntax, a real run and a visual for each feature below.

Feature What it is Maturity
ANSI mode by default Invalid casts and divide by zero raise errors instead of returning NULL Default
VARIANT A binary type for semi-structured data such as JSON Default; GA in 4.1
SQL pipe syntax Read a query top to bottom with |> Default
SQL user-defined functions Scalar and table functions written in SQL Default
Session variables Typed variables with DECLARE and SET VAR Default
String collation Case-insensitive, accent-aware and locale-aware comparison Default
Built-in XML source Read, write and parse XML without an external package Default
Python Data Source API and UDTFs Write a data source or table function in Python Default, needs pyarrow
GROUP BY on maps and DESCRIBE ... AS JSON Group by a map column; get a table description as one JSON document Default
transformWithState and the state data source Custom per-key streaming state, read back as a table Default; needs the RocksDB state store and protobuf
Polymorphic Python UDTFs A table function whose schema follows its argument types Default
Named and unnamed parameter markers :name and ? placeholders bound outside the SQL text Default

Also in 4.0, listed in the release notes:

  • transformWithState for custom stateful processing in Scala, Java and Python, the state data source reader, and state store improvements such as SST file reuse
  • Polymorphic Python UDTFs whose output schema is decided at call time
  • Named and unnamed parameter markers for parameterized queries
  • Structured JSON logging, seen in every error the 4.0 runs logged
  • A 1.5 MB lightweight Python client, spark.api.mode to switch Connect on, and community Spark Connect clients for Go, Swift and Rust
  • Native Plotly-based plotting on PySpark DataFrames (SPARK-49530)
  • Java 21 support, the Spark Kubernetes operator (SPARK-45923), Spark ML on Connect, and unified PySpark UDF profiling

Run the examples yourself

Every example is a runnable file in ranga-spark4-examples, organised by release. Each deep-dive post has a Run it yourself section for its release: the tarball and image, the Python floor, what the smoke test printed, and the PySpark, pipeline or Kafka runs that release needs. The download-and-verify script and the SQL runner for the plain Apache tarballs are in RUNNING_ON_TARBALLS.md.

Line Release run Tarball Python for PySpark Run it yourself
4.0 4.0.5 523 MB 3.9 or newer 4.0 post
4.1 4.1.4 546 MB 3.10 or newer 4.1 post
4.2 4.2.1 529 MB 3.10 or newer 4.2 post
4.3 4.3.0 535 MB 3.11 or newer 4.3 post

The Python column decides which examples run from a tarball. A machine with Python 3.9 runs the SQL and Scala examples on all four releases and the PySpark examples on 4.0 only.

When these features bite

Almost every failure in this line falls into five shapes: a stricter default, a feature that parses and then does nothing, a feature that is off until you switch it on, a Python environment that is not ready, and real-time mode with no free slots. Each deep-dive post lists the failures for its release, with the text each produced, the cause and the fix, so you can grep for it: 4.0, 4.1, 4.2 and 4.3. The same posts list the settings that gate each feature and what to budget for under Settings and costs.

Release cadence, support and connectors

Cadence. The versioning policy makes 4.3.0 the first quarterly feature release: feature releases come every three months and majors annually. Its maintenance windows are 6 months for a major or feature release and 18 months for a long-term-support (LTS) release. The 4.x LTS is planned as 4.5.0, and the policy keeps the existing 18-month commitment for 4.2.x. It lists a 4.4 branch cut on 16 November 2026 with a first release candidate by 7 December 2026, and a tentative 4.5 in February 2027, all subject to discussion on the dev list. Patch releases have run longer than the stated windows, for example 4.1.4 on 27 October 2026, ten months after 4.1.0, so read a window as a minimum.

Connectors. A lakehouse stack upgrades with its connectors, so check them first. This is what Maven Central showed on 18 November 2026:

Line Latest patch Iceberg iceberg-spark-runtime Hudi hudi-spark4.x-bundle Delta delta-spark_2.13
4.0 4.0.5 1.12.0 1.2.1 4.0.1, built against Spark 4.0.1
4.1 4.1.4 1.12.0 1.2.1 4.1.0, built against Spark 4.1.0
4.2 4.2.1 none published none published 4.4.1, built against Spark 4.2.0
4.3 4.3.0 none published none published none built against 4.3

So 4.1 is the newest line that all three table formats cover today. The release posts say more: 4.1, 4.2 and 4.3.

Managed platforms. Microsoft’s Fabric documentation lists Runtime 2.0 as Spark 4.1 with Delta 4.2, so Fabric users get the 4.1 line, not 4.3. Check your platform’s runtime page before reading a feature as available to you.

Which upgrades are worth it

Upgrade by upgrade

This part is my judgement, drawn from what ran, not a measurement.

  • To 4.0. Not optional once you leave 3.x, because Scala 2.13 and Java 17 are the baseline. The work is dependency and ANSI-mode testing, and the language gains (pipe syntax, SQL functions, session variables, collations) come with it.
  • 4.0 to 4.1. Worth it for SQL scripting, recursive CTEs and VARIANT colon paths if you have logic living in driver code. Declarative Pipelines is worth a trial on one pipeline, with dry-run, before you commit a team to it.
  • 4.1 to 4.2. QUALIFY and metric views pay back quickly for analysts. The geospatial types are a foundation: five functions today, no distance or containment.
  • 4.2 to 4.3. JSON_TABLE, UNNEST and the VARIANT editing functions help any pipeline that handles nested documents. Stateful real-time mode is for the few queries that need sub-second latency and a Kafka source. 4.3.0 shipped without preview builds, so a cautious team waits for the first patch release.

Before you upgrade

  1. Test in this order: ANSI errors on your real data first, then the gating settings listed in each release’s post for anything a job relies on, then the Python environment.
  2. Pin the interpreter and the packages with the release. The Python floor moved from 3.9 to 3.11 across the four releases.
  3. Switch on one flag at a time, in the session that uses it rather than cluster-wide, so a failure points at the feature.
  4. Check the connector before the engine. For Auto CDC, CHANGES, schema evolution and transactions, the connector decides whether the feature exists for your table.
  5. Print spark.version at the top of every run. It is the cheapest check against running the wrong install.
  6. Read the migration guides. The official SQL and PySpark guides list far more default changes than any release post, each with the setting that restores the old behaviour.

The line is moving faster than at any point in the 4.x series. Treat the tables here as a snapshot, re-check the maturity of each feature against the release note of the version you deploy, and keep the smoke files in the examples repo as a test you can rerun on the next release.

References

  • Introducing Apache Spark 4.0, 4.1, 4.2 and 4.3 from Databricks, used to find the features this post lists as not run
  • Apache Spark 4 release overview from Decube
  • ranga-spark4-examples with every runnable example in this post
  • Spark 4.0.0 release notes, 4.1.0, 4.2.0 and 4.3.0 for the feature lists and ticket numbers used throughout
  • Every Apache Spark release, and the problem each one was built to solve for removals, changed defaults and upgrade risks
  • Spark Connect: the driver becomes a server for the client and server split behind the thin client and the pipelines CLI
  • Structured Streaming internals for state and checkpoints behind real-time mode
  • JOIN syntax, including NEAREST BY, QUALIFY and SET PATH in the 4.2.1 documentation
  • JSON_TABLE, ASOF JOIN and UNNEST in the 4.3.0 documentation
  • Spark Declarative Pipelines programming guide for the project spec, the CLI, and Auto CDC with its target requirements
  • RealTimeModeAllowlist.scala for the sources, sinks and operators real-time mode accepts
  • Apache Spark downloads and archive for the release tarballs and their checksums
  • SQL migration guide and PySpark migration guide, the source of the behaviour-change tables in the release posts
  • Apache Spark versioning policy, for the quarterly cadence and the maintenance windows

Capability 4.0 4.1 4.2 4.3 New query syntax Pipe syntax (SPARK-49555) Recursive CTEs (SPARK-24497), query parameter markers anywhere (SPARK-53573) QUALIFY (SPARK-31561), NEAREST BY join (SPARK-56395) ASOF JOIN (SPARK-58092), JSON_TABLE (SPARK-58366), UNNEST in FROM (SPARK-58419) Procedural SQL Session variables (SPARK-42849), SQL user-defined functions (SPARK-46057) SQL scripting, enabled by default (SPARK-54499) Cursors in scripting (SPARK-54759) none in the headlines Data types VARIANT (SPARK-45827), string collations (SPARK-46830) VARIANT generally available (SPARK-54454) GEOMETRY and GEOGRAPHY (SPARK-51658) VARIANT editing functions (SPARK-57804), nanosecond timestamps in preview (SPARK-56876) Name resolution none none SET PATH and CURRENT_PATH() (SPARK-54806, behind a flag) none Teams used to write logic in Python or Scala because SQL could not express it, and paid for it in code analysts could not read and the optimiser could not see through. Putting the constructs into the language fixes that. The cost is that each one is another thing the parser, analyzer and optimiser must keep correct, and several arrive behind a flag first. Batch and streaming converge on one declarative layer Streaming and batch meet in one declarative layer, and the streaming side gets a second, lower-latency mode. Capability 4.0 4.1 4.2 4.3 Pipelines none Spark Declarative Pipelines (SPARK-51727) Auto CDC, SCD Type 1 (SPARK-56249) Auto CDC, SCD Type 2 (SPARK-58321 and others) Change data none none CHANGES clause and DataFrame APIs for row-level changes (SPARK-55668) consumed by Auto CDC SCD Type 2 Streaming latency Arbitrary state API v2, state data source Real-time mode, stateless (SPARK-53736) none in the headlines Real-time mode with state: aggregation, dropDuplicates, transformWithState (SPARK-58635 and others) Writes none stored procedures API for catalogs (SPARK-44167) Data Source V2 transaction management (SPARK-55855) dynamic table options for UPDATE, MERGE, DELETE A pipeline used to need an orchestrator for ordering, a streaming job for freshness and hand-written merge logic for change data, written in different dialects by different teams. Declaring the datasets and letting Spark derive the graph removes that, and the cost is that you hand the execution graph to the framework: when a run behaves oddly, the schedule is not code you wrote. An external orchestrator with micro-batch triggers is still the better fit for pipelines that mix many engines. Python and Connect move off the JVM path The client and the language runtime change shape, not just the API. Capability 4.0 4.1 4.2 4.3 Spark Connect A lightweight Python client, ML over Connect JDBC driver for Connect (SPARK-53484), ML on Connect generally available for Python (SPARK-51236) RDD API compatibility (SPARK-55227) REST endpoints for sessions and operations (SPARK-57941), more complete JDBC driver Python UDFs Python UDTFs, unified UDF profiling Arrow-native UDF and UDTF decorators (SPARK-52214, SPARK-52979) Arrow-optimized UDFs and Arrow IPC on by default (SPARK-54555) Python performance work Python data Python Data Source API (SPARK-44076), plotting API (SPARK-49530) filter pushdown for Python data sources grouped-aggregation UDFs in Arrow and pandas none in the headlines Small data none none none opt-in single-task execution and Arrow-native caching (SPARK-57851, SPARK-57268) Python was the most used language and the slowest path through Spark, because every row crossed the JVM boundary through pickling, and a client that only talks to a server still needed a full PySpark install. The fix is Arrow end to end, a thin client (4.0 added a 1.5 MB pyspark-client), and a server reachable by JDBC and REST. A default that changes how data crosses the boundary changes behaviour at the edges, in types, nulls and timestamps, which is why 4.2 is the release to test on your own UDFs. The features, release by release Each table row gives the feature, what it is and a maturity tag. The deep-dive post for the release has the syntax, the output of a run, and the reasoning. Tag Meaning Default Works with no configuration on the release that introduced it GA, on by default Was experimental earlier and is now enabled and supported Behind a flag Present, but off until you set a configuration Preview The release note says so; syntax or behaviour can still change Needs a connector The engine defines the syntax; a data source has to implement it The last tag is the one that surprises people. A feature that exists in Spark SQL does not exist for your table until the connector for that table supports it, which is true of change data capture, data source transactions and several INSERT extensions. Every example is a runnable file in ranga-spark4-examples, organised by release: spark-4.0/, spark-4.1/, spark-4.2/ and spark-4.3/. ./run.sh 4.2 spark-4.2/02_qualify.sql runs one in Docker. Each deep-dive post links the example file for every feature it covers, and Run the examples yourself says how to run them. Spark 4.3: stateful real-time mode, semi-structured SQL, and history tracking Everything in Spark 4.3. Stateful queries move onto the real-time trigger, SQL gains standard answers for JSON, time series and history tracking, and several new types sit behind flags. 4.3.0 shipped without preview builds, so a cautious team waits for the first patch release. Deep dive: What’s new in Apache Spark 4.3, with the syntax, a real run and a visual for each feature below. Feature What it is Maturity Stateful real-time mode Running counts, de-duplication and transformWithState under the real-time trigger, over a pipelined shuffle Default for supported operators; needs a task slot per partition Auto CDC with SCD Type 2 Keep every version of a record, bounded by __START_AT and __END_AT, inside a pipeline Needs a connector JSON_TABLE The SQL-standard way to turn a JSON document into typed rows Default, flat form only UNNEST in FROM ANSI array expansion, in place of explode and LATERAL VIEW Default ASOF JOIN Match each row to the closest preceding row on the other side Behind a flag VARIANT editing functions Set, insert, delete and append inside a variant Default BIN BY Spread a measure over fixed time bins in proportion to the overlap Behind a flag TIME(p) and nanosecond timestamps Time of day and timestamps with up to nine fractional digits Behind flags; timestamps are a preview DataFrame.zip Append the columns of a second DataFrame row by row, with no join key Default Single-task execution Run a small query as one task, with no shuffles (Project Feather) Behind a flag Also in 4.3, listed in the release notes: Project Feather: opt-in shuffle-free single-task execution and Arrow-native caching for small data (the two flags are in the 4.3 settings table) Items that need a connector: @ time travel on table names (SPARK-57421, SPARK-58012) and dynamic table options for UPDATE, MERGE and DELETE Spark Connect REST endpoints (SPARK-57941), operation IDs for tracing, and a JDBC driver that returns ARRAY, MAP and STRUCT timestamp_nanos and unix_nanos, and VARIANT field-extraction pushdown for aggregate, sort and join queries Default whole-stage code generation for eligible UNIONs, opt-in null join key spreading for outer and anti joins, and pruning of unused fields inside arrays of structs Spark 4.2: new types, new joins, and a clearer SQL surface Everything in Spark 4.2. Spatial types, vector distance functions and a top-K join arrive in the engine, alongside SQL for filtering windows, resolving names and defining metrics once. Three of the headline items, change data capture, INSERT ... WITH SCHEMA EVOLUTION and Data Source V2 transactions, are defined by the engine but implemented by a connector, so built-in sources cannot show them. Deep dive: What’s new in Apache Spark 4.2, with the syntax, a real run and a visual for each feature below. Feature What it is Maturity GEOMETRY and GEOGRAPHY Spatial column types that carry an SRID, with five functions today Default NEAREST BY join Return the K best rows on the right for each row on the left; brute force today Default Vector functions Cosine similarity, L2 distance, inner product and norm over ARRAY<FLOAT> Default QUALIFY Filter on a window function without a subquery Default SET PATH An ordered schema search path for unqualified names Behind a flag Metric views Define dimensions and measures once in YAML and query them with MEASURE Default, built-in catalog time_bucket and IGNORE NULLS Fixed-width time buckets, and explicit null handling in collect_list Default The CHANGES clause Read what changed between two table versions; the catalog must implement it Needs a connector Cursors in SQL scripts DECLARE, OPEN, FETCH and CLOSE in a script Behind two internal flags Also in 4.2, listed in the release notes: Items that need a connector: the CHANGES clause and CDC APIs (SPARK-55668), INSERT ... WITH SCHEMA EVOLUTION and REPLACE ON/USING (SPARK-54971, SPARK-56001), and Data Source V2 transactions (SPARK-55855) Tuple sketches, and broader TIME support across file formats SYSTEM.BUILTIN and SYSTEM.SESSION qualification for built-in functions and temporary views Arrow-optimized Python UDFs on by default (SPARK-54555), so test your own UDFs before trusting it, and zero-copy hand-off of DataFrames to Polars or DuckDB through the Arrow C Data Interface Auto CDC with SCD Type 1 (SPARK-56249), and stateless PySpark queries in real-time mode Spark Connect: RDD API compatibility, YARN cluster mode, and DataFrame inputs to spark.read.* Faster MERGE INTO, operation summaries for UPDATE and DELETE, a web UI rebuilt on Bootstrap 5 with dark mode, heterogeneous Kubernetes executors, Spark History Server scalability, and JDK 25 support Spark 4.1: pipelines, procedural SQL, and real-time mode Everything in Spark 4.1. Pipelines become declarative, SQL gains scripts and recursion, and Structured Streaming gets a real-time trigger for stateless Scala queries on Kafka. Deep dive: What’s new in Apache Spark 4.1, with the syntax, a real run and a visual for each feature below. Feature What it is Maturity Spark Declarative Pipelines Declare datasets; Spark derives the run order from their references Default, via the spark-pipelines CLI Real-time mode, stateless Long-lived tasks instead of micro-batches, in Scala, with a Kafka source Default, stateless only SQL scripting BEGIN ... END blocks with variables, loops and error handlers GA, on by default Recursive CTEs A CTE that refers to itself, for hierarchies and graph walks Default VARIANT GA and colon paths Read a field with v:path::type GA, on by default Parameter markers anywhere :name markers in identifiers, limits and scripts Default Sketch functions Top-k, KLL quantile and Theta sketches that can be stored and merged Default Arrow-native UDFs and UDTFs @arrow_udf hands the function whole PyArrow arrays Default, needs pyarrow Also in 4.1, listed in the release notes: CONTINUE HANDLER and multi-variable DECLARE in SQL scripting, and shredding for faster VARIANT reads Spark ML on Connect generally available for Python, zstd compression for protobuf plans, chunked Arrow result streaming, and no 2 GB limit on local relations python_worker_logs() to query Python worker logs, and filter pushdown for Python data sources through pushFilters A JDBC driver for Spark Connect (SPARK-53484) Spark 4.0: the break, and a far more expressive SQL Everything in Spark 4.0. Scala 2.13 and Java 17 become the baseline, ANSI mode turns on by default, and SQL gains a type for JSON, functions, variables, collations and a top-to-bottom syntax. Deep dive: What’s new in Apache Spark 4.0, with the syntax, a real run and a visual for each feature below. Feature What it is Maturity ANSI mode by default Invalid casts and divide by zero raise errors instead of returning NULL Default VARIANT A binary type for semi-structured data such as JSON Default; GA in 4.1 SQL pipe syntax Read a query top to bottom with |> Default SQL user-defined functions Scalar and table functions written in SQL Default Session variables Typed variables with DECLARE and SET VAR Default String collation Case-insensitive, accent-aware and locale-aware comparison Default Built-in XML source Read, write and parse XML without an external package Default Python Data Source API and UDTFs Write a data source or table function in Python Default, needs pyarrow GROUP BY on maps and DESCRIBE ... AS JSON Group by a map column; get a table description as one JSON document Default transformWithState and the state data source Custom per-key streaming state, read back as a table Default; needs the RocksDB state store and protobuf Polymorphic Python UDTFs A table function whose schema follows its argument types Default Named and unnamed parameter markers :name and ? placeholders bound outside the SQL text Default Also in 4.0, listed in the release notes: transformWithState for custom stateful processing in Scala, Java and Python, the state data source reader, and state store improvements such as SST file reuse Polymorphic Python UDTFs whose output schema is decided at call time Named and unnamed parameter markers for parameterized queries Structured JSON logging, seen in every error the 4.0 runs logged A 1.5 MB lightweight Python client, spark.api.mode to switch Connect on, and community Spark Connect clients for Go, Swift and Rust Native Plotly-based plotting on PySpark DataFrames (SPARK-49530) Java 21 support, the Spark Kubernetes operator (SPARK-45923), Spark ML on Connect, and unified PySpark UDF profiling Run the examples yourself Every example is a runnable file in ranga-spark4-examples, organised by release. Each deep-dive post has a Run it yourself section for its release: the tarball and image, the Python floor, what the smoke test printed, and the PySpark, pipeline or Kafka runs that release needs. The download-and-verify script and the SQL runner for the plain Apache tarballs are in RUNNING_ON_TARBALLS.md. Line Release run Tarball Python for PySpark Run it yourself 4.0 4.0.5 523 MB 3.9 or newer 4.0 post 4.1 4.1.4 546 MB 3.10 or newer 4.1 post 4.2 4.2.1 529 MB 3.10 or newer 4.2 post 4.3 4.3.0 535 MB 3.11 or newer 4.3 post The Python column decides which examples run from a tarball. A machine with Python 3.9 runs the SQL and Scala examples on all four releases and the PySpark examples on 4.0 only. When these features bite Almost every failure in this line falls into five shapes: a stricter default, a feature that parses and then does nothing, a feature that is off until you switch it on, a Python environment that is not ready, and real-time mode with no free slots. Each deep-dive post lists the failures for its release, with the text each produced, the cause and the fix, so you can grep for it: 4.0, 4.1, 4.2 and 4.3. The same posts list the settings that gate each feature and what to budget for under Settings and costs. Release cadence, support and connectors Cadence. The versioning policy makes 4.3.0 the first quarterly feature release: feature releases come every three months and majors annually. Its maintenance windows are 6 months for a major or feature release and 18 months for a long-term-support (LTS) release. The 4.x LTS is planned as 4.5.0, and the policy keeps the existing 18-month commitment for 4.2.x. It lists a 4.4 branch cut on 16 November 2026 with a first release candidate by 7 December 2026, and a tentative 4.5 in February 2027, all subject to discussion on the dev list. Patch releases have run longer than the stated windows, for example 4.1.4 on 27 October 2026, ten months after 4.1.0, so read a window as a minimum. Connectors. A lakehouse stack upgrades with its connectors, so check them first. This is what Maven Central showed on 18 November 2026: Line Latest patch Iceberg iceberg-spark-runtime Hudi hudi-spark4.x-bundle Delta delta-spark_2.13 4.0 4.0.5 1.12.0 1.2.1 4.0.1, built against Spark 4.0.1 4.1 4.1.4 1.12.0 1.2.1 4.1.0, built against Spark 4.1.0 4.2 4.2.1 none published none published 4.4.1, built against Spark 4.2.0 4.3 4.3.0 none published none published none built against 4.3 So 4.1 is the newest line that all three table formats cover today. The release posts say more: 4.1, 4.2 and 4.3. Managed platforms. Microsoft’s Fabric documentation lists Runtime 2.0 as Spark 4.1 with Delta 4.2, so Fabric users get the 4.1 line, not 4.3. Check your platform’s runtime page before reading a feature as available to you. Which upgrades are worth it Upgrade by upgrade This part is my judgement, drawn from what ran, not a measurement. To 4.0. Not optional once you leave 3.x, because Scala 2.13 and Java 17 are the baseline. The work is dependency and ANSI-mode testing, and the language gains (pipe syntax, SQL functions, session variables, collations) come with it. 4.0 to 4.1. Worth it for SQL scripting, recursive CTEs and VARIANT colon paths if you have logic living in driver code. Declarative Pipelines is worth a trial on one pipeline, with dry-run, before you commit a team to it. 4.1 to 4.2. QUALIFY and metric views pay back quickly for analysts. The geospatial types are a foundation: five functions today, no distance or containment. 4.2 to 4.3. JSON_TABLE, UNNEST and the VARIANT editing functions help any pipeline that handles nested documents. Stateful real-time mode is for the few queries that need sub-second latency and a Kafka source. 4.3.0 shipped without preview builds, so a cautious team waits for the first patch release. Before you upgrade Test in this order: ANSI errors on your real data first, then the gating settings listed in each release’s post for anything a job relies on, then the Python environment. Pin the interpreter and the packages with the release. The Python floor moved from 3.9 to 3.11 across the four releases. Switch on one flag at a time, in the session that uses it rather than cluster-wide, so a failure points at the feature. Check the connector before the engine. For Auto CDC, CHANGES, schema evolution and transactions, the connector decides whether the feature exists for your table. Print spark.version at the top of every run. It is the cheapest check against running the wrong install. Read the migration guides. The official SQL and PySpark guides list far more default changes than any release post, each with the setting that restores the old behaviour. The line is moving faster than at any point in the 4.x series. Treat the tables here as a snapshot, re-check the maturity of each feature against the release note of the version you deploy, and keep the smoke files in the examples repo as a test you can rerun on the next release. References Introducing Apache Spark 4.0, 4.1, 4.2 and 4.3 from Databricks, used to find the features this post lists as not run Apache Spark 4 release overview from Decube ranga-spark4-examples with every runnable example in this post Spark 4.0.0 release notes, 4.1.0, 4.2.0 and 4.3.0 for the feature lists and ticket numbers used throughout Every Apache Spark release, and the problem each one was built to solve for removals, changed defaults and upgrade risks Spark Connect: the driver becomes a server for the client and server split behind the thin client and the pipelines CLI Structured Streaming internals for state and checkpoints behind real-time mode JOIN syntax, including NEAREST BY, QUALIFY and SET PATH in the 4.2.1 documentation JSON_TABLE, ASOF JOIN and UNNEST in the 4.3.0 documentation Spark Declarative Pipelines programming guide for the project spec, the CLI, and Auto CDC with its target requirements RealTimeModeAllowlist.scala for the sources, sinks and operators real-time mode accepts Apache Spark downloads and archive for the release tarballs and their checksums SQL migration guide and PySpark migration guide, the source of the behaviour-change tables in the release posts Apache Spark versioning policy, for the quarterly cadence and the maintenance windows Trademarks Apache Spark, Apache Kafka, Apache Iceberg, Apache Parquet, Apache Arrow and Apache are either registered trademarks or trademarks of The Apache Software Foundation in the United States and other countries.

entry.content:

  • 9. DataFrame.zip
    • Before Spark 4.3
    • With Spark 4.3: sample code
