If you need the joined rows themselves, isolate that customer: filter them out, join them separately — their side of the dimension table is one row, so it broadcasts — and union the result back (Fix 4). Salting works too, but it makes every other customer pay for the one. If this is a recurring pipeline, the durable answer is layout: bucket the fact table on customer_id so the shuffle stops happening at all (Fix 6). In production 29. How would you optimize a production pipeline suffering from severe data skew? Treat it as a measurement problem before a tuning one: Instrument. Log the max-to-median partition ratio for the keyed stages, so skew is a metric with a history rather than an incident. Fix the data if you can. Placeholder keys deleted upstream, or a layout change at the source, fix it for every job that reads that table rather than for yours. Take the free fixes: confirm AQE is on and that the partitions actually clear the 256 MB threshold; broadcast whatever fits. Then change the job, cheapest first — filter, pre-aggregate, isolate, salt. Assert correctness in the job. Any fix that replicates or splits can change the answer; a row-count check is one line. Alert on the ratio, not the duration. Duration drifts for many reasons; a ratio that climbs from 3x to 30x is skew arriving, usually before anyone notices the job is slow. 30. Describe a real-world scenario where you identified and resolved data skew. A useful answer has four parts, and the structure matters more than the anecdote: The symptom. “A nightly join sat at 199 of 200 tasks for 40 minutes; the cluster was idle.” The measurement. “Stage summary metrics showed a median shuffle read of 8 MB and a max of 4 GB. Counting by the join key, one merchant_id held 60% of the rows — it was the placeholder the upstream system wrote for card-present transactions.” The fix and why that one. “Those rows were not joinable, so they were filtered before the shuffle rather than salted. Max-to-median went to 3x and the stage to 4 minutes.” What stopped it recurring. “A check on the share of the top key, alerting when it exceeds a threshold, plus the filter pushed upstream.” The strongest version names a fix you rejected and why — the honest answer is usually that salting was considered and dropped because the hot key turned out to be garbage data, which is Fix 9. Shuffle internals Shuffle internals: which writer you get, what lands on disk, the reduce side and tuning. The answers link into the shuffle internals post, where each mechanism is measured. What a shuffle is, and what it costs 1. What is a shuffle in Spark, and why does one exist? A redistribution of rows across partitions so that all records needing to be processed together end up in the same place. It exists because operations like a join or a groupBy need every row with a given key on one machine, and the partitioning the data arrived with says nothing about that key. Structurally it is a disk barrier between two stages: map tasks write their output to local disk, the stage ends, and reduce tasks fetch what belongs to them. That barrier is why a shuffle is the expensive thing in most jobs. 2. Which operations cause a shuffle? Anything that has to repartition by key: groupByKey, reduceByKey, aggregateByKey, join, cogroup, distinct, sortBy, repartition, and window functions with a PARTITION BY. coalesce to a smaller count does not shuffle, which is exactly why it can leave you with uneven partitions. map, filter and mapPartitions are narrow and never shuffle. See which operations shuffle. 3. Where does the cost of a shuffle actually go? Four places, and they are not equal: serializing records, writing them to local disk, transferring them over the network, and on the reduce side deserializing and often sorting or spilling them again. The one people underweight is disk. Every shuffled record is written to local disk by the map side even when the consumer is on the same host — the write is not optional, because the reduce side may fetch it much later or after a retry. 4. What is the difference between a narrow and a wide dependency? A narrow dependency means each parent partition feeds at most one child partition, so the work can be pipelined inside one stage with no data movement. A wide dependency means a child partition draws from many parents, which requires a shuffle. Stage boundaries in Spark are exactly the wide dependencies. Counting Exchange nodes in a plan is counting wide dependencies. 5. Why did sort-based shuffle replace hash-based shuffle? File count. Hash shuffle wrote one file per map-and-reduce pair: M x R files, so 1000 map tasks into 1000 partitions produced a million files and a million open file handles’ worth of pressure. Sort-based shuffle writes one data file per map task with the records ordered by partition id, plus a small index of offsets — M files rather than M x R. Collapsing that count is what let the shuffle scale. See why hash shuffle lost. Which writer you get 6. What are the three shuffle writers? BypassMergeSortShuffleWriter, UnsafeShuffleWriter and SortShuffleWriter. SortShuffleManager.registerShuffle picks one per shuffle, once, and the choice is fixed for that shuffle’s life. They correspond to three handle classes — BypassMergeSortShuffleHandle, SerializedShuffleHandle and BaseShuffleHandle — which is what you look at if you want to know which one you got. See what decides which writer you get. 7. How does Spark decide between them? One if/else if/else on three properties of the dependency: Bypass if there is no map-side combine and the partition count is at most spark.shuffle.sort.bypassMergeThreshold (200). Otherwise serialized (UnsafeShuffleWriter) if the serializer supports relocation, there is no map-side combine, and there are at most 16777216 partitions. Otherwise SortShuffleWriter, the general path. Note what is absent: the data size. The decision is structural — aggregation, partition count, serializer — not based on how much data there turns out to be. 8. How can you tell which writer a shuffle actually used? Nothing in the Spark UI names it, but the handle is reachable from the dependency: val dep = rdd.dependencies.head.asInstanceOf[ShuffleDependency[_, _, _]] println(dep.shuffleHandle.getClass.getSimpleName) Run against four shuffles that differ only in the three deciding properties, that prints each branch of the tree in turn: Shuffle Handle 200 partitions, no combine, (Int, Int) records BypassMergeSortShuffleHandle 201 partitions, no combine, (Int, Int) records SerializedShuffleHandle 201 partitions, no combine, (Int, (Int, Int)) records BaseShuffleHandle 201 partitions, reduceByKey, (Int, Int) records BaseShuffleHandle Every row is one predicate changing. That is the decision tree, observed rather than described. 9. What exactly is the bypass threshold, and is the comparison inclusive? spark.shuffle.sort.bypassMergeThreshold, default 200, and the comparison is <=. So a shuffle with 200 partitions takes the bypass path and the same shuffle with 201 does not — the boundary is exact, not approximate, and the table above shows it flipping. This matters more than it looks, because spark.sql.shuffle.partitions also defaults to 200. A SQL shuffle at the default sits exactly on the boundary. 10. Why does the bypass writer have a threshold at all? Because it opens one file and one buffer per partition, per map task, and skips sorting entirely by writing each record straight to its partition’s file, concatenating them at the end. That is cheap for few partitions and expensive for many. At 2000 partitions each map task would want 2000 open files and, at the 32k default for spark.shuffle.file.buffer, around 62 MiB of buffers. The default of 200 is roughly where that trade stops paying. See what should you configure. 11. What does "serializer relocation" mean, and which serializers support it? The serialized path sorts records without deserializing them — it moves already-serialized bytes around inside a buffer and expects them to still be readable afterwards. A serializer that writes stream-level state, such as a back-reference table, breaks under that. Asked directly of the JVM: Serializer supportsRelocationOfSerializedObjects JavaSerializer false KryoSerializer true So Java serialization disqualifies UnsafeShuffleWriter outright. The 16777216 partition ceiling on the same path comes from PackedRecordPointer, which packs a partition id and a memory address into one 64-bit long, leaving the partition id 24 bits — and 2^24 is exactly 16777216. 12. If the default serializer is Java, how does any RDD shuffle reach the fast path? Because spark.serializer is not the whole answer. ShuffledRDD asks SerializerManager for a serializer, and it auto-selects Kryo when both the key and the value class tags are primitives, primitive arrays or String — regardless of what spark.serializer says. So (Int, Int) records get Kryo automatically and can reach UnsafeShuffleWriter, while spark.serializer remains unset at its JavaSerializer default. Setting spark.serializer to Kryo changes the fallback for types the auto-pick rejects; it does not override the auto-pick and it does not help when there is map-side aggregation. 13. Can changing a value type change which writer runs? Yes, and it is the most surprising consequence of the above. Changing a value from Int to (Int, Int) makes the value class tag a tuple rather than a primitive, the auto-pick declines Kryo, the serializer falls back to Java, Java cannot relocate — and the same job moves from SerializedShuffleHandle to BaseShuffleHandle. That is rows two and three of the table in question 8, and the only thing that changed is a type. SortShuffleWriter then pays to deserialize and re-serialize records when merging spills, which the serialized path avoids entirely. What lands on disk 14. What files does a map task write? Three, whichever writer ran: a .data file holding every partition’s bytes concatenated, a .index file of partition offsets, and a .checksum file. shuffle_0_0_0.data # the records shuffle_0_0_0.index # numPartitions + 1 offsets, as 8-byte longs shuffle_0_0_0.checksum.ADLER32 # one checksum per partition The sizes are arithmetic rather than mystery: for 4 partitions the index is (4 + 1) x 8 = 40 bytes and the checksum file 4 x 8 = 32 bytes. See what lands on disk. 15. Why is the last component of shuffle_0_0_0 always zero? It is IndexShuffleBlockResolver.NOOP_REDUCE_ID, a placeholder kept so the block id keeps its three-part shape. Its constancy is the entire point of sort-based shuffle: there is no per-reducer file, so there is no reducer id to put there. Under hash shuffle that component was meaningful, and that is precisely why there were M x R files. 16. How does a reduce task find its bytes without reading the whole file? The index file holds one 8-byte offset per partition plus a final end-of-file offset. A reduce task reads the two offsets bracketing its partition and then reads exactly that byte range from the data file. So locating a partition is two small reads of the index rather than a scan, which is what makes one-file-per-map-task workable. 17. How is a shuffle write committed, and why does that make speculation safe? The map task writes data and index to temporary files, then calls IndexShuffleBlockResolver.writeMetadataFileAndCommit, which renames them into place under a lock. That rename is the commit. Which is why speculative execution is safe here: two attempts at the same map task can both write their temporaries, whichever commits first wins, and the loser’s files are discarded. There is never a half-written file visible to a reader. 18. Does sort-based shuffle sort your data? It sorts records by partition id, so each partition’s bytes are contiguous in the data file. It does not order records by key within a partition unless a key ordering was explicitly requested. People assume a sortBy came free with the shuffle. It did not. The reduce side 19. What does the reduce side actually do? Asks the driver’s MapOutputTracker where the blocks for its partition live, fetches those byte ranges from each map output — locally where it can, over the network where it cannot — decompresses and deserializes them, and then aggregates or sorts if the operation needs it. spark.reducer.maxSizeInFlight, 48m by default, bounds how much fetched data one reduce task holds at a time. See what the reduce side does. 20. What is a FetchFailedException, and why is it expensive? A reduce task could not retrieve a block it needs. It is expensive because the recovery is not a task retry — the map output is gone, so Spark must re-run the map stage to regenerate it, and everything downstream waits. spark.shuffle.io.maxRetries (3) and spark.shuffle.io.retryWait govern how hard a fetch tries before giving up. On a busy or flaky cluster raising them converts expensive stage recomputation into cheap waiting. See what happens when a fetch fails. 21. Who serves shuffle files when the executor that wrote them is gone? The external shuffle service, if it is enabled. It runs per node rather than per executor, so shuffle output survives the executor exiting — which is what makes dynamic allocation viable, since Spark can only release an idle executor if something else can still serve its files. Without it, losing an executor means losing its map output and re-running the stage that produced it. See who serves the files. 22. What does push-based shuffle change? Map tasks additionally push their blocks to remote shuffle services, which merge the fragments belonging to each reduce partition. The reduce side then reads a few large sequential merged blocks rather than thousands of small random ones. The problem it targets is the many-small-reads pattern that hurts most at large scale, not correctness. See why hash shuffle lost. 23. What does adaptive execution change about a shuffle? It cannot un-write a shuffle that already happened, but at the boundary it can coalesce many small post-shuffle partitions into fewer reasonable ones, split skewed partitions, and switch a sort-merge join to a broadcast now that it knows the real size. The evidence is AQEShuffleRead in the final plan. See what AQE changes. Spill, memory and tuning 24. What is spilling, and when does it happen? Writing the in-memory collection to disk because the sorter’s share of execution memory is exhausted. ExternalSorter and ExternalAppendOnlyMap spill sorted runs and merge them later. It is a symptom of the partition being too large for the memory available to that task, which is why raising the partition count is usually a better first move than raising spark.memory.fraction. See what does spilling actually cost. 25. Why are memoryBytesSpilled and diskBytesSpilled so different? They measure different things. memoryBytesSpilled is the in-memory object size of what was spilled; diskBytesSpilled is the serialized, compressed bytes that actually reached disk. On the measured run the disk figure was about a tenth of the memory one. So a large memoryBytesSpilled is not “we wrote that much” — it is “objects of that size left memory”. Compare the two rather than reading either alone. 26. Which shuffle metrics are worth reading? Shuffle write and read bytes for volume; shuffle read records against bytes to spot pathological record sizes; spill (both kinds) for memory pressure; and the max-to-median gap across tasks for skew. The ratio that most often explains a slow stage is not a shuffle metric at all — it is the largest task’s shuffle read against the median. See which numbers tell you something. 27. What is actually worth configuring? Mostly one number, and it is not a shuffle setting: the partition count. It decides which writer runs, how many files exist, how large each reduce partition is, and whether tasks spill. For SQL that is spark.sql.shuffle.partitions, and better still whatever AQE coalesces it to. After that, in rough order of usefulness: bypassMergeThreshold if you understand the file-count trade, spark.shuffle.file.buffer (32k) on large shuffles, spark.reducer.maxSizeInFlight (48m) when fetch-bound, and spark.shuffle.io.maxRetries on a flaky cluster. Leave compression and checksums alone unless measuring — spark.io.compression.codec defaults to lz4. 28. How do you avoid a shuffle entirely? Broadcast the small side of a join — no exchange at all. Bucket both tables on the join key, so the data arrives pre-partitioned and the exchange disappears permanently. Combine before the shuffle: reduceByKey over groupByKey, or a DataFrame aggregation that gets a map-side partial automatically. Filter and project first, so less is shuffled even when a shuffle remains. coalesce instead of repartition when only reducing partitions, since it merges without shuffling. See how to avoid the shuffle. 29. When is the shuffle not the problem? When the stage is slow but shuffle read and write are small, spill is zero, and task durations are even. Then you are looking at a scan, a UDF, a skewed input rather than a skewed shuffle, or simply too little parallelism. The check is cheap: compare shuffle bytes against input bytes. If the shuffle is a small fraction of what the job read, tuning it cannot help much. See when the shuffle is not your problem. 30. A stage is slow and you suspect the shuffle. What do you check, in order? Is it skew? Max-versus-median shuffle read across tasks. One oversized partition defeats everything else, and the fix is different — see the data skew post. Is it volume? Shuffle bytes against input bytes. If they are comparable, the work is to shuffle less, not to tune the shuffle. Is it spill? Both spill metrics non-zero means partitions too large for the memory available; raise the partition count first. Is it fetch failures? FetchFailedException in the logs means stage re-runs, and the answer is retries or the external shuffle service, not partition tuning. Only then the writer. If the shuffle is large, has no aggregation, and your record types are forcing BaseShuffleHandle, making the types Kryo-friendly moves it onto the serialized path — check with the one-liner in question 8. Performance optimization Performance optimization: proving a change worked, reading less, shuffling less and everything else. The answers link into the performance optimization post, where each mechanism is measured. Proving a change worked 1. How do you know a Spark optimization actually fired? Read the plan, not the clock. df.explain("formatted") names the optimization directly — PartitionFilters, PushedFilters, ReadSchema, BroadcastHashJoin, AQEShuffleRead — and those attributes do not move when the cluster is busy. This matters because most Spark optimizations are conditional: pushdown needs the filter to be expressible in the format, a broadcast needs the build side to be small enough at planning time, partition pruning needs the filter to name the partition column. Each silently does nothing when its condition is not met, and a slow job looks identical either way. See how do you read the proof? 2. Why is a before-and-after timing comparison unreliable? Because on a shared cluster the difference you measured is usually smaller than the variance between two runs of the unchanged job. The input was cached differently, the executors landed on different hosts, another job was competing for the same disks. A plan attribute is binary and reproducible: the filter either appears under PushedFilters or it does not. That is why every technique in this post is justified by a plan line or a counted number rather than a duration. 3. What is the difference between explain(), explain("extended") and explain("formatted")? explain() prints the physical plan only. explain("extended") prints all four trees — parsed, analyzed, optimized logical, and physical — which is what you want when you are asking why the optimizer did something. explain("formatted") prints a compact tree plus a numbered details section listing each node’s attributes, which is where PushedFilters and ReadSchema actually appear. For tuning, "formatted" is the one to reach for, because the attributes are the evidence. 4. What is isFinalPlan, and why can inspecting a plan mislead you? With adaptive execution on, the plan printed before execution is a proposal. Spark re-plans at shuffle boundaries using measured statistics, so what ran may differ from what you printed. isFinalPlan=true marks the plan that actually executed. The trap is subtle: calling count() to force execution before inspecting builds a different query — one whose plan is not the plan you were asking about — and reports isFinalPlan=false. Run the real action, then read the plan. 5. Which plan attributes are worth knowing by name? Attribute Means PartitionFilters partition pruning applied — whole directories never opened PushedFilters predicate pushed into the scan ReadSchema the columns actually decoded; the proof of column pruning BroadcastHashJoin / BroadcastExchange the small side was broadcast Exchange a shuffle; count them, and try to remove them AQEShuffleRead adaptive execution coalesced or split partitions at runtime BatchEvalPython a Python UDF, and a codegen boundary *(n) a whole-stage codegen stage; fewer distinct n is better A change that alters none of these did not do anything, however much the wall clock moved. Reading less 6. What is partition pruning, and what turns it off? Skipping whole directories because the filter names the partition column, so those files are never opened. It is the cheapest optimization available, because the data is not read at all. It turns off when the filter does not reference the partition column directly — wrapping it in a function, comparing it against a differently-typed literal, or filtering on a derived column instead. The evidence is PartitionFilters in the plan; if that list is empty, pruning did not happen. See prune partitions. 7. What is predicate pushdown, and does it only work on Parquet? Pushing the filter down into the scan so rows are eliminated as early as possible. And no — PushedFilters appears for CSV and JSON too. What differs is what the format can do with the pushed filter. Parquet holds min/max statistics per row group, so it can skip entire blocks without decoding them. A row format still parses every record and simply discards non-matching rows sooner. Same plan attribute, very different saving. See pushdown and pruning. 8. What does select * actually cost? Column pruning. On the same query against the same data, an explicit projection gave a ReadSchema of 2 columns and select * gave 5. On a columnar format that is a direct multiple on bytes decoded. It also makes every downstream optimization work harder and makes the job fragile to upstream schema changes. ReadSchema in the plan is the proof. 9. How much does file format choice matter? More than most settings. Converting the measured dataset from JSON to Parquet was 7.5x on read — and unlike a tuning flag, it applies to every job that reads that table afterwards. Parquet gives columnar decoding, per-row-group statistics for skipping, and better compression on typed columns. See file format and compression. 10. Does compression codec choice matter, and what is splittability? A file is splittable if Spark can start reading it from the middle, which is what lets one file be processed by many tasks. A gzipped CSV is not splittable, so a 10 GB file becomes exactly one task no matter how large the cluster. Inside Parquet this is less of a concern, because compression is per column chunk and the file remains splittable at row-group boundaries. Snappy is the usual default — cheaper CPU, larger files; zstd trades the other way. Shuffling less 11. Why is a shuffle the thing to attack? Because it is the only operation that writes every row to disk and sends it over the network, and it forces a stage boundary. Everything inside a stage is pipelined in memory; everything between stages is materialised. The plan shows them as Exchange nodes. Counting Exchange before and after a change is one of the most useful tuning habits there is: removing a join’s broadcast turned one BroadcastExchange into a SortMergeJoin with two Exchange nodes. 12. When does Spark choose a broadcast join? When one side’s estimated size at planning time is under spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold, 10 MB by default. The small side is sent whole to every executor and the join happens locally, removing the shuffle entirely. Two things commonly stop it: the estimate being wrong because statistics are missing or stale, and the build side genuinely being too large. With adaptive execution on, Spark can also switch to a broadcast at runtime once it has measured the real size — which is one of the better arguments for leaving AQE alone. See broadcast joins. 13. What is the difference between a broadcast join and a broadcast variable? A broadcast join is a join strategy the optimizer picks; you influence it with a threshold or a hint, and the evidence is BroadcastHashJoin in the plan. A broadcast variable is an API for shipping a read-only value to every executor once instead of once per task — a lookup map used inside a UDF, say. It does not make joins faster and it does not appear in the plan. They share a word and nothing else. See broadcast variables. 14. reduceByKey or groupByKey, and why does it matter? reduceByKey combines on the map side before the shuffle; groupByKey ships every row and combines after. Same answer, 11x the shuffle bytes measured. The DataFrame API makes this mostly moot — groupBy().agg() gets a partial aggregate automatically for algebraic aggregations — which is itself an argument for the DataFrame API over RDD lambdas. See combine early. 15. repartition or coalesce? repartition(n) shuffles and can increase or decrease the count, producing even partitions. coalesce(n) only decreases, and avoids a shuffle by merging existing partitions — which is why it can leave you with uneven ones. The trap is coalesce(1) before a write: because it avoids the shuffle, it pushes single-threaded execution back up into the stage that produces the data. repartition(1) shuffles into one partition and leaves the upstream stage parallel. They are not interchangeable. See repartition versus coalesce. 16. What do partitioning and bucketing do, and when is bucketing worth it? Partitioning splits data into directories by column value, which enables partition pruning at read time. Bucketing pre-hashes rows into a fixed number of files by a key, so a join on that key needs no shuffle at all — the exchange disappears permanently rather than being tuned. Bucketing costs a write-time shuffle and locks in the bucket count, so it pays off for a table joined the same way repeatedly, not for ad-hoc analysis. See partitioning and bucketing. Adaptive query execution 17. What does AQE actually change, and what does it leave alone? It re-plans at shuffle boundaries using statistics it has just measured, rather than estimated beforehand. Three things: it coalesces small post-shuffle partitions, it switches a join to a broadcast when the measured size allows, and it splits skewed partitions. What it does not do is change the logical plan — it will not push a filter you did not write or reorder your joins. It is on by default (spark.sql.adaptive.enabled is true). See let adaptive execution finish. 18. If AQE coalesces partitions, does spark.sql.shuffle.partitions still matter? It becomes an upper bound rather than a target. AQE cannot create more partitions than the shuffle produced, so the setting still decides the ceiling; it merges downward toward spark.sql.adaptive.advisoryPartitionSizeInBytes, 64 MB by default. So the modern advice inverts: set shuffle.partitions generously and let AQE coalesce, rather than trying to guess the right number in advance. The evidence is AQEShuffleRead coalesced in the final plan. 19. Why does AQE sometimes appear to do nothing about skew? Because its skew rule requires two conditions, and the absolute one is easy to miss. A partition must be larger than spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.skewedPartitionFactor (5.0) times the median and larger than spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.skewedPartitionThresholdInBytes (256 MB). A partition can be a hundred times the median and be left alone because it is under 256 MB — which is exactly the situation on laptop-scale test data, where people conclude the feature is broken. The data skew post covers this in detail. 20. Should you ever turn AQE off? Rarely, and mostly for diagnosis — turning it off makes the pre-execution plan the plan that runs, which is convenient when you are trying to reason about the optimizer in isolation. In production the argument for leaving it on is that it has information you do not: the real size of a shuffle it has already written. Guessing partition counts in advance is strictly worse than measuring them after the fact. Boundaries and APIs 21. What does a Python UDF really cost? More than “a bit slower”. It inserts BatchEvalPython into the plan and splits whole-stage code generation around itself, because the generated JVM code cannot contain Python. Measured on the same trivial query, the built-in version planned as one codegen stage and the UDF version as three — identical on Spark 3.5.9 and 4.1.3. On top of that, every row crosses a serialization boundary into a Python worker and back. So the cost is structural, not proportional: it does not shrink because your function is simple. See keep the work inside the JVM. 22. When is a UDF justified, and what should you try first? Check pyspark.sql.functions first — the built-in library is much larger than most people assume, and anything there stays inside the JVM and inside codegen. If you genuinely need Python, prefer a pandas UDF (functionType of SCALAR, GROUPED_MAP, and so on): it moves data in Arrow batches rather than row by row, which removes most of the serialization cost though not the codegen split. A plain row-at-a-time UDF should be the last resort. 23. RDD, DataFrame or Dataset? DataFrame by default. It is the only one the Catalyst optimizer can see into: an RDD map with a lambda is an opaque function, so no predicate pushdown, no column pruning, no join reordering, no codegen. Dataset gives compile-time type safety in Scala at the cost of some deserialization; typed lambdas on a Dataset are similarly opaque to the optimizer. RDDs remain right for genuinely unstructured work and fine control over partitioning. See which API. 24. What is whole-stage code generation? Spark compiling a chain of operators into a single generated Java method, so rows move through filter, project and join in tight loops rather than via a virtual call per operator per row. You can read it in the plan: stages are marked *(1), *(2) and so on. Fewer distinct stage numbers means longer fused pipelines. Anything the generator cannot express — a Python UDF being the common case — forces a boundary and a new stage. Memory, caching and serialization 25. When does caching make a job slower? When the DataFrame is read once. Caching costs the time to materialise it plus the memory it then occupies, and that memory comes out of the same pool execution wants. A read-once DataFrame is slower cached than not. Cache when something is genuinely reused across multiple actions, and unpersist when done. See caching. 26. Which storage level should you cache in? MEMORY_AND_DISK is the DataFrame default and usually right. The choice that actually moves the needle is serialized versus deserialized: the deserialized form held 3x the memory of the serialized one on the measured data. Deserialized is faster to read and much larger. Serialized costs CPU on every access and fits far more in the same pool. On a memory-pressured job that trade is usually worth taking. 27. What is the default serializer, and should you change it? spark.serializer is unset by default, which means JavaSerializer — on both Spark 3.5.9 and 4.1.3. This is worth checking rather than assuming, because so many cluster images and templates set Kryo in spark-defaults.conf that people report Kryo as “the default”. Kryo is faster and more compact and is worth enabling for RDD-heavy or cache-heavy jobs. It matters less than people expect for DataFrame work, which mostly uses Spark’s own Tungsten encoders rather than spark.serializer at all. See serialization. 28. How is executor memory divided, and what causes OOM? Broadly: a reserved slice, then a unified region split between execution (shuffle, sort, join buffers) and storage (cache), which borrow from each other, and outside the JVM heap the overhead region for off-heap and Python workers. OOM usually comes from one of a few places rather than “not enough memory overall”: a skewed task asked to hold far more than its share, a broadcast build side larger than estimated, an unbounded aggregation like collect_list on a hot key, or collect() pulling a large result into the driver. See memory and GC. Cluster, stragglers and method 29. Why doesn't speculative execution fix a straggler caused by skew? Because speculation re-runs the same partition on another node. It is designed for stragglers caused by a slow or failing node — bad disk, noisy neighbour — where a fresh attempt elsewhere finishes sooner. A skewed task is slow because of the data it was given, so the duplicate gets the same oversized partition and is equally slow. You have spent twice the resources for the same duration. Diagnose which kind you have before enabling it — see resources, locality and speculation. 30. You are handed a slow Spark job. What do you do, in order? Work down the list, because each step reduces what the later ones have to be clever about: Measure skew first. It is the exception that jumps the queue — one oversized partition defeats everything below. Read less. Partition pruning, column pruning, columnar format. Usually a one-line change; JSON to Parquet was 7.5x on its own. Shuffle less. Broadcast what fits, combine before the shuffle, bucket if the join repeats. Nothing you tune inside a shuffle beats not having it. Let AQE size the shuffles you keep. Use the API the optimizer can see — DataFrame over RDD lambdas. Remove boundary crossings — built-ins over Python UDFs. Then representation — storage level, serializer, what you cache. Only then cluster settings — executor sizing, locality, speculation. And at each step, confirm from the plan that the change did what you think. See in what order? References Handling data skew in Spark for the measured fixes behind the skew questions Spark shuffle internals for the writers, the files and the reduce side Spark performance optimization for the tuning questions Top Apache Spark interview questions for the broader question bank Trademarks Apache Spark, Apache Parquet and Apache are either registered trademarks or trademarks of The Apache Software Foundation in the United States and other countries.

entry.title: Six URL rewrites that turn any GitHub repository into an editor, a prompt, a diagram or an MCP server

link.title: Six URL rewrites that turn any GitHub repository into an editor, a prompt, a diagram or an MCP server

entry.content:
• Why read a repository without cloning it
    • The test repository
  • What the URL rewrite actually does
    • Three jobs, three places the work happens
    • The trade-off all six share
  • Hands-on demo: each tool, step by step, on a real repository
    • Tool 1: github1s, a read-only VS Code in the tab
    • Tool 2: GitIngest, the whole repository as one prompt
    • Tool 3: GitDiagram, an architecture diagram from the file tree
    • Tool 4: GitMCP, the repository as a tool your assistant can call
    • Tool 5: GitHubBox, a running dev environment, for the right repo
    • Tool 6: DeepWiki, a generated wiki, if someone has indexed it
  • Real-world scenarios and production failures
    • Failure 1: the prompt is bigger than the model can use
    • Failure 2: the diagram says something the repository does not
    • Failure 3: the same URLs refuse a script
    • Failure 4: a stale snapshot treated as current
    • Failure 5: what you paste and what you sign up for
    • Failure 6: wrong tool for the repository
  • Optimisation, tuning knobs and best practices
    • Pick the tool by the question, not by the novelty
    • A pipeline that uses three of them
    • Scope before you paste
    • Check what you are about to send
    • Prompt template for a dump
    • Cost and trade-offs against a local clone
  • Key takeaways
  • References
  • Trademarks

TL;DR

  • Six sites work by rewriting the host or the path of a GitHub URL. No install, no clone, and for public repositories no sign-in.
  • They split into three jobs: read a repo (github1s), feed a repo to an LLM (GitIngest, GitMCP), and understand a repo (GitDiagram, DeepWiki). GitHubBox is the odd one out: it runs a repo, and only helps if the repo is a JavaScript project.
  • Every screenshot in this post comes from one real repository, rangareddy/ranga_spark_experiments: 280 text files, Scala and Java, Maven build. That choice exposes the limits as well as the wins.
  • Two of the tools did not work for this repo, and the post says so and shows why.

Why read a repository without cloning it

A pull request link, a Stack Overflow answer or a colleague’s message lands you in a repository you have never seen. The default move is git clone, then an IDE import, then a Maven or sbt dependency download, all to answer a question like “where does this job write its output?”. For a repository you will not touch again, that is minutes of setup for a thirty-second question.

A family of small sites removes the setup by taking the GitHub URL itself as input. You change github.com to another host, or put another host in front of the path, and the page you land on has done the work: an editor with search, a single text file ready to paste into a chat, a diagram, or a server your AI assistant can query.

This post runs each of them, in order, on the same repository so the outputs are comparable. It is a tutorial first: each tool has numbered steps and a screenshot taken during the run. It also records where each tool stops, because “works on any repo” is only true of some of them.

The test repository

All runs use rangareddy/ranga_spark_experiments. It is a good subject because it is awkward in the ways real repositories are:

Property Value Why it matters
Files 280 text files analysed by GitIngest Large enough that a naive dump is cropped
Layout 34 top-level folders, 32 of them Maven modules (each has a pom.xml), one per Spark integration A diagram has to summarise, not list
Languages Scala 153,704 bytes, Java 41,228, Shell 23,514, Python 5,074 (GitHub languages API) Not JavaScript, which matters for GitHubBox
History 102 commits, one branch, last commit eaf9e23 Small enough to read, old enough to be unmaintained

What the URL rewrite actually does

None of these sites is magic. Each one is a web application that receives owner/repo in the URL, fetches the repository from GitHub on the server side (or, for github1s, in your browser), and renders a different view of it. The rewrite is the cheapest possible interface: you already have the GitHub URL, so the only thing you type is the part that changes.

  https://github.com/rangareddy/ranga_spark_experiments
        |
        |  swap the host, keep owner/repo
        v
  github1s.com   /rangareddy/ranga_spark_experiments   -> VS Code in the browser
  gitingest.com  /rangareddy/ranga_spark_experiments   -> one text file for an LLM
  gitdiagram.com /rangareddy/ranga_spark_experiments   -> architecture diagram
  gitmcp.io      /rangareddy/ranga_spark_experiments   -> MCP server URL
  githubbox.com  /rangareddy/ranga_spark_experiments   -> redirects to CodeSandbox
  deepwiki.com   /rangareddy/ranga_spark_experiments   -> generated wiki, if indexed

All six take the same two path segments. Only the host differs, so the habit to build is: open the repository on GitHub, then retype the host.

Three jobs, three places the work happens

The tools differ less in what they show than in where the computation runs and what they cost you.

Tool Job Where the work runs What you get Needs sign-in
github1s Read and search Your browser, which loads a VS Code web build A read-only VS Code workbench No
GitIngest Feed an LLM Server One text file: summary, tree, file contents No
GitMCP Feed an LLM, live Server, over MCP A URL your assistant calls as tools No
GitDiagram Understand Server, using an LLM A Mermaid diagram of the architecture No
DeepWiki Understand Server, using an LLM A wiki, after an indexing job Email to index
GitHubBox Run CodeSandbox A cloud dev environment Not to open

“Needs sign-in” is for a public repository, as observed in this run. Private repositories need tokens or accounts on most of these, and none was tried here.

The trade-off all six share

Each tool trades privacy and completeness for speed. The server-side ones receive the repository name, and GitHubBox, GitIngest and GitDiagram each run on someone else’s infrastructure, so none of them belongs anywhere near a private repository you have not cleared. The model-backed ones (GitDiagram, DeepWiki) also summarise: they read a slice of the repository, which the sections below quantify (GitDiagram reported reading 40 source files out of 280).

The alternative is the tool you already have: git clone --depth 1, then tree, rg and your IDE. It is complete, private and offline, and it costs the clone plus the import. The six tools win on the first minute and lose on everything after it.

Hands-on demo: each tool, step by step, on a real repository

Every step below was run on 12 November 2026 in Chrome against the repository above, signed in to nothing but GitHub. The screenshots are from those runs, unedited apart from file size. Each tool section ends with what it did not do, because that is the part the landing pages leave out.

Tool 1: github1s, a read-only VS Code in the tab

What it is for. Browsing and searching code with a real editor’s tree, tabs and search panel, without cloning. It is the right first move when you want to read, not run.

Steps

  1. Open the repository on GitHub: https://github.com/rangareddy/ranga_spark_experiments.
  2. Edit the host in the address bar: replace github.com with github1s.com. The full URL is https://github1s.com/rangareddy/ranga_spark_experiments.
  3. Wait for the workbench to load. It opens the README as a preview tab and the whole folder tree in the Explorer. The status bar shows master, the branch the URL resolved to.

  1. To land on a file directly, keep the whole GitHub path and change only the host. This opens the Delta Lake example:
https://github1s.com/rangareddy/ranga_spark_experiments/blob/master/spark-delta-lake-integration/src/main/scala/com/ranga/spark/delta/lake/SparkDeltaLakeIntegrationApp.scala

  1. Search across the repository. Click the magnifier in the activity bar, or press Cmd+Shift+F on macOS (Ctrl+Shift+F elsewhere), and type format("delta"). The panel reported 2 results in 1 file, and both matches are highlighted in the open editor.

Where it stops

  • No syntax highlighting for Scala. The status bar showed Plain Text for the .scala file. Navigation and search work; colour does not.
  • Read-only. The Search view has a Replace box, but this is a viewer for a public repository. There is nothing to run, build or debug.
  • A “Leave site?” prompt. After I used Search, Chrome asked for confirmation before navigating away from the page. It is a browser prompt from the editor page, not data loss, because nothing can be saved.

Tool 2: GitIngest, the whole repository as one prompt

What it is for. Pasting a repository into an LLM chat. It produces a summary, a directory tree and the file contents as a single text document.

Steps

  1. Open https://gitingest.com/rangareddy/ranga_spark_experiments. The path is the same owner/repo, so the page starts processing immediately.
  2. Wait for the spinner. This run took under half a minute for 280 files.
  3. Read the Summary panel. For this repository it reported:
Repository: rangareddy/ranga_spark_experiments
Commit: eaf9e23df97e7f3dbe720223b027fb24352f3f5f
Files analyzed: 280

Estimated tokens: 173.5k

  1. Use the controls above the result before you ingest, not after. The form has an Exclude (or Include) pattern box such as *.md, src/, an Include files under slider that defaults to 50 kB, and a Private Repository checkbox. Typing *.xml, *.sh, *.md, *.properties into the Exclude box and clicking Ingest again took the result from 280 files and 173.5k estimated tokens to 151 files and 64.1k tokens, with the same commit.

  1. Click Copy all to put the document on the clipboard, or Download to save it as a file. Paste it into a chat with the question you actually have, for example “Which modules write to Kafka and which read from it?”

Where it stops

  • The on-page view is cropped. The panel begins with (Files content cropped to 300k characters, download full ingest to see more). The 173.5k-token estimate is for the whole repository, so only Download gives you everything.
  • 173.5k tokens does not fit everywhere. It is a large prompt even for long-context models. Exclude patterns are not optional for a repository this size.
  • A snapshot, not a live view. The summary pins commit eaf9e23. A later push is not in the document you copied.

Tool 3: GitDiagram, an architecture diagram from the file tree

What it is for. The first ninety seconds with an unfamiliar repository: what are the parts and how do they connect.

Steps

  1. Open https://gitdiagram.com/rangareddy/ranga_spark_experiments.
  2. Watch the progress panel. It shows Understanding the architecture with a timer and an Info line, 40 source files read. The diagram appeared after roughly half a minute.
  3. The first render fits the whole diagram into the page. For this repository it is too wide to read:

  1. Click Enable zoom. The diagram becomes pannable and zoomable (the first view opened at 467%), with -, + and FIT controls. Scroll and drag to read a cluster:

  1. The toolbar also has Export and Regenerate. For use in your own notes, add .md to the URL:
https://gitdiagram.com/rangareddy/ranga_spark_experiments.md

That returned 200 with text/markdown, about 15 KB, containing an Overview, the diagram as a Mermaid block, a Components list with links to source files, and Connections. It is built for pasting into an agent’s context instead of screenshotting the page.

Where it stops

  • It reads a sample. Forty files out of 280. Its own markdown says it is generated “from its file tree, README and a sample of source files” and that it “is an AI-made overview: check details against the source.”
  • It invents hubs. The top node, Example runner, fans out to every cluster. This repository is a set of independent examples, and the generated overview itself says each is “independently initiated”. The hub is the model’s way to draw a tree, not a program in the repo. Read diagrams like this as a table of contents, not a call graph.
  • Wide repositories shrink. Thirty-two sibling modules produce a diagram that only works zoomed. A repository with a deeper structure would read better than a flat monorepo of samples.

Tool 4: GitMCP, the repository as a tool your assistant can call

What it is for. Instead of pasting a snapshot, give an AI assistant a URL that it queries on demand, so it reads current files rather than a stale dump.

Steps

  1. Open https://gitmcp.io/rangareddy/ranga_spark_experiments. The page is a setup guide titled GitMCP Documentation Server, with the server URL:
https://gitmcp.io/rangareddy/ranga_spark_experiments
  1. Pick your client from the tabs: Cursor, Claude Desktop, Windsurf, VSCode, Cline, Highlight AI, Augment Code or Msty AI. For Cursor, add this to ~/.cursor/mcp.json:
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "ranga_spark_experiments Docs": {
      "url": "https://gitmcp.io/rangareddy/ranga_spark_experiments"
    }
  }
}

  1. For Claude Desktop the page gives a different shape, because that client starts a local process and bridges to the remote server with mcp-remote. Add this to claude_desktop_config.json:
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "ranga_spark_experiments Docs": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": [
        "mcp-remote",
        "https://gitmcp.io/rangareddy/ranga_spark_experiments"
      ]
    }
  }
}

  1. Restart the client and ask a question that needs the repository, such as “In ranga_spark_experiments, how does the graceful shutdown example stop a streaming job?”

Where it stops

  • Not run end to end in this post. The configuration above is exactly what the page shows. I did not connect an assistant to the server or list its tools, so what the assistant does with the URL is not claimed here.
  • Claude Desktop needs Node. npx mcp-remote means a local Node.js install, which cancels some of the “no install” appeal for that client.
  • Editing the config file is the install. A remote MCP URL means the assistant sends your questions, and what it fetches, to a third-party server.

Tool 5: GitHubBox, a running dev environment, for the right repo

What it is for. Opening a repository as an editable, runnable project in CodeSandbox, which suits JavaScript and Node projects.

Steps

  1. Open https://githubbox.com/rangareddy/ranga_spark_experiments.
  2. It redirects to https://codesandbox.io/p/sandbox/github/rangareddy/ranga_spark_experiments, shows “Fetching details…”, then opens the editor. It opened without a sign-in, with a Sign In button still available.

Where it stops, and this one stopped. The preview pane is blank. The template label reads nodebox, a Node runtime in the browser, and this repository is Scala and Java built with Maven: no package.json, nothing for a Node sandbox to start. It is a useful negative result. GitHubBox is for JavaScript repositories, and nothing in this post is evidence that it works for anything else. I did not test it on a Node repository.

Tool 6: DeepWiki, a generated wiki, if someone has indexed it

What it is for. An LLM-written wiki of a repository, with pages by topic.

Steps

  1. Open https://deepwiki.com/rangareddy/ranga_spark_experiments.
  2. For this repository the page showed Repository Not Indexed: “This repository hasn’t been indexed yet”, with the estimate “Indexing typically takes 2-10 minutes”.

  1. Indexing requires an email to notify (required) and a click on Index Repository. I stopped here. Submitting someone’s email address to a third-party service is not part of a read-only demonstration, so the wiki itself is not covered in this post.

Where it stops. It does not work on first visit for a repository nobody has indexed, and the index step has a cost in personal data. For well-known projects that are already indexed it is the lowest-effort tool of the six, but I have not shown that here.

Real-world scenarios and production failures

These tools are for reading, so “production failure” here means the moment a workflow built on one of them gives a wrong answer or quietly stops working. Each case below was observed in this run unless it says otherwise.

Failure 1: the prompt is bigger than the model can use

The GitIngest summary for the unfiltered repository says Estimated tokens: 173.5k. Pasting that into a chat either fails the length limit or, worse, fits and leaves little room for the answer. The page does not stop you. It crops its own preview to 300k characters and leaves the decision with you.

The fix is to cut before copying, not after. Excluding build files, shell scripts, Markdown and properties files removed 129 of 280 files and cut the estimate from 173.5k to 64.1k tokens at the same commit. Mind what you removed: that exclude list also drops the pom.xml files, so a question about dependencies now has no evidence to read.

Run Files Estimated tokens
Defaults (50 kB file limit) 280 173.5k
Exclude *.xml, *.sh, *.md, *.properties 151 64.1k

Failure 2: the diagram says something the repository does not

GitDiagram’s top node is Example runner, with a labelled runs edge to every cluster. Read at face value it says one entry point launches all the examples. The same tool’s text overview says the opposite: “Each example is independently initiated.” Both statements came out of one generation.

The root cause is structural. A diagram needs a root, a flat collection of 32 independent modules does not have one, and the model supplies a hub. The tool also states it read 40 files, so any behaviour that lives in the other 240 is a guess from names. Treat the diagram as an index of where to look, then confirm in the source (github1s is the quickest way to do that).

Failure 3: the same URLs refuse a script

All of these loaded in the browser. Requested from a shell with curl, the same hosts answered differently:

URL (path /rangareddy/ranga_spark_experiments) Browser curl status
githubbox.com Redirected to CodeSandbox and opened 403
deepwiki.com “Repository Not Indexed” page 429
uithub.com Not opened in the browser 401
gitmcp.io Setup page 200
gitingest.com Result page 200
gitdiagram.com Result page 200

The page-level 200 for GitIngest, GitDiagram and GitMCP only proves that a page was served. I did not trace how each one fetches its results, so a bare curl of the page is not shown here to be a way to automate them. If you want repeatable output in CI, use the repository’s own tooling: git clone --depth 1 and a local packer, not these sites. The one exception observed is GitDiagram’s .md endpoint, which returned the generated text over plain curl with a 200.

Failure 4: a stale snapshot treated as current

GitIngest pins the commit in its summary (eaf9e23...). Anything pushed after that is not in your document, and nothing in the pasted text tells the model so. If you are asking an assistant about a fast-moving repository, put the commit hash into the prompt and refresh the dump before a long session. This repository last changed in December 2023, so staleness did not bite here, and I did not test a repository that changes daily.

Failure 5: what you paste and what you sign up for

  • Everything included is sent to the model. GitIngest includes every file under the size limit that your pattern does not exclude. If a repository has a committed credential in a config file, it is in the dump. Scan or exclude before copying. This is a general risk with any dump tool, not something I found in this repository.
  • Private repositories. GitIngest has a Private Repository checkbox and GitDiagram has API Key and Private Repos entries in its header. I did not test either, and handing a private repository’s code to a free third-party service is a decision for your security team, not a URL trick.
  • DeepWiki asks for an email. To index a repository you must give an address. The post stopped there on purpose.
  • Ads and sponsors. GitIngest shows Carbon ads and GitDiagram a sponsor banner. This is how free tools pay for the servers that read your repository, and a reason to keep them off pages with sensitive context.

Failure 6: wrong tool for the repository

GitHubBox is the clean example. For this Scala and Java repository, the editor opened and the preview was empty, which looks like an error on your side, not a mismatch. The test before you open any of these tools is one question about the repository: what is its main language, and what do I want out of it?

If the repository is Reach for Skip
JavaScript or Node, and you want to run it GitHubBox Nothing, but expect to wait for installs
Any language, and you want to read it github1s GitHubBox
Any language, and you want to ask an LLM GitIngest for a one-off, GitMCP for repeated use Pasting the unfiltered dump
Large, unfamiliar, and you want the shape GitDiagram, then verify in github1s Trusting the hub node
Popular open source project DeepWiki, if already indexed Indexing someone else’s repo with your email

Optimisation, tuning knobs and best practices

The tools have few settings, so the tuning is mostly about what you decide before you open them and what you do with the output afterwards.

Pick the tool by the question, not by the novelty

  What do you want to know?
        |
        +-- "Where is X, and how is it written?" ---------> github1s
        |                                                    (read, search)
        +-- "What are the parts and how do they connect?" -> GitDiagram
        |                                                    (then verify in github1s)
        +-- "Answer questions about it, once" ------------> GitIngest
        |                                                    (scope with excludes first)
        +-- "Answer questions about it, repeatedly" ------> GitMCP
        |                                                    (the assistant fetches on demand)
        +-- "Does it run?" (Node/JS only) ----------------> GitHubBox
        +-- "A wiki for a well-known project" ------------> DeepWiki
                                                             (only if already indexed)

Walk the diagram top to bottom. The first two branches need no AI at all for the answer: github1s is plain browsing. The AI-backed branches (GitIngest, GitMCP, GitDiagram, DeepWiki) are where you should check the result.

A pipeline that uses three of them

For an unfamiliar repository, in this order:

  1. GitDiagram for the shape. Open the .md version if you want to paste the overview and component list into your notes. Write down the two or three clusters that matter to you.
  2. github1s to confirm. Open one file from each cluster and read it. This is where the Example runner hub gets caught.
  3. GitIngest, scoped for the deep question. Exclude everything outside the clusters you picked, so the token count matches the question.
  4. GitMCP if you will keep asking. A configured MCP URL beats re-pasting a dump every session, and does not go stale the way a pinned dump does. (Configuration shown above; not exercised end to end in this post.)

Scope before you paste

GitIngest’s controls are the only real tuning surface in the set.

Control Default seen What it does Use it when
Exclude / Include pattern empty Glob patterns, comma separated, e.g. *.md, src/ Always, for anything over a few dozen files
Include files under 50 kB Skips larger files Generated or data files dominate
Private Repository off Checkbox for private repositories Not tested here

Measured on this repository, one exclude list changed the result like this:

Exclude list Files Estimated tokens
None 280 173.5k
*.xml, *.sh, *.md, *.properties 151 64.1k

Patterns worth trying, as starting points and not measured here: exclude test folders when the question is about production code, exclude *.json and *.csv for data-heavy repositories, and use Include mode to keep only one module’s directory. Verify the file count after each change, because a pattern that matches more than you meant removes the evidence for your question.

Check what you are about to send

Before pasting a dump anywhere, run two local commands on a shallow clone. They cost almost nothing and they are the check the web tools do not give you:

git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/rangareddy/ranga_spark_experiments
cd ranga_spark_experiments
git ls-files | wc -l
grep -rIn --exclude-dir=.git -E 'AKIA|password *=|secret' .

On this repository that printed 313 tracked files, and the grep produced a handful of hits that were all configuration key names and placeholders: Hadoop fs.s3a.secret.key settings that read the value from a variable, a usage string with the literal arguments ranga_aws_access_key ranga_aws_secret_key, and a spark.datasource.hive.warehouse.password=hive line in a run script. No real credential. That outcome is the point of the exercise: a pattern search finds names, so a person has to triage it, and it is quicker to do that on a terminal than after the text is in a chat.

The file counts differ by tool and the post did not reconcile them: git ls-files says 313, GitIngest analysed 280, and 151 after excludes. Different tools count binary files, ignored files and size limits differently. Compare counts within a tool, not across tools.

Prompt template for a dump

A pasted repository answers better when the prompt says what the text is.

Below is a snapshot of github.com/<owner>/<repo> at commit <sha>,
filtered to <what you kept>. Answer only from this text. If the answer is
not in it, say which file you would need. Quote file paths.

Question: <your question>

The commit hash comes from the Summary panel (eaf9e23... here). It tells the assistant, and your future self, which snapshot the answer is about. The “which file you would need” line is the cheap guard against a cropped or filtered dump producing a confident answer from missing evidence.

Cost and trade-offs against a local clone

  Browser tools (this post) git clone --depth 1 plus local tools
Setup None Network fetch and disk
Disk used None 1,812 KB for this repository, of which 304 KB is .git
Completeness Sampled (GitDiagram read 40 files) or cropped (GitIngest preview at 300k characters) Everything tracked
Privacy The repository name and content go to a third party Stays on your machine
Repeatable in CI Not shown to work (see Failure 3) Yes
Freshness A snapshot, or live through GitMCP git pull
Cost Free, with ads or sponsors Free

For this 313-file repository the clone is 1,812 KB on disk, with a 304 KB .git. The browser tools do not save you bytes at this size. They save you the decision to set anything up, which matters for a repository you will open once and does not matter for one you will work in. Timings are left out on purpose: they depend on the network and the day.

Key takeaways

  • The trick is the same in every case. Open the repository on GitHub, then retype the host. github1s.com, gitingest.com, gitdiagram.com, gitmcp.io, githubbox.com and deepwiki.com all take owner/repo after it.
  • Match the tool to the question. Reading and searching: github1s. Shape of an unfamiliar repository: GitDiagram. One-off questions to an LLM: GitIngest. Repeated questions: GitMCP. Running a JavaScript project: GitHubBox.
  • Scope before you paste. One exclude list took the test repository from 280 files and 173.5k estimated tokens to 151 files and 64.1k.
  • Verify the AI-generated views. GitDiagram read 40 of 280 files and drew a hub node the repository does not have. Use it as a table of contents and confirm in the source.
  • Know what did not work. GitHubBox showed a blank preview for a Maven project, DeepWiki had not indexed the repository and asks for an email, and GitMCP was configured from its page but not run end to end here.
  • Do not use these on private code unless cleared. The server-side tools run on someone else’s infrastructure.
  • For anything repeatable, clone. A shallow clone of this repository is 1,812 KB on disk, runs offline, and scripts cleanly.

References

  • github1s, the VS Code web viewer for GitHub repositories
  • GitIngest, which turns a repository into a prompt-ready text file
  • GitDiagram, which generates an architecture diagram and a Markdown overview
  • GitMCP, which serves a repository as a remote MCP endpoint
  • GitHubBox, which opens a repository in CodeSandbox
  • DeepWiki, which hosts generated wikis for indexed repositories
  • The test repository, rangareddy/ranga_spark_experiments
  • Model Context Protocol for what an MCP server and client are

No install, no clone, and for public repositories no sign-in. They split into three jobs: read a repo (github1s), feed a repo to an LLM (GitIngest, GitMCP), and understand a repo (GitDiagram, DeepWiki). GitHubBox is the odd one out: it runs a repo, and only helps if the repo is a JavaScript project. Every screenshot in this post comes from one real repository, rangareddy/ranga_spark_experiments: 280 text files, Scala and Java, Maven build. That choice exposes the limits as well as the wins. Two of the tools did not work for this repo, and the post says so and shows why. Why read a repository without cloning it A pull request link, a Stack Overflow answer or a colleague’s message lands you in a repository you have never seen. The default move is git clone, then an IDE import, then a Maven or sbt dependency download, all to answer a question like “where does this job write its output?”. For a repository you will not touch again, that is minutes of setup for a thirty-second question. A family of small sites removes the setup by taking the GitHub URL itself as input. You change github.com to another host, or put another host in front of the path, and the page you land on has done the work: an editor with search, a single text file ready to paste into a chat, a diagram, or a server your AI assistant can query. This post runs each of them, in order, on the same repository so the outputs are comparable. It is a tutorial first: each tool has numbered steps and a screenshot taken during the run. It also records where each tool stops, because “works on any repo” is only true of some of them. The test repository All runs use rangareddy/ranga_spark_experiments. It is a good subject because it is awkward in the ways real repositories are: Property Value Why it matters Files 280 text files analysed by GitIngest Large enough that a naive dump is cropped Layout 34 top-level folders, 32 of them Maven modules (each has a pom.xml), one per Spark integration A diagram has to summarise, not list Languages Scala 153,704 bytes, Java 41,228, Shell 23,514, Python 5,074 (GitHub languages API) Not JavaScript, which matters for GitHubBox History 102 commits, one branch, last commit eaf9e23 Small enough to read, old enough to be unmaintained What the URL rewrite actually does None of these sites is magic. Each one is a web application that receives owner/repo in the URL, fetches the repository from GitHub on the server side (or, for github1s, in your browser), and renders a different view of it. The rewrite is the cheapest possible interface: you already have the GitHub URL, so the only thing you type is the part that changes. https://github.com/rangareddy/ranga_spark_experiments | | swap the host, keep owner/repo v github1s.com /rangareddy/ranga_spark_experiments -> VS Code in the browser gitingest.com /rangareddy/ranga_spark_experiments -> one text file for an LLM gitdiagram.com /rangareddy/ranga_spark_experiments -> architecture diagram gitmcp.io /rangareddy/ranga_spark_experiments -> MCP server URL githubbox.com /rangareddy/ranga_spark_experiments -> redirects to CodeSandbox deepwiki.com /rangareddy/ranga_spark_experiments -> generated wiki, if indexed All six take the same two path segments. Only the host differs, so the habit to build is: open the repository on GitHub, then retype the host. Three jobs, three places the work happens The tools differ less in what they show than in where the computation runs and what they cost you. Tool Job Where the work runs What you get Needs sign-in github1s Read and search Your browser, which loads a VS Code web build A read-only VS Code workbench No GitIngest Feed an LLM Server One text file: summary, tree, file contents No GitMCP Feed an LLM, live Server, over MCP A URL your assistant calls as tools No GitDiagram Understand Server, using an LLM A Mermaid diagram of the architecture No DeepWiki Understand Server, using an LLM A wiki, after an indexing job Email to index GitHubBox Run CodeSandbox A cloud dev environment Not to open “Needs sign-in” is for a public repository, as observed in this run. Private repositories need tokens or accounts on most of these, and none was tried here. The trade-off all six share Each tool trades privacy and completeness for speed. The server-side ones receive the repository name, and GitHubBox, GitIngest and GitDiagram each run on someone else’s infrastructure, so none of them belongs anywhere near a private repository you have not cleared. The model-backed ones (GitDiagram, DeepWiki) also summarise: they read a slice of the repository, which the sections below quantify (GitDiagram reported reading 40 source files out of 280). The alternative is the tool you already have: git clone --depth 1, then tree, rg and your IDE. It is complete, private and offline, and it costs the clone plus the import. The six tools win on the first minute and lose on everything after it. Hands-on demo: each tool, step by step, on a real repository Every step below was run on 12 November 2026 in Chrome against the repository above, signed in to nothing but GitHub. The screenshots are from those runs, unedited apart from file size. Each tool section ends with what it did not do, because that is the part the landing pages leave out. Tool 1: github1s, a read-only VS Code in the tab What it is for. Browsing and searching code with a real editor’s tree, tabs and search panel, without cloning. It is the right first move when you want to read, not run. Steps Open the repository on GitHub: https://github.com/rangareddy/ranga_spark_experiments. Edit the host in the address bar: replace github.com with github1s.com. The full URL is https://github1s.com/rangareddy/ranga_spark_experiments. Wait for the workbench to load. It opens the README as a preview tab and the whole folder tree in the Explorer. The status bar shows master, the branch the URL resolved to. To land on a file directly, keep the whole GitHub path and change only the host. Click the magnifier in the activity bar, or press Cmd+Shift+F on macOS (Ctrl+Shift+F elsewhere), and type format("delta"). The panel reported 2 results in 1 file, and both matches are highlighted in the open editor. Where it stops No syntax highlighting for Scala. The status bar showed Plain Text for the .scala file. Navigation and search work; colour does not. Read-only. The Search view has a Replace box, but this is a viewer for a public repository. There is nothing to run, build or debug. A “Leave site?” prompt. After I used Search, Chrome asked for confirmation before navigating away from the page. It is a browser prompt from the editor page, not data loss, because nothing can be saved. Tool 2: GitIngest, the whole repository as one prompt What it is for. Pasting a repository into an LLM chat. It produces a summary, a directory tree and the file contents as a single text document. Steps Open https://gitingest.com/rangareddy/ranga_spark_experiments. The path is the same owner/repo, so the page starts processing immediately. Wait for the spinner. This run took under half a minute for 280 files. Read the Summary panel. It is built for pasting into an agent’s context instead of screenshotting the page. Where it stops It reads a sample. Forty files out of 280. Its own markdown says it is generated “from its file tree, README and a sample of source files” and that it “is an AI-made overview: check details against the source.” It invents hubs. The top node, Example runner, fans out to every cluster. This repository is a set of independent examples, and the generated overview itself says each is “independently initiated”. The hub is the model’s way to draw a tree, not a program in the repo. Read diagrams like this as a table of contents, not a call graph. Wide repositories shrink. Thirty-two sibling modules produce a diagram that only works zoomed. A repository with a deeper structure would read better than a flat monorepo of samples. Tool 4: GitMCP, the repository as a tool your assistant can call What it is for. Instead of pasting a snapshot, give an AI assistant a URL that it queries on demand, so it reads current files rather than a stale dump. Steps Open https://gitmcp.io/rangareddy/ranga_spark_experiments. The page is a setup guide titled GitMCP Documentation Server, with the server URL: https://gitmcp.io/rangareddy/ranga_spark_experiments Pick your client from the tabs: Cursor, Claude Desktop, Windsurf, VSCode, Cline, Highlight AI, Augment Code or Msty AI.
