Iceberg’s manifests point at the Parquet files Hudi wrote, in place. What it needs Hudi 1.2.x. The adapter loads Hudi classes that 1.1.1 does not have. The playground’s Spark 3.5.9 image ships Hudi 1.1.1, and with the adapter jars on top of it the write fails with ClassNotFoundException: org.apache.hudi.common.schema.HoodieSchema. The Hudi 1.2.1 Spark bundle fixes that. Four XTable jars and an Iceberg runtime. xtable-iceberg-pluggable-tf, xtable-core, xtable-api and xtable-hudi-support-utils, plus the Iceberg Spark runtime. The Iceberg runtime is needed on the writer, not only for reads. Without it the write dies with ClassNotFoundException: org.apache.iceberg.exceptions.AlreadyExistsException. A source build. At the time of writing the module is not on Maven Central. The jars below were built from XTable commit 0e97d0a, whose version is 0.5.0-SNAPSHOT. A 0.5.0-incubating-rc1 candidate is on the Apache dev distribution site. Pin whatever you build. Under the hood: what a commit leaves on disk One folder, two metadata trees Run the demo in the next section and the table folder looks like this: orders/ |-- eu/ <uuid>-0_0-..._<instant>.parquet <- data files written by Hudi |-- us/ <uuid>-0_1-..._<instant>.parquet (Iceberg points at these) | |-- .hoodie/ <- Hudi's metadata | |-- hoodie.properties hoodie.table.format=ICEBERG | '-- timeline/ | |-- 20261109055454773.commit.requested | |-- 20261109055454773.inflight | |-- 20261109055454773_20261109055500898.commit | '-- ... one triple per commit | '-- metadata/ <- Iceberg's metadata |-- v1.metadata.json ... v5.metadata.json |-- version-hint.text contains: 5 |-- snap-<snapshot-id>-1-<uuid>.avro one manifest list per commit '-- <uuid>-m0.avro, <uuid>-m1.avro manifests There is no .hoodie/metadata directory, because the Hudi metadata table is off. That is a requirement, and the reason is in the next subsection. An Iceberg reader that opens the folder by path reads version-hint.text, which holds the number of the current v<N>.metadata.json, and follows it to a snapshot, a manifest list, manifests and then the Parquet files. A Hudi reader ignores metadata/ and reads the timeline. Both end at the same files. Each Hudi instant becomes one Iceberg snapshot The demo writes an insert, an upsert and a delete. These are the three Hudi instants and the three Iceberg snapshots they produced: Hudi write Hudi instant (requested time) Iceberg snapshot operation insert of 3 orders 20261109055454773 append upsert of order 2 and 4 20261109055505444 overwrite delete of order 3 20261109055509672 overwrite The snapshot records which instant it mirrors in its summary, under the key XTABLE_METADATA. For the third snapshot of an earlier run, the value decodes to this: { "sourceTableFormat": "HUDI", "sourceIdentifier": "20261107065224958", "latestTableOperationIdentifier": "{\"action\":\"commit\",\"ts\":\"20261107065224958\", \"state\":\"COMPLETED\",\"requestedTime\":\"20261107065224958\", \"completionTime\":\"20261107065226457\"}" } That string is the join key between the two formats. It also explains the operations. This is a copy-on-write table, so an update or delete rewrites a whole base file: Iceberg sees one file added and one file deleted, which is overwrite, with added-data-files and deleted-data-files both at 1 in the summary. Only the first write, which adds files and removes none, is append. Why five metadata files for three commits The table folder holds v1 to v5 for three commits. The Iceberg table is created in two steps before the first snapshot lands: File Snapshots Schemas Partition specs What changed v1.metadata.json 0 1 1 Table created, empty schema, unpartitioned v2.metadata.json 0 2 2 Real schema and the region partition spec added v3.metadata.json 1 2 2 First snapshot (the insert) v4.metadata.json 2 2 2 Second snapshot (the upsert) v5.metadata.json 3 2 2 Third snapshot (the delete) So a table with N commits has N + 2 metadata files. A reader never opens the older ones; version-hint.text points at the newest. The table property write.metadata.delete-after-commit.enabled is true, so Iceberg removes metadata files once they fall outside its retained-versions limit. All five were still present in this run. The Iceberg schema is Hudi’s, with field ids assigned Parquet files written by Hudi carry no Iceberg field ids. The adapter assigns them in column order and records the names so that Iceberg can match columns by name: Field id Name Type 1 to 5 _hoodie_commit_time, _hoodie_commit_seqno, _hoodie_record_key, _hoodie_partition_path, _hoodie_file_name string 6 order_id long 7 region string 8 amount double 9 updated_at string The five Hudi meta columns appear as ordinary Iceberg columns. An Iceberg query that runs SELECT * returns them, and you can use _hoodie_commit_time in Iceberg to ask which Hudi commit last wrote a row. The mapping from names to ids is stored in the table property schema.name-mapping.default, and the partition spec is identity(region), which is the only kind of partitioning the adapter supports. Why the metadata table has to be off Hudi’s metadata table normally answers file listings and column statistics. For an Iceberg-format table the metadata factory is IcebergBackedTableMetadata, and its documentation says it deliberately lists the file system rather than reading Iceberg manifests. An enabled metadata table would fail with Unsupported operation: getColumnsStats. The adapter therefore refuses the combination up front, which is the error you will see in the failures section. The cost is on the Hudi side: every file listing Hudi does on this table is a real storage listing. The source calls the design a placeholder, because Iceberg’s manifests already carry the file lists and column bounds this class should eventually serve. Rollback, clean and archive go through the same hook commit is not the only callback. clean and archive each convert their instant into Iceberg changes (read from the source, not run here), and a rollback commits a snapshot too. The earlier failure run shows it: after a rollback the Iceberg snapshot list reads append for the first commit, overwrite with the action rollback for the rollback, and overwrite with the action commit for the next write. A restore is refused outright, which is covered in the limits below. Hands-on demo: write once, read as Hudi and as Iceberg Prerequisites and the stack Every command below ran on a laptop. The demo needs Docker and nothing else: the XTable build runs inside a Maven container, so no local Java or Maven is installed. The datalake-playground gives you the Spark image and the same stack the other posts use; see the setup post. git clone https://github.com/rangareddy/datalake-playground.git cd datalake-playground SPARK_VERSION=3.5.9 sh run_datalake.sh start sh run_datalake.sh status The adapter does not run on the Hudi 1.1.1 that stack ships, so this demo does not use the running spark-master. It starts a throwaway container from the same Spark 3.5.9 image, which keeps the shared stack untouched, and loads Hudi 1.2.1 and the XTable jars with --jars. The image is linux/amd64, so Apple Silicon runs it under emulation. Step 1: build the XTable jars mkdir work && cd work git clone https://github.com/apache/incubator-xtable.git cd incubator-xtable git checkout 0e97d0a docker run --rm -v "$PWD":/src -v "$HOME/.m2":/root/.m2 -w /src \ maven:3.9-eclipse-temurin-17 \ mvn -B -q -pl xtable-hudi-support/xtable-iceberg-pluggable-tf -am \ package -DskipTests -Dspotless.check.skip=true -Dspotless.apply.skip=true cd .. Collect the four jars and the Hudi 1.2.1 bundle into one folder: mkdir jars X=incubator-xtable cp $X/xtable-hudi-support/xtable-iceberg-pluggable-tf/target/xtable-iceberg-pluggable-tf_2.12-0.5.0-SNAPSHOT.jar \ $X/xtable-core/target/xtable-core_2.12-0.5.0-SNAPSHOT.jar \ $X/xtable-api/target/xtable-api-0.5.0-SNAPSHOT.jar \ $X/xtable-hudi-support/xtable-hudi-support-utils/target/xtable-hudi-support-utils-0.5.0-SNAPSHOT.jar \ jars/ curl -sSfO --output-dir jars \ https://repo1.maven.org/maven2/org/apache/hudi/hudi-spark3.5-bundle_2.12/1.2.1/hudi-spark3.5-bundle_2.12-1.2.1.jar ls jars Step 2: the script Save this as hudi_iceberg_demo.py. It writes three batches to a Hudi table with the two settings that matter, compares the Hudi and Iceberg reads after each one, and then prints each Iceberg snapshot with the Hudi instant it records. import json import sys from pyspark.sql import SparkSession BASE = sys.argv[1] # for example file:///data/orders spark = ( SparkSession.builder.appName("hudi-writes-iceberg") .config("spark.serializer", "org.apache.spark.serializer.KryoSerializer") .config("spark.sql.extensions", "org.apache.spark.sql.hudi.HoodieSparkSessionExtension") .config("spark.sql.catalog.spark_catalog", "org.apache.spark.sql.hudi.catalog.HoodieCatalog") .config("spark.kryo.registrator", "org.apache.spark.HoodieSparkKryoRegistrar") .config("spark.sql.shuffle.partitions", "2") .getOrCreate() ) spark.sparkContext.setLogLevel("ERROR") COLUMNS = ["order_id", "region", "amount", "updated_at"] HUDI_OPTIONS = { "hoodie.table.name": "orders", "hoodie.datasource.write.recordkey.field": "order_id", "hoodie.datasource.write.precombine.field": "updated_at", "hoodie.datasource.write.partitionpath.field": "region", "hoodie.datasource.write.table.type": "COPY_ON_WRITE", # The two settings that matter for this post. "hoodie.table.format": "ICEBERG", "hoodie.metadata.enable": "false", } def write(rows, operation, mode): df = spark.createDataFrame(rows, COLUMNS) (df.write.format("hudi").options(**HUDI_OPTIONS) .option("hoodie.datasource.write.operation", operation) .mode(mode).save(BASE)) def read(fmt): df = spark.read.format(fmt).load(BASE) return sorted(tuple(r) for r in df.select("order_id", "region", "amount").collect()) def compare(label): hudi, iceberg = read("hudi"), read("iceberg") print(f"== {label}") print("hudi :", hudi) print("iceberg:", iceberg) print("same :", hudi == iceberg) write([(1, "eu", 10.0, "2026-11-01"), (2, "us", 20.0, "2026-11-01"), (3, "eu", 30.0, "2026-11-01")], "upsert", "overwrite") compare("after insert") write([(2, "us", 25.0, "2026-11-02"), (4, "us", 40.0, "2026-11-02")], "upsert", "append") compare("after upsert") write([(3, "eu", 30.0, "2026-11-03")], "delete", "append") compare("after delete") print("== iceberg snapshots and the Hudi instant each one records") snapshots = spark.read.format("iceberg").load(BASE + "#snapshots").orderBy("committed_at") for s in snapshots.collect(): instant = json.loads(s.summary["XTABLE_METADATA"])["sourceIdentifier"] print(s.snapshot_id, s.operation, "hudi instant", instant) first = snapshots.first().snapshot_id as_of_first = (spark.read.format("iceberg").option("snapshot-id", first).load(BASE) .select("order_id", "region", "amount")) print("== iceberg time travel to the first snapshot") print(sorted(tuple(r) for r in as_of_first.collect())) Step 3: run it mkdir -p data docker run -d --name hudi-iceberg --user root --entrypoint bash \ -v "$PWD/jars":/jars:ro -v "$PWD":/work -v "$PWD/data":/data \ rangareddy1988/ranga-spark:1.0.0 -c 'sleep infinity' docker exec hudi-iceberg bash -c ' JARS=$(ls /jars/*.jar | tr "\n" ","),$(ls $ICEBERG_HOME/iceberg-spark-runtime*.jar) $SPARK_HOME/bin/spark-submit --master "local[2]" \ --conf spark.eventLog.enabled=false --conf spark.ui.enabled=false \ --conf spark.sql.catalogImplementation=in-memory \ --jars $JARS /work/hudi_iceberg_demo.py file:///data/orders' Three flags need a word. spark.eventLog.enabled=false avoids an event-log directory the image preconfigures but does not create. The Iceberg runtime comes from $ICEBERG_HOME, which the playground image sets, so there is nothing to download for it. spark.sql.catalogImplementation=in-memory is needed because this container is not on the stack’s network: without it the image’s defaults point Hudi’s reader at a Hive Metastore it cannot reach, and the first read fails with Unable to instantiate SessionHiveMetaStoreClient. Step 4: the output == after insert hudi : [(1, 'eu', 10.0), (2, 'us', 20.0), (3, 'eu', 30.0)] iceberg: [(1, 'eu', 10.0), (2, 'us', 20.0), (3, 'eu', 30.0)] same : True == after upsert hudi : [(1, 'eu', 10.0), (2, 'us', 25.0), (3, 'eu', 30.0), (4, 'us', 40.0)] iceberg: [(1, 'eu', 10.0), (2, 'us', 25.0), (3, 'eu', 30.0), (4, 'us', 40.0)] same : True == after delete hudi : [(1, 'eu', 10.0), (2, 'us', 25.0), (4, 'us', 40.0)] iceberg: [(1, 'eu', 10.0), (2, 'us', 25.0), (4, 'us', 40.0)] same : True == iceberg snapshots and the Hudi instant each one records 1579142869345373296 append hudi instant 20261109055454773 6206417245994243896 overwrite hudi instant 20261109055505444 6278283655811247997 overwrite hudi instant 20261109055509672 == iceberg time travel to the first snapshot [(1, 'eu', 10.0), (2, 'us', 20.0), (3, 'eu', 30.0)] The Hudi and Iceberg readers agree after every write, there is one snapshot per Hudi instant, and the Iceberg time travel returns the table as it was after the insert. Your snapshot ids and instants will differ; the shape will not. Look at the folder to see both metadata trees: ls data/orders data/orders/.hoodie/timeline data/orders/metadata | grep -v crc grep table.format data/orders/.hoodie/hoodie.properties The last command prints hoodie.table.format=ICEBERG. That is the property every later writer reads from the table, so only the first write needs to set it. Step 5: clean up docker rm -f hudi-iceberg rm -rf data The container only ever wrote into data/, so there is nothing to remove from the shared stack. Real-world scenarios and production failures Most failures of this feature are quiet, because the fallback to a native table raises nothing. Each one below was reproduced on the demo setup with the exact output shown. The write that succeeds and then disappears Three writers touch one table. The first and third have the adapter jars. The second does not, because it is a different job with a different classpath. Writer Adapter jars Writes Hudi reader sees Iceberg reader sees 1 yes order 1 orders 1 orders 1 2 no order 2 orders 1, 2 orders 1 3 yes order 3 orders 1, 3 orders 1, 3 Writer 2 raised nothing and its data is in the Hudi table, but the Iceberg side never heard about it: the property hoodie.table.format=ICEBERG was set, no jar answered to it, and Hudi fell back to native. Then writer 3 started. It found a completed Hudi instant with no Iceberg snapshot, treated it as pending, and rolled it back. After writer 3, order 2 is gone from both formats. The timeline shows the rollback: 20261109055001528_20261109055007254.commit writer 1 20261109055044928.rollback.inflight writer 3 rolls back writer 2 20261109055044928.rollback.requested 20261109055044928_20261109055046624.rollback 20261109055047824_20261109055053164.commit writer 3 Writer 2’s .commit file is no longer there, and the Iceberg snapshot list is append (commit), overwrite (rollback), overwrite (commit). A Hudi writer without the adapter is therefore not a harmless degraded mode. It acknowledges data that the next correct writer will delete. What to do. Put the jars on every job that touches the table, including the ones nobody thinks of as writers: clean, clustering and compaction run as separate jobs in many deployments. Then check the invariant instead of trusting it. Every completed Hudi commit must be recorded by an Iceberg snapshot. This script compares the two and needs only the Iceberg runtime, not the adapter: import json import os import re import sys from pyspark.sql import SparkSession TABLE = sys.argv[1] # a local table folder, for example /data/orders spark = SparkSession.builder.config("spark.sql.catalogImplementation", "in-memory").getOrCreate() spark.sparkContext.setLogLevel("ERROR") # Hudi instants that the timeline calls completed. completed = set() for name in os.listdir(f"{TABLE}/.hoodie/timeline"): m = re.match(r"(\d+)_\d+\.commit$", name) if m: completed.add(m.group(1)) # Hudi instants that an Iceberg snapshot records. snapshots = spark.read.format("iceberg").load(f"file://{TABLE}#snapshots").collect() recorded = {json.loads(s.summary["XTABLE_METADATA"])["sourceIdentifier"] for s in snapshots} pending = sorted(completed - recorded) print(f"completed hudi commits: {len(completed)}, iceberg snapshots: {len(snapshots)}") print("completed in hudi but missing from iceberg:", pending or "none") Run against the table above after writer 3, it printed 2 completed commits, 3 snapshots (the rollback adds one) and none. Run against the next table, it finds the problem. For an object store, replace the os.listdir with a listing of .hoodie/timeline/ through your storage client. The metadata table left on hoodie.metadata.enable defaults to true in Hudi. A writer that forgets to set it to false on a table with the Iceberg format fails with: UnsupportedOperationException: The Iceberg table format does not support the Hudi metadata table, but table orders has one; set hoodie.metadata.enable=false on every writer of the table and remove the metadata table The error message is accurate and the damage is instructive. The failure happens in the hook, after Hudi has completed its own instant, so the timeline holds a completed .commit for the failed write and no snapshot for it. What each reader sees right after that failed write depends on whether it has the adapter: Reader Adapter jars Result Hudi yes order 1 only; the failed commit is pending Iceberg n/a order 1 only Hudi no orders 1 and 2; the native timeline says completed A Hudi reader without the jars reads the native timeline and shows the write the adapter considers uncommitted. The next write, with the metadata table off, rolled the failed commit back, so the row that reader saw is gone. The rule from the previous failure extends to readers: any Hudi job that reads this table needs the jars as well. Merge-on-read A merge-on-read table is refused at the first write, before any files appear: UnsupportedOperationException: The Iceberg table format only supports COPY_ON_WRITE tables, but table orders is MERGE_ON_READ No metadata/ folder is created. If you need the merge-on-read write profile, this feature is not available to that table today. Classpath failures that look like data problems Symptom Cause Fix ClassNotFoundException: org.apache.iceberg.exceptions.AlreadyExistsException on write The Iceberg runtime is not on the writer’s classpath. The adapter commits with it. Add iceberg-spark-runtime to the writer’s --jars, not only to the reader’s. ClassNotFoundException: org.apache.hudi.common.schema.HoodieSchema on write The adapter is running on Hudi 1.1.1, which lacks a class the adapter loads. Use the Hudi 1.2.1 Spark bundle. Unable to instantiate SessionHiveMetaStoreClient on the first read The container is not on the stack network, so the image’s Hive Metastore default is unreachable. Set spark.sql.catalogImplementation=in-memory, or join the datalake network. hoodie.table.format=ICEBERG in hoodie.properties, no metadata/ folder The adapter jars were not on the classpath of that writer. The first failure above. Add the jars and rerun the consistency check. The limits that come with the format These come from the adapter’s source and the XTable documentation for the feature, and they were not all run here. Only the first two were reproduced above. Copy-on-write tables only. Reproduced above. The metadata table stays off on every write. Reproduced above. Identity partitioning only. The adapter maps each Hudi partition field to an Iceberg identity partition. Timestamp-based and custom key generators with typed partition fields are refused. No restore. A Hudi restore is refused before it changes the table. One writer at a time. Compare this with the locking options in Hudi concurrency control, which describes what Hudi alone does with two writers. Iceberg format version 2. The metadata.json files in the demo say format-version: 2. Hudi is the only writer. Other engines read the table as Iceberg. A commit made by an Iceberg writer is invisible to Hudi, which does not see snapshots it did not make. Optimisation, tuning knobs and best practices Choosing between the ways to give a Hudi table an Iceberg face Pluggable table format XTableSyncTool in the writer Standalone XTable job Iceberg commit In the Hudi commit path After the Hudi commit, in the writer Separate job, on a schedule Failure mode Hudi operation fails, instant pending Hudi write succeeded, Iceberg lags or is missing Iceberg lags by the schedule Table types Copy-on-write See the XTable documentation See the XTable documentation Hudi metadata table Must be off Not restricted by the sync tool Not restricted Released today No, source build Yes Yes Hudi versions I ran it on 1.2.1 0.14.1 Not run here Operates as A table property plus jars on every job Three writer options plus a jar A job to deploy and monitor The sync tool is the right answer when you need a released artifact today and can accept lag. It is also strict about versions. XTable 0.4.0 worked against Hudi 0.14.1 on Spark 3.4.4, with Iceberg 1.9.2: an insert and an upsert both read identically in both formats. The same jar against Hudi 0.15.0 and against Hudi 1.1.1 failed with the same error: NoSuchMethodError: HoodieTableMetaClient$Builder.setConf(org.apache.hadoop.conf.Configuration) That method exists in the Hudi 0.14 line the jar was built against and not in 0.15.0 or 1.1.1, so a jar built against 0.14 does not load on later lines. The sync tool also needs the jars in a particular order. The XTable bundle carries its own unshaded copy of org.apache.iceberg.parquet, and when it comes before the Iceberg runtime on the classpath it shadows the runtime’s shaded copy, so reads fail with NoClassDefFoundError: org/apache/parquet/conf/ParquetConfiguration. Listing the Iceberg runtime first fixed it. The pluggable adapter was not subject to either problem in the demo, because it was built against the Hudi line it runs on. What the choice costs Listings replace the metadata table. With the metadata table off, Hudi lists storage for every file listing it needs. On a local disk that is invisible. On an object store it is a request per partition per write, and the cost scales with partition count. Keep partition counts bounded, and expect list latency to show up in write time before it shows up on a bill. The index you pick also changes: the demo ran on Hudi’s default index, and an index that lives in the metadata table, such as the record-level index, is off the table by implication of the requirement. Snapshots accumulate. Every Hudi commit adds an Iceberg snapshot, and so does every rollback. Hudi’s cleaner and archiver get callbacks and convert their instants into Iceberg changes, but how Iceberg’s own snapshot expiry interacts with that was not tested here. The XTable documentation says to write the table only through Hudi, so do not schedule Iceberg maintenance procedures against it without testing them on a copy. Storage does not double. The demo’s data is one set of Parquet files. The Iceberg metadata for three commits was a few kilobytes of JSON and Avro: each metadata.json was under 7 KB, and each manifest or manifest list about 4 to 8 KB. The cost of the feature is in operations, not bytes. The Iceberg runtime version is yours to choose. The XTable jars were built against Iceberg 1.9.2. The snapshots in the demo carry iceberg-version: Apache Iceberg 1.11.0, the runtime on the classpath at write time, and the Iceberg 1.11.0 reader read them back. You do not have to match the build version, but pin whichever you run, on writers and readers alike. Best practices Pin the build. Record the XTable commit and Hudi bundle version beside the job, as this post does, because the artifact is a source build. Put the same jars on every job. Writers, table services and Hudi readers. Treat a job without them as a defect, not a configuration choice. Set hoodie.metadata.enable=false explicitly on every write, including SQL sessions, rather than relying on it being off in hoodie.properties. Run the consistency check on a schedule, and alert on a non-empty result. It is the only signal that the silent fallback happened. Make Hudi the only writer and give Iceberg readers read-only credentials. Test on a copy first if you operate Iceberg maintenance or a catalog on top of the folder. Key takeaways The mental model is short. A table format is the layer that records commits. Hudi made that layer replaceable, and XTable supplies an Iceberg implementation, so one Hudi write commits twice in the same operation: once to Hudi’s timeline and once to an Iceberg snapshot that names the Hudi instant it mirrors. The data files are shared. Iceberg’s snapshot ancestry decides which Hudi commits count. The parameters are small and the prerequisites are not. The table property and hoodie.metadata.enable=false are two lines. The prerequisites are Hudi 1.2.x, four XTable jars built from source, the Iceberg runtime on the writer and a copy-on-write table. Failure is silent by default. A writer without the jars writes a native table without a warning, and the next correct writer rolls its commit back. The jars are a table-wide contract. Every writer, table service and Hudi reader needs them. Verify the invariant. Every completed Hudi commit needs an Iceberg snapshot that records it. The check in this post tests exactly that. Choose the sync tool when you need a released artifact now. Choose the pluggable format when removing the lag matters more than building the jars. The feature is young. Its metadata serving is explicitly a placeholder, restore is refused, and the artifact is a release candidate away from Maven Central. That is a reason to pin, test on a copy and automate the check, not a reason to avoid a design that removes a whole class of two-commit divergence. References RFC-93, pluggable table formats for the design behind hoodie.table.format HoodieTableFormat.java, the interface an implementation provides HoodieTableConfig.java for hoodie.table.format and the ServiceLoader lookup with its fallback IcebergTableFormat.java, the adapter, including the copy-on-write and metadata-table checks IcebergActiveTimeline.java for how the timeline is rebuilt from snapshot ancestry IcebergBackedTableMetadata.java for why the metadata table must be off Apache XTable documentation for the sync tool and the standalone job Hudi catalog sync documentation for XTable for the writer-side sync route One table, three formats for how translation compares with writing natively Life of a write query in Iceberg for the manifest, manifest list and metadata file this adapter writes Time travel and rollback in Iceberg for the snapshot-id reads used in the demo Trademarks Apache Hudi, Apache Iceberg, Apache XTable, Apache Spark, Apache Parquet, Apache Avro and Apache are either registered trademarks or trademarks of The Apache Software Foundation in the United States and other countries.

entry.content:

    • Design 2: CDC from an OLTP database to the lakehouse in under five minutes

    • Design 4: log aggregation for 10,000 servers

    • Design 6: IoT telemetry from one million devices

    • Design 9: a data quality platform for 500 tables
    • Design 10: GDPR right to erasure across the lake

  • Optimisation, tuning knobs and best practices

    • Tuning interview questions
  • Key takeaways
  • References
  • Trademarks

TL;DR

  • Start from the consumer and the decision the data supports. Tools come last. An answer that opens with “Kafka, Spark, Snowflake” has skipped the part being graded.
  • State freshness, completeness and correctness as separate targets. “Real time” is not a requirement until it has a number and a consumer.
  • Estimate before you draw: events per second at peak, bytes per day, log disk with replication, lake storage after compression, and the partition count those numbers imply.
  • Exactly-once is a property of a boundary, not of a pipeline. Name the boundary, then make the sink idempotent so that replay is safe.
  • Every design needs a replay story: where the raw data lives, how far back it goes, and how a backfill runs without starving the live path.
  • Monitor the data, not just the jobs. A job that succeeds with zero rows is the most expensive failure in data engineering because nobody gets paged.
  • Close every choice with its cost: “X buys A at the cost of B, and we rejected Y because C”.

Reading paths and setup

A pipeline that double-counts revenue after a node restart is a system design failure, not a Spark bug. The data engineering design round tests whether you can see that failure coming: whether you ask what one row means, where the data can be replayed from, and which write is allowed to happen twice. This guide gives you a repeatable way to answer that round and the mechanics you need to defend each answer.

It follows the order you would use in the room:

  1. A framework for any design prompt, with a capacity estimate you can do in two minutes.
  2. The building blocks in the order data flows through them: ingestion, the log, processing, delivery guarantees, storage, serving, orchestration and quality.
  3. A runnable demo of the property interviewers probe hardest: a Kafka to Iceberg stream that is replayed after a simulated crash, with one sink that duplicates and one that does not.
  4. Ten worked designs of the prompts that come up most often, from clickstream analytics to GDPR erasure.
  5. Production failures and tuning knobs, so the trade-offs you name are ones you can back with a config key or an error message.

Interview questions with model answers close the framework, building-block, demo, design and tuning sections. Each answer is written the way an interviewer wants to hear it: the decision, the mechanism, and what it costs.

If you have not yet read them, the companion guides cover the ground this one assumes: the data modeling guide for grain, SCD history, CDC patterns and Lambda versus Kappa in depth, and the Structured Streaming internals post for the micro-batch engine the demo runs on.

Running the examples

The demo scripts run on the public datalake-playground stack, which ships Spark 3.5.9 with the Iceberg runtime on disk. Start it from its root:

git clone https://github.com/rangareddy/datalake-playground.git
cd datalake-playground
SPARK_VERSION=3.5.9 sh run_datalake.sh start
sh run_datalake.sh status

The demo reads from Kafka, which only the all profile starts (the broker is kafka:29092), so start the stack with that profile instead:

PROFILE=all SPARK_VERSION=3.5.9 sh run_datalake.sh start

The PySpark scripts use an Iceberg catalog named sd of type hadoop, whose warehouse is file:///tmp/sd_blog/warehouse inside the spark-master container, and one Kafka topic, sd_blog_orders. They do not touch the shared Hive Metastore or MinIO buckets. Spark reads Kafka on this stack without extra --jars. The capacity estimate in the next section is plain Python and runs anywhere.

A framework for any design prompt

Why the data design round is different

A backend design round asks whether a service stays up and answers fast. A data design round asks whether the numbers are still right after the system has failed, been replayed, and been changed by three teams over a year. The state that matters is not a request in flight; it is every row ever written.

Concern Backend system design Data system design
Unit of work A request A record, a batch, or a table commit
Main failure Latency and availability Wrong, missing or duplicated data, often silent
Time Request time Event time, processing time, and the gap between them
Recovery Retry the request Replay a range of history without double-counting
Change Deploy a new version Evolve a schema that years of stored data already use
Success metric p99 latency, error rate Freshness, completeness, correctness, cost per TB

That difference is why the framework below spends two of its seven steps on contracts and recovery, which a backend round barely touches.

The seven-step framework

 45-minute round
 ┌────────┬──────────┬────────┬──────────┬────────────┬────────┬─────────┐
 │ 1      │ 2        │ 3      │ 4        │ 5          │ 6      │ 7       │
 │Consumer│Numbers & │Data    │End-to-end│Correctness │Ops &   │Trade-   │
 │and     │non-funct.│contract│flow      │and recovery│govern- │offs and │
 │decision│targets   │        │(diagram) │            │ance    │stress   │
 ├────────┼──────────┼────────┼──────────┼────────────┼────────┼─────────┤
 │ ~4 min │ ~5 min   │ ~4 min │ ~10 min  │ ~10 min    │ ~5 min │ ~7 min  │
 └────────┴──────────┴────────┴──────────┴────────────┴────────┴─────────┘
   ask        estimate   define     draw       defend       operate  attack

The timings are a budget, not a script. What matters is the order: an architecture drawn before step 3 has no grain to be correct about, and a diagram defended before step 5 has never been replayed.

Step 1, the consumer and the decision. Ask who reads the output and what they do with it. “The fraud team blocks a card within 200 ms” and “finance closes the month on day 3” lead to different systems from the same events. Write the consumer and the decision at the top of the whiteboard.

Step 2, numbers and non-functional targets. Turn adjectives into numbers: volume, peak rate, record size, key cardinality, retention, growth. Then set the targets in the next subsection.

Step 3, the data contract. Define the key, the grain (what one row means), the event timestamp, the schema format and its compatibility rule, and who owns it. Most double-counting starts with a grain nobody wrote down.

Step 4, the end-to-end flow. Producers, ingestion, durable log, processing, storage layers, serving, and the control plane around them. Draw it left to right and walk one record through it.

Step 5, correctness and recovery. Delivery semantics at each boundary, deduplication, late data, dead-letter handling, replay and backfill. This is where most candidates lose the round.

Step 6, operations, security and governance. Freshness and volume alerts, lineage, access control, PII masking, retention and deletion, ownership.

Step 7, trade-offs and stress tests. Attack your own design: peak traffic at 10x, a hot key, a source outage of six hours, a breaking schema change, a backfill of a year. Say what bends and what breaks.

Step 1 in practice: the questions to ask

Area Question Why it changes the design
Consumer Who reads it: a dashboard, a model, an API, a regulator? Sets the serving store and the latency target
Decision What action does the data trigger? Separates “nice to be fresh” from “must be fresh”
Sources Databases, events, files, third-party APIs? Push or pull, CDC or extract, rate limits
Volume Events per day, peak hour, average and largest record? Partition counts, cluster size, cost
Freshness How old may the newest data be when read? Batch, micro-batch or continuous
Correctness Is approximate acceptable? Can a number change after publish? Exactly-once effort, restatement policy
History How far back must it be queryable, and replayable? Log retention, lake retention, tiering
Change Do source records update or delete? Append-only versus upsert and CDC
Compliance PII? Right to erasure? Residency? Encryption, masking, deletion path
Team Who operates it, and what do they already run? Managed versus self-hosted

Ask five or six of these, not all ten. Then confirm the one constraint that dominates: “So the binding requirement is fraud decisions under 200 ms, and analytics can be an hour behind. Correct?”

Step 2 in practice: freshness, completeness and correctness are three targets

“Real time” fuses three properties that a design trades against each other:

Target Definition Example SLO
Freshness Age of the newest data a consumer can read Dashboard data at most 2 minutes old at p95
Completeness Share of events for a period that have arrived 99.9% of an hour’s events present 15 minutes after the hour
Correctness Each event counted once, at the right grain and time Daily revenue matches the payment ledger to the cent
Latency Time from event to decision Fraud score returned in under 100 ms
Durability Data that may be lost Zero acknowledged events lost
Replayability How far back the raw input can be reprocessed 7 days from the log, 3 years from the lake

A dashboard can be fresh and incomplete at the same time: at 10:02 the 10:00-10:01 bucket is visible but late mobile events have not arrived yet. Stating both targets forces the late-data question that step 5 answers.

Step 2 in practice: capacity estimation

Estimation earns its time when it changes a decision. Do it in this order: average rate, peak rate, bytes per day, log disk, lake storage, and the partition count. Every input is an assumption to say out loud.

"""Back-of-envelope sizing for an event pipeline, as done in an interview.

Every input is an assumption to state out loud. The per-partition budget and
the compression ratio in particular must be measured on your own data.
"""
import math

events_per_day = 2_000_000_000      # stated by the interviewer
avg_event_bytes = 1_000             # JSON, measured from a sample
peak_to_avg = 3                     # evening peak vs daily average
kafka_retention_days = 7
kafka_replication = 3
partition_budget_mb_s = 5           # per-partition write budget, measured
parquet_ratio = 5                   # JSON -> zstd Parquet, measured
lake_retention_days = 365

SECONDS_PER_DAY = 86_400
MB, GB, TB = 10**6, 10**9, 10**12

avg_eps = events_per_day / SECONDS_PER_DAY
avg_mb_s = avg_eps * avg_event_bytes / MB
peak_mb_s = avg_mb_s * peak_to_avg
raw_per_day = events_per_day * avg_event_bytes
kafka_disk = raw_per_day * kafka_retention_days * kafka_replication
lake_per_day = raw_per_day / parquet_ratio
partitions = math.ceil(peak_mb_s / partition_budget_mb_s)

print(f"average rate     : {avg_eps:,.0f} events/s, {avg_mb_s:.1f} MB/s")
print(f"peak rate        : {avg_eps * peak_to_avg:,.0f} events/s, "
      f"{peak_mb_s:.1f} MB/s")
print(f"raw per day      : {raw_per_day / TB:.1f} TB")
print(f"kafka disk       : {kafka_disk / TB:.0f} TB "
      f"({kafka_retention_days} days x RF {kafka_replication})")
print(f"min partitions   : {partitions} at {partition_budget_mb_s} MB/s each")
print(f"lake per day     : {lake_per_day / GB:,.0f} GB Parquet")
print(f"lake per year    : {lake_per_day * lake_retention_days / TB:,.0f} TB")

Run with python3 capacity_estimate.py:

average rate     : 23,148 events/s, 23.1 MB/s
peak rate        : 69,444 events/s, 69.4 MB/s
raw per day      : 2.0 TB
kafka disk       : 42 TB (7 days x RF 3)
min partitions   : 14 at 5 MB/s each
lake per day     : 400 GB Parquet
lake per year    : 146 TB

Read the numbers back as decisions. 69 MB/s at peak is a modest Kafka load, so the cluster is sized by retention disk, 42 TB, not by throughput. Fourteen partitions is the floor from throughput; the real count is set by consumer parallelism and headroom, so 24 or 48 is a defensible answer if you say why. 400 GB of Parquet a day means daily partitions hold hundreds of 512 MB files, which is healthy; hourly partitions would hold about 17 GB each, also fine. 146 TB a year puts a lifecycle policy on the table.

The two inputs marked “measured” are the ones an interviewer may challenge. Say that the per-partition budget comes from a load test on your brokers and message sizes, and the compression ratio from writing a day of real data. A number you can explain beats a number that sounds precise.

Step 3 in practice: the data contract

 event: order_status_changed            owner: orders-service team
 ┌──────────────┬───────────┬──────────────────────────────────────────┐
 │ field        │ type      │ contract                                 │
 ├──────────────┼───────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────┤
 │ event_id     │ string    │ unique per emitted event; dedup key      │
 │ order_id     │ string    │ entity key; Kafka message key            │
 │ status       │ enum      │ PLACED, PAID, SHIPPED, CANCELLED         │
 │ amount       │ decimal   │ order total in minor units, never float  │
 │ order_ts     │ timestamp │ business time the order was placed (UTC) │
 │ updated_ts   │ timestamp │ event time of this change; orders events │
 │ schema_ver   │ int       │ registry id; BACKWARD compatible only    │
 └──────────────┴───────────┴──────────────────────────────────────────┘
 grain of the sink table: one row per order_id, latest status wins

Three fields carry most of the correctness: a dedup key (event_id), an entity key that becomes the Kafka message key and the upsert key (order_id), and an event time that orders versions of the same entity (updated_ts). Without the last one, “latest wins” means “last to arrive wins”, and a retried old event silently overwrites a newer one. The demo in this guide feeds exactly that stale event into the pipeline.

Step 4 in practice: the reference architecture

  SOURCES        INGEST            LOG            PROCESS         STORE / SERVE
 ┌────────┐   ┌───────────┐   ┌───────────┐   ┌────────────┐   ┌──────────────┐
 │OLTP DB │──►│CDC        │──►│           │──►│stream      │──►│bronze (raw)  │
 │(WAL)   │   │(Debezium) │   │  Kafka    │   │(Spark /    │   │silver (clean)│
 ├────────┤   ├───────────┤   │  topics,  │   │ Flink)     │   │gold (agg)    │
 │apps,   │──►│SDK /      │──►│  keyed,   │   ├────────────┤   │ Iceberg/Hudi/│
 │devices │   │collector  │   │  RF = 3   │   │batch       │──►│ Delta on S3  │
 ├────────┤   ├───────────┤   └───────────┘   │(Spark,     │   ├──────────────┤
 │files,  │──►│landing    │──────────────────►│ dbt)       │──►│OLAP / KV /   │
 │SaaS API│   │zone + pull│                   └────────────┘   │search / APIs │
 └────────┘   └───────────┘                                    └──────────────┘
 ─────────────────────────────── CONTROL PLANE ────────────────────────────────
  schema registry · catalog & lineage · orchestration (Airflow) · data quality
  checks · freshness / volume / lag alerts · access control & PII masking · cost

Walk one record through it. An order row changes in PostgreSQL; the change lands in the write-ahead log; Debezium reads the log and publishes a keyed event to Kafka, which replicates it to three brokers before acknowledging. A stream job reads it, validates it against the registered schema, and appends it to bronze. A second step deduplicates and upserts it into silver at the order grain. Batch jobs build gold aggregates from silver, and a serving store answers dashboards and APIs. Files and SaaS APIs skip the log and land in an object-store landing zone, from which the batch path picks them up.

The bottom band is not decoration. A design without a schema registry, a catalog, quality checks and freshness alerts works on the day it ships and degrades silently afterwards.

Step 5 in practice: correctness and recovery

Answer five questions for every boundary in the diagram:

  1. What are the delivery semantics here? At-most-once, at-least-once, or effectively-once, and what makes it so.
  2. Where is the dedup key, and who applies it? Usually the sink, through a MERGE on the entity key or a unique constraint.
  3. What happens to late data? Updated in place, written to a correction partition, or dropped behind a watermark and counted.
  4. Where do bad records go? A dead-letter topic or table with the error, the raw payload and the source offset, plus an alert on its rate.
  5. How do we replay? From which store, how far back, at what rate, and what stops the replay from overwriting newer data.

Step 7 in practice: trade-off sentences

Interviewers grade the trade-off, not the tool. Use one sentence shape:

“Micro-batches every 30 seconds buy us idempotent, transactional table commits at the cost of about a minute of freshness. We rejected per-record streaming into the warehouse because each record would be a commit.”

Then stress-test: “At 10x the peak, the Kafka cluster holds because it is sized by disk; the stream job falls behind, lag grows, and maxOffsetsPerTrigger keeps each batch bounded while autoscaling catches up.”

What interviewers grade, and the mistakes that cost the round

Graded dimension Strong signal Common mistake
Requirements and SLOs Names consumer, volume, freshness and completeness with numbers Picks tools in the first minute
Contracts and modeling Defines keys, grain, event time, schema owner Treats “the data” as one undifferentiated blob
Correctness Scopes guarantees to boundaries; idempotent sinks; reconciliation Claims end-to-end exactly-once with no boundary named
Scale and reliability Partitioning, skew, backpressure, checkpoints, replay Forgets replay and backfill entirely
Operations and quality Freshness, volume, lag, quality assertions, cost Monitors jobs, not data
Trade-offs and communication Every choice has a cost and a rejected alternative Lists features of a tool instead of reasons

Framework interview questions

1. You are asked to "design a real-time analytics pipeline". What do you do in the first five minutes?

I do not draw anything yet. I ask who consumes the output and what decision it drives, the event volume at peak, how fresh the data must be and how complete, whether source records change after they are emitted, and how far back we must be able to reprocess. Then I restate the binding constraint, for example “dashboards two minutes fresh, finance numbers final after one hour”, and get agreement on it. Those answers decide batch versus streaming and how much exactly-once machinery is justified; the tool names come after.

2. How do you choose between batch and streaming?

From the freshness target and the decision it serves, not from preference. If the consumer acts on data within seconds or minutes (fraud, alerting, operational dashboards), stream. If the consumer reads daily or hourly (finance, most BI), batch is cheaper to build, test, backfill and operate. A common middle ground is micro-batch on a schedule, such as Spark Structured Streaming with trigger(availableNow=True) every 15 minutes, which keeps one code path and gets incremental processing without an always-on cluster. I also say what I give up: streaming costs state management, late-data handling and on-call load; batch costs freshness.

3. Walk me through a capacity estimate for 2 billion events a day.

Two billion over 86,400 seconds is about 23,000 events per second on average. At 1 KB an event that is 23 MB/s, and with a 3x evening peak about 70 MB/s. Raw volume is 2 TB a day; seven days in Kafka at replication 3 is 42 TB of broker disk, so retention, not throughput, sizes the cluster. If Parquet compresses the JSON 5x, the lake grows 400 GB a day, roughly 146 TB a year, which justifies lifecycle tiering. Fourteen partitions is the floor at a 5 MB/s per-partition budget, and I would pick 24 or 48 for consumer parallelism and growth. I would flag the compression ratio and partition budget as numbers to measure.

4. What is a data contract, and what goes in one?

A data contract is the producer’s promise about a dataset that consumers can build on. It names the owner, the schema and its compatibility rule (for example backward compatible in the schema registry), the grain, the keys (a unique event id for dedup and an entity key for ordering and upserts), the event-time field and its time zone, allowed values, nullability, and the freshness and volume a consumer can expect. It turns a breaking change into a failed CI check or a rejected registration instead of a broken dashboard.

5. Freshness and completeness: why state both?

Because a pipeline can meet one and fail the other. A dashboard can show data from 30 seconds ago (fresh) while 2% of the last hour’s mobile events are still buffered on phones (incomplete). If I only promise freshness, consumers treat the latest hour as final and make decisions on partial numbers. Stating “fresh within 2 minutes, 99.9% complete 15 minutes after the hour, final at T+1 day” tells consumers when a number can still move, and it forces the design to decide how late data updates published results.

Under the hood: the building blocks, in data-flow order

Ingestion: how data enters the platform

Pattern How it works Captures deletes Source load Typical use
Full extract SELECT * on a schedule, replace the target Yes, by absence High Small reference tables
Incremental query WHERE updated_at > :high_water_mark No Medium Sources without log access
Log-based CDC Read the WAL or binlog (Debezium) Yes Low OLTP replication to the lake
Event push Apps send events through an SDK or collector Not applicable None Clickstream, telemetry
File drop Partners write files to object storage or SFTP By convention None B2B feeds, exports
API pull Poll a SaaS API with pagination and rate limits Rarely External CRM, ads, payments data

The incremental-query row hides a race that interviewers like: a transaction that started before the high-water mark was read but commits after it gets an updated_at below the mark and is skipped forever. Log-based CDC reads committed changes in commit order, so it has no such gap. The data modeling guide covers CDC mechanics in detail, including replication-slot retention.

For files and APIs, land the raw bytes first, unchanged, in an object-store prefix keyed by source and arrival time. Parsing comes after. If the parser has a bug, you re-parse from the landing zone instead of asking a partner to resend last month.

The log: Kafka as the system’s buffer and replay store

A durable log decouples producers from consumers in time. Producers write at their rate, consumers read at theirs, and the log holds the difference. Most data platform designs put one in the middle for three reasons: it absorbs bursts, it lets several consumers read the same events independently, and it is the first replay store.

 topic: orders  (3 partitions, replication factor 3)

 producer: key = order_id ──► partition = hash(key) % 3
                               (Kafka's default partitioner uses murmur2)
 partition 0  [o1 o4 o7 ...]  leader broker 1, followers 2, 3
 partition 1  [o2 o5 o8 ...]  leader broker 2, followers 3, 1
 partition 2  [o3 o6 o9 ...]  leader broker 3, followers 1, 2
               offset 0 1 2 ... append-only, ordered within a partition only

 consumer group "lake-writer"        consumer group "fraud"
   consumer A ◄─ partition 0, 1        consumer X ◄─ partition 0
   consumer B ◄─ partition 2           consumer Y ◄─ partition 1
                                       consumer Z ◄─ partition 2
 each group tracks its own committed offsets in __consumer_offsets

Read it from the top. The producer hashes the message key to pick a partition, so every event for o1 lands in partition 0 and stays in order relative to other o1 events. Ordering holds within a partition only; there is no global order across the topic. Each partition has a leader that takes writes and followers that copy it. A consumer group splits the partitions among its members, so a group can have at most as many active consumers as there are partitions, and the extra members sit idle. Each group commits its own offsets, which is why the fraud team and the lake writer can read the same topic at different speeds.

The settings below decide whether an acknowledged event can be lost:

Setting Scope Default Design choice
replication.factor Topic 1 (default.replication.factor) 3 in production
min.insync.replicas Topic / broker 1 2 with RF 3: a write needs two copies
acks Producer all since Kafka 3.0 all; 1 loses data if the leader dies before followers copy
enable.idempotence Producer true since Kafka 3.0 Keep it; retries no longer create duplicates in the log
retention.ms Topic 604800000 (7 days) Sized from the replay window and disk
isolation.level Consumer read_uncommitted read_committed when producers use transactions

acks=all with min.insync.replicas=2 and RF 3 means an acknowledged write exists on at least two brokers, and the cluster tolerates one broker loss without refusing writes. The cost is write latency: the leader waits for a follower. The idempotent producer attaches a producer id and a sequence number per partition, so a retried batch that the broker already has is discarded rather than appended twice. It removes duplicates caused by producer retries; it does nothing for an application that sends the same business event twice, which is why the contract still carries an event_id.

Choosing the key. The key decides ordering and load. Key by the entity whose events must stay ordered (order_id, account_id, device_id). If one key dominates, such as one huge merchant, its partition becomes hot. The fixes are a composite key (merchant_id plus a bucket) when per-merchant order does not matter, or a dedicated topic for the outlier. Increasing the partition count later changes hash(key) % n, so keys move partitions and per-key ordering breaks across the change. Over-provision partitions up front instead.

Processing: batch, micro-batch and continuous

Model Unit Latency State Failure recovery Engines
Batch A bounded input, often a date partition Minutes to hours Recomputed each run Re-run the partition Spark, dbt, Trino
Micro-batch A range of offsets per trigger Seconds to minutes Checkpointed state store Replay the last uncommitted batch Spark Structured Streaming
Continuous One record at a time Milliseconds to seconds Keyed state with periodic snapshots Restore snapshot, rewind sources Flink, Kafka Streams

The micro-batch engine is worth knowing in detail, because its recovery rule is what the demo exercises:

 Spark Structured Streaming, one micro-batch (batch N)

  1. plan    ── read latest Kafka offsets ──► write offsets/N to checkpoint
  2. execute ── read offsets(N-1)..offsets(N) ──► transform ──► sink
  3. commit  ── write commits/N to checkpoint
                ▲
                └─ crash here: offsets/N exists, commits/N does not.
                   On restart, Spark re-runs batch N with the SAME offsets.

The offsets log is written before the batch runs (a write-ahead log) and the commit log after the sink returns. If the process dies between steps 2 and 3, the restart finds an offset entry without a commit entry and re-executes batch N over exactly the same offset range. The engine guarantees the replay is the same input. Whether the output is duplicated depends entirely on the sink. A sink that appends writes the batch twice; a sink that upserts on a key writes the same final state twice, which is the same as writing it once.

Event time and watermarks. For aggregations by event time, the engine has to decide when a window is complete. A watermark is that decision: “no event older than the maximum event time seen minus 10 minutes is expected”. withWatermark("event_ts", "10 minutes") lets Spark finalise windows and drop state behind the watermark. Events older than the watermark are dropped by stateful operators. That is a correctness trade-off you should state: a larger delay keeps more state and publishes later; a smaller one drops more late data. Count the late events you drop, or route them to a correction path, rather than losing them silently.

State. Windowed aggregations, stream-stream joins and streaming deduplication keep state per key. Spark’s default state store provider is HDFSBackedStateStoreProvider, which holds state in executor JVM memory and checkpoints it to files. For large state, switch spark.sql.streaming.stateStore.providerClass to org.apache.spark.sql.execution.streaming.state.RocksDBStateStoreProvider, which keeps it in native RocksDB instances outside the JVM heap. Spark 3.5 also added dropDuplicatesWithinWatermark, which deduplicates on a key while bounding state with the watermark.

Delivery semantics: where exactly-once actually lives

Guarantee Meaning How you get it Cost
At-most-once Each event is processed zero or one times Commit offsets before processing Data loss on crash
At-least-once Each event is processed one or more times Commit offsets after the sink succeeds Duplicates on replay
Effectively-once Each event affects the output once At-least-once delivery plus an idempotent or transactional sink Sink design and keys

“Exactly-once” is always scoped to a boundary. The mechanisms differ by boundary:

Boundary Mechanism
Producer to Kafka Idempotent producer (sequence numbers per partition)
Kafka to Kafka Kafka transactions: consume, produce and commit offsets atomically; readers use read_committed
Kafka to a table format Replayable source, deterministic batch, idempotent MERGE or a sink that records the batch id it committed
Kafka to a database Write the rows and the consumed offset in one database transaction
Anything to an external API Idempotency key on the request; the API must deduplicate
Flink to Kafka or files Two-phase commit tied to checkpoints (KafkaSink with DeliveryGuarantee.EXACTLY_ONCE)

The sentence interviewers want: “Delivery is at-least-once everywhere; I make the effect exactly-once at the sink by upserting on a deterministic key, so a replay rewrites the same rows.”

Storage: lake, warehouse and lakehouse tables

A plain data lake is a directory of Parquet files: cheap, open, and with no transactions. Two writers can interleave, a reader can see half a job’s output, and an update means rewriting a partition by hand. A warehouse gives transactions and fast SQL but stores data in its own format, so every other engine pays to copy it out. An open table format (Iceberg, Hudi, Delta Lake) adds a transaction log over Parquet files in object storage, which is what a lakehouse is.

 Iceberg table commit: an atomic swap of one pointer

 catalog: shop.orders ──► metadata/v12.metadata.json   (current)
                               │ snapshots: [..., s11, s12]
                               ▼
                         snap-s12 manifest list (.avro)
                          ├─► manifest A (.avro) ──► day=2026-10-28/00001.parquet
                          │                      ──► day=2026-10-28/00002.parquet
                          └─► manifest B (.avro) ──► day=2026-10-27/00417.parquet

 writer: write new data files ──► write manifests ──► write v13.metadata.json
         ──► ask catalog: "swap v12 → v13 if current is still v12"
             success: readers see s13 atomically
             conflict: re-read, re-validate, retry (commit.retry.num-retries)

Writers never modify files in place. A commit writes new files and then compare-and-swaps the catalog pointer to a new metadata file. Readers resolve the pointer once and read a consistent snapshot, so they never see a half write. Concurrent writers use optimistic concurrency: the loser of the swap re-reads, checks that its change does not conflict, and retries up to commit.retry.num-retries times (default 4). Because each commit is a metadata file and a manifest, a design that commits every second creates thousands of snapshots and tiny files an hour. That is why streaming into a table format uses micro-batches of tens of seconds or more, plus scheduled compaction and snapshot expiry.

Choice Option A Option B Rule of thumb
Format of record Warehouse-native Open table format Open format when several engines read it or cost of copies matters
Write mode for upserts Copy-on-write: rewrite affected files Merge-on-read: write delete files, merge at read MOR for frequent small updates, COW for read-heavy tables
Partitioning By event date By ingestion date Event date for queries; handle late data by rewriting old partitions
File size Small, frequent commits Fewer, larger files Target hundreds of MB; Iceberg’s write.target-file-size-bytes defaults to 512 MB

The open table formats comparison goes deeper on how Iceberg, Hudi and Delta Lake differ.

Serving: pick the store by the query

Query pattern Store Why
Ad hoc SQL over months of history Trino, Spark SQL, or a warehouse over the lakehouse Scans columnar files, prunes partitions
Sub-second aggregates for dashboards ClickHouse, Apache Pinot, Apache Druid Pre-aggregation and columnar indexes
Point lookup by key in milliseconds Redis, DynamoDB, Cassandra Key-value access, no scans
Full-text and log search Elasticsearch or OpenSearch Inverted indexes
Time series per device TimescaleDB, InfluxDB Time-partitioned storage and downsampling
Operational tools need warehouse data Reverse ETL to the SaaS tool Pushes rows to where the user works

Most designs have two or three serving stores fed from one lakehouse. Say which is the source of truth (usually silver or gold in the lakehouse) and which are disposable projections you can rebuild by replay.

Orchestration and backfills

An orchestrator (Airflow, Dagster, or a managed equivalent) runs batch steps in dependency order, retries them and records what ran. Two properties make a DAG safe to retry and to backfill:

Tasks are idempotent per partition. Each run writes one logical partition, for example order_date = 2026-10-27, with an overwrite or a MERGE, never a blind append. Re-running the same date gives the same result.

Inputs are pinned. A run for 2026-10-27 reads the inputs for that date, not “everything new since the last run”. Then a backfill of last March is the same code with a different date, and it can run in parallel with a separate compute pool so it does not starve the live schedule.

For streaming jobs, the backfill is a replay: a second instance of the job with its own checkpoint reads a historical range (from the lake if the log has expired) and writes through the same idempotent sink.

Data quality and observability

Monitor five signals per dataset, not just job status:

Signal Check Example alert
Freshness Max event time versus now orders silver is 45 minutes behind a 10-minute SLO
Volume Row count versus same hour last week Rows dropped 50% day over day, or zero rows
Schema Columns and types versus the contract A new nullable column, or a type change
Validity Null rates, ranges, enums, uniqueness amount < 0 in 0.3% of rows
Reconciliation Totals against the source of record Lakehouse revenue differs from the ledger by more than 0.01%

Place the checks as gates. Bronze warns and continues, because blocking raw ingestion loses data. Silver and gold halt the publish step, so consumers keep the last good version instead of reading a bad one. Tie each alert to the dataset’s owner, and record lineage (OpenLineage, a catalog such as DataHub or OpenMetadata) so the alert can say which dashboards are affected.

Architecture patterns in one table

Pattern Idea Choose when Cost
Lambda Batch layer for correctness, speed layer for freshness, merged at serving A legacy batch path must stay and fresh numbers are also needed Two code paths that drift
Kappa One streaming path; reprocess by replaying the log Logic is the same for live and history, and replay is affordable Long log retention or lake replay
Medallion Bronze raw, silver cleaned and conformed, gold business-ready Almost every lakehouse Extra copies; layers without contracts become sprawl
CDC Stream database changes from the log Database is the source of truth Slot and binlog retention, schema changes
Outbox Service writes business row and event in one transaction; CDC publishes the event A service must update its DB and emit an event atomically One more table and relay
Event sourcing Store events; derive state Audit, ledgers, undo Snapshots, ever-growing logs, schema evolution of history
Data mesh Domains own data products on a shared platform Many domains, a central team is the bottleneck Needs strong standards and platform investment

The data modeling guide’s Lambda versus Kappa section walks both architectures step by step.

Building-block interview questions

6. Why put Kafka between the database and the lake instead of writing straight to the lake?

Three reasons. It decouples rates: a slow lake commit or a compaction does not push back on the source. It allows several independent consumers, such as the lake writer, a search indexer and a fraud service, to read the same changes with their own offsets. And it is a replay buffer: if a bug corrupts silver, I can rewind a consumer group and reprocess the retained days. The cost is another system to operate and size, mostly by retention disk. For a single consumer with hourly freshness I might skip it and land CDC files directly.

7. How does Kafka guarantee ordering, and when does it not?

Ordering is per partition. The producer picks the partition from the message key, so all events with one key go to one partition in send order, and a consumer reads a partition in offset order. There is no order across partitions. Ordering breaks if producers use no key, if the partition count is increased (keys rehash to different partitions), or if a non-idempotent producer with several in-flight requests retries a failed batch after a later one succeeded. The idempotent producer, the default since Kafka 3.0, preserves order for up to five in-flight requests.

8. Explain at-least-once versus exactly-once in a Spark streaming job writing to a table.

Spark’s source and checkpoint give replayable, deterministic input: the offsets for batch N are written before it runs, and on restart an uncommitted batch N is re-run over the same offsets. So delivery to the sink is at-least-once. The effect is exactly-once only if the sink tolerates the replay. An Iceberg MERGE on the entity key does: replaying the batch writes the same final rows. A plain append does not: it adds the batch twice. I would show this with a deleted commit file, which is what the demo below does.

9. What is a watermark, and what does it cost?

A watermark is the engine’s rule for when event-time results are final: the maximum event time seen minus an allowed delay. It lets the engine emit windows and discard state. The cost is late data: events older than the watermark are dropped by stateful operators. A long delay keeps more state and publishes later; a short one drops more. I size it from the observed lateness distribution of the slowest source, count what is dropped, and route very late events to a batch correction job if the numbers must be exact.

10. How does an open table format make a commit atomic on object storage?

Files are immutable. A writer writes its new data files and manifests, then a new metadata file, and finally asks the catalog to swap the table’s pointer from the old metadata file to the new one, only if the pointer has not moved. That compare-and-swap is the commit. Readers resolve the pointer once and see a full snapshot. If another writer moved the pointer first, the loser re-reads, checks for conflicts with what changed, and retries. Object storage only has to store files; the catalog provides the atomic step.

11. How do you make a batch pipeline safe to re-run and to backfill?

Each task writes one logical partition with overwrite or MERGE, never append, so a re-run replaces rather than adds. Each run reads inputs pinned to its logical date, not “since last run”, so a backfill is the same code with a different date. Backfills run on separate compute, throttled, so the live schedule keeps its SLO. And I check the result with the same quality gates, including a reconciliation against the source for the backfilled range.

12. What would you monitor on a new pipeline on day one?

Freshness (max event time against now), volume against the same period last week, schema drift against the contract, a handful of validity checks on keys and amounts, and consumer lag for streaming jobs. Job success alone is not enough: the worst incidents are jobs that succeed with zero or half the rows. Each alert has an owner and lineage, so it says which consumers are affected. P1 alerts page someone; data-quality warnings open tickets.

Hands-on demo: an exactly-once Kafka to Iceberg pipeline

The claim to prove: a replayed micro-batch duplicates rows in an append sink and leaves an idempotent MERGE sink unchanged. The demo also shows two contract rules from step 3: duplicates from producer retries are removed, and a stale event that arrives late does not overwrite newer state.

 produce_orders.py ──► Kafka sd_blog_orders (3 partitions, key = order_id)
                                │  maxOffsetsPerTrigger = 400
                                ▼
                     orders_stream.py  (Structured Streaming, availableNow)
                       foreachBatch(batch_df, batch_id)
                         ├─► append ──► sd.shop.orders_append   (naive)
                         └─► dedup in batch, MERGE on order_id
                                    ──► sd.shop.orders           (idempotent)
                       checkpoint: /tmp/sd_blog/checkpoints/orders
                                   offsets/N  commits/N

Step 1: create the topic

docker exec kafka kafka-topics --bootstrap-server kafka:29092 \
  --create --topic sd_blog_orders --partitions 3 --replication-factor 1

Replication factor 1 is only because the playground runs one broker.

Step 2: the producer

Run 1 publishes 1,000 orders plus 50 exact copies, the duplicates a producer retry creates when an acknowledgement is lost after the broker stored the write. Run 2 publishes 500 new orders, 30 SHIPPED updates for earlier orders, and 10 PENDING events whose updated_ts is older than the stored PLACED version.

"""Publish order events to Kafka for the system design demo.

Run 1 sends 1,000 new orders plus 50 exact duplicates, the way a producer
retry after a lost ack would. Run 2 sends 500 new orders, 30 status updates
for run-1 orders, and 10 stale updates that arrive out of order.
"""
import sys
from datetime import datetime, timedelta

from pyspark.sql import SparkSession

TOPIC = "sd_blog_orders"
BOOTSTRAP = "kafka:29092"
BASE = datetime(2026, 10, 28, 10, 0, 0)


def order(i, status, updated):
    return {
        "event_id": f"o{i:05d}-{status}",
        "order_id": f"o{i:05d}",
        "customer_id": f"c{i % 97:03d}",
        "amount": round(10 + (i * 7.31) % 490, 2),
        "status": status,
        "order_ts": (BASE + timedelta(seconds=i * 2)).isoformat(),
        "updated_ts": updated.isoformat(),
    }


def run_1():
    rows = [order(i, "PLACED", BASE + timedelta(seconds=i * 2))
            for i in range(1, 1001)]
    return rows + rows[:50]                       # retried sends


def run_2():
    rows = [order(i, "PLACED", BASE + timedelta(seconds=i * 2))
            for i in range(1001, 1501)]
    shipped_at = BASE + timedelta(hours=2)
    rows += [order(i, "SHIPPED", shipped_at) for i in range(1, 31)]
    # Older than the PLACED event already stored: must not win.
    rows += [order(i, "PENDING", BASE - timedelta(hours=1))
             for i in range(31, 41)]
    return rows


if __name__ == "__main__":
    spark = SparkSession.builder.appName("sd-produce-orders").getOrCreate()
    rows = run_1() if sys.argv[1] == "1" else run_2()
    df = spark.createDataFrame(rows)
    (df.selectExpr("order_id AS key", "to_json(struct(*)) AS value")
       .write.format("kafka")
       .option("kafka.bootstrap.servers", BOOTSTRAP)
       .option("topic", TOPIC)
       .save())
    print(f"published {len(rows)} events to {TOPIC}")
    spark.stop()

Step 3: the streaming job

Inside foreachBatch, each micro-batch goes to both sinks. Before the MERGE, a window keeps one row per order_id within the batch, the newest by updated_ts. That step is required, not a nicety: a MERGE whose source has two rows for one target row fails, as the last step shows. The MERGE itself only updates when the incoming version is newer, which is what rejects the stale events.

"""Kafka -> Spark Structured Streaming -> Iceberg, with an idempotent sink.

Each micro-batch is written twice: a naive append to orders_append, and a
deduplicating MERGE into orders keyed on order_id. Replaying a batch shows
which of the two sinks survives a crash between write and checkpoint commit.
"""
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession, Window
from pyspark.sql import functions as F
from pyspark.sql.types import (DoubleType, StringType, StructField,
                               StructType, TimestampType)

WAREHOUSE = "file:///tmp/sd_blog/warehouse"
CHECKPOINT = "file:///tmp/sd_blog/checkpoints/orders"

spark = (
    SparkSession.builder.appName("sd-orders-stream")
    .config("spark.sql.extensions",
            "org.apache.iceberg.spark.extensions."
            "IcebergSparkSessionExtensions")
    .config("spark.serializer",
            "org.apache.spark.serializer.KryoSerializer")
    .config("spark.sql.catalog.sd", "org.apache.iceberg.spark.SparkCatalog")
    .config("spark.sql.catalog.sd.type", "hadoop")
    .config("spark.sql.catalog.sd.warehouse", WAREHOUSE)
    .config("spark.sql.shuffle.partitions", "4")
    .getOrCreate()
)

spark.sql("CREATE NAMESPACE IF NOT EXISTS sd.shop")
for table in ("orders", "orders_append"):
    spark.sql(f"""
        CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS sd.shop.{table} (
            order_id STRING, customer_id STRING, amount DOUBLE,
            status STRING, order_ts TIMESTAMP, updated_ts TIMESTAMP,
            kafka_partition INT, kafka_offset BIGINT)
        USING iceberg
        PARTITIONED BY (days(order_ts))""")

schema = StructType([
    StructField("event_id", StringType()),
    StructField("order_id", StringType()),
    StructField("customer_id", StringType()),
    StructField("amount", DoubleType()),
    StructField("status", StringType()),
    StructField("order_ts", TimestampType()),
    StructField("updated_ts", TimestampType()),
])

events = (
    spark.readStream.format("kafka")
    .option("kafka.bootstrap.servers", "kafka:29092")
    .option("subscribe", "sd_blog_orders")
    .option("startingOffsets", "earliest")
    .option("maxOffsetsPerTrigger", "400")
    .load()
    .select(F.from_json(F.col("value").cast("string"), schema).alias("e"),
            F.col("partition").alias("kafka_partition"),
            F.col("offset").alias("kafka_offset"))
    .select("e.*", "kafka_partition", "kafka_offset")
    .drop("event_id")
)


def write_batch(batch_df, batch_id):
    batch_df.persist()
    batch_df.writeTo("sd.shop.orders_append").append()

    # Keep the newest version of each order inside the batch, so MERGE
    # never sees two source rows for one target row.
    latest = Window.partitionBy("order_id").orderBy(
        F.col("updated_ts").desc(), F.col("kafka_offset").desc())
    (batch_df.withColumn("rn", F.row_number().over(latest))
        .where("rn = 1").drop("rn")
        .createOrReplaceTempView("batch_orders"))
    batch_df.sparkSession.sql("""
        MERGE INTO sd.shop.orders t
        USING batch_orders s
        ON t.order_id = s.order_id
        WHEN MATCHED AND s.updated_ts > t.updated_ts THEN UPDATE SET *
        WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT *""")
    print(f"batch {batch_id}: {batch_df.count()} events")
    batch_df.unpersist()


query = (
    events.writeStream
    .foreachBatch(write_batch)
    .option("checkpointLocation", CHECKPOINT)
    .trigger(availableNow=True)
    .start()
)
query.awaitTermination()

for table in ("orders", "orders_append"):
    # foreachBatch writes through a cloned session with its own catalog
    # cache; without REFRESH this session still sees the empty table.
    spark.sql(f"REFRESH TABLE sd.shop.{table}")
    n = spark.table(f"sd.shop.{table}").count()
    print(f"{table}: {n} rows")
spark.sql("""SELECT status, count(*) AS orders FROM sd.shop.orders
             GROUP BY status ORDER BY status""").show()
spark.stop()

The MERGE table now has 1,500 orders: 30 moved to SHIPPED, and the 10 stale PENDING events were rejected by s.updated_ts > t.updated_ts, so no order shows PENDING. Step 5: why the in-batch dedup matters

Remove the window and feed a MERGE two copies of one key, and Spark refuses the whole statement:

"""Show what MERGE does when one micro-batch carries the same key twice."""
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession

spark = (
    SparkSession.builder.appName("sd-merge-dup")
    .config("spark.sql.extensions",
            "org.apache.iceberg.spark.extensions."
            "IcebergSparkSessionExtensions")
    .config("spark.serializer",
            "org.apache.spark.serializer.KryoSerializer")
    .config("spark.sql.catalog.sd", "org.apache.iceberg.spark.SparkCatalog")
    .config("spark.sql.catalog.sd.type", "hadoop")
    .config("spark.sql.catalog.sd.warehouse", "file:///tmp/sd_blog/warehouse")
    .getOrCreate()
)
spark.sql("CREATE NAMESPACE IF NOT EXISTS sd.shop")
spark.sql("DROP TABLE IF EXISTS sd.shop.merge_dup PURGE")
spark.sql("CREATE TABLE sd.shop.merge_dup (order_id STRING, status STRING) "
          "USING iceberg")
spark.sql("INSERT INTO sd.shop.merge_dup VALUES ('o00001', 'PLACED')")
spark.createDataFrame(
    [("o00001", "SHIPPED"), ("o00001", "SHIPPED")],
    "order_id STRING, status STRING",
).createOrReplaceTempView("retried_batch")
try:
    spark.sql("""
        MERGE INTO sd.shop.merge_dup t USING retried_batch s
        ON t.order_id = s.order_id
        WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET *
        WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT *""")
except Exception as err:                     # the failure is the point
    code = "MERGE_CARDINALITY_VIOLATION"
    print(f"MERGE failed: {code}" if code in str(err) else err)
spark.sql("DROP TABLE sd.shop.merge_dup PURGE")
spark.stop()

MERGE failed: MERGE_CARDINALITY_VIOLATION

The full error is SparkRuntimeException: [MERGE_CARDINALITY_VIOLATION] The ON search condition of the MERGE statement matched a single row from the target table with multiple rows of the source table. In a streaming job this fails the batch, and every restart replays the same batch and fails again, so the query is stuck until the code changes. Deduplicate inside each batch before merging.

What the demo proves, and a pitfall it found

Replay is the engine’s job; idempotency is yours. Spark re-ran batch 2 with identical input, as its checkpoint protocol promises. Only the sink design decided whether that produced duplicates.

The catalog cache pitfall. The first version of orders_stream.py counted the tables at the end without REFRESH TABLE and printed 0 rows for both, although the data was there. Structured Streaming runs each query in a cloned SparkSession, and foreachBatch hands you a DataFrame bound to that clone, whose Iceberg catalog has its own table cache. The driver session still held the table it loaded at creation time, before any batch committed. REFRESH TABLE invalidates the cached entry. A monitoring job that reads row counts from a long-lived session can report stale numbers in the same way.
