The demo also shows two contract rules from step 3: duplicates from producer retries are removed, and a stale event that arrives late does not overwrite newer state. produce_orders.py ──► Kafka sd_blog_orders (3 partitions, key = order_id) │ maxOffsetsPerTrigger = 400 ▼ orders_stream.py (Structured Streaming, availableNow) foreachBatch(batch_df, batch_id) ├─► append ──► sd.shop.orders_append (naive) └─► dedup in batch, MERGE on order_id ──► sd.shop.orders (idempotent) checkpoint: /tmp/sd_blog/checkpoints/orders offsets/N commits/N Step 1: create the topic docker exec kafka kafka-topics --bootstrap-server kafka:29092 \ --create --topic sd_blog_orders --partitions 3 --replication-factor 1 Replication factor 1 is only because the playground runs one broker. Step 2: the producer Run 1 publishes 1,000 orders plus 50 exact copies, the duplicates a producer retry creates when an acknowledgement is lost after the broker stored the write. Run 2 publishes 500 new orders, 30 SHIPPED updates for earlier orders, and 10 PENDING events whose updated_ts is older than the stored PLACED version. """Publish order events to Kafka for the system design demo. Run 1 sends 1,000 new orders plus 50 exact duplicates, the way a producer retry after a lost ack would. Run 2 sends 500 new orders, 30 status updates for run-1 orders, and 10 stale updates that arrive out of order. """ import sys from datetime import datetime, timedelta from pyspark.sql import SparkSession TOPIC = "sd_blog_orders" BOOTSTRAP = "kafka:29092" BASE = datetime(2026, 10, 28, 10, 0, 0) def order(i, status, updated): return { "event_id": f"o{i:05d}-{status}", "order_id": f"o{i:05d}", "customer_id": f"c{i % 97:03d}", "amount": round(10 + (i * 7.31) % 490, 2), "status": status, "order_ts": (BASE + timedelta(seconds=i * 2)).isoformat(), "updated_ts": updated.isoformat(), } def run_1(): rows = [order(i, "PLACED", BASE + timedelta(seconds=i * 2)) for i in range(1, 1001)] return rows + rows[:50] # retried sends def run_2(): rows = [order(i, "PLACED", BASE + timedelta(seconds=i * 2)) for i in range(1001, 1501)] shipped_at = BASE + timedelta(hours=2) rows += [order(i, "SHIPPED", shipped_at) for i in range(1, 31)] # Older than the PLACED event already stored: must not win. rows += [order(i, "PENDING", BASE - timedelta(hours=1)) for i in range(31, 41)] return rows if __name__ == "__main__": spark = SparkSession.builder.appName("sd-produce-orders").getOrCreate() rows = run_1() if sys.argv[1] == "1" else run_2() df = spark.createDataFrame(rows) (df.selectExpr("order_id AS key", "to_json(struct(*)) AS value") .write.format("kafka") .option("kafka.bootstrap.servers", BOOTSTRAP) .option("topic", TOPIC) .save()) print(f"published {len(rows)} events to {TOPIC}") spark.stop() Step 3: the streaming job Inside foreachBatch, each micro-batch goes to both sinks. Before the MERGE, a window keeps one row per order_id within the batch, the newest by updated_ts. That step is required, not a nicety: a MERGE whose source has two rows for one target row fails, as the last step shows. The MERGE itself only updates when the incoming version is newer, which is what rejects the stale events. """Kafka -> Spark Structured Streaming -> Iceberg, with an idempotent sink. Each micro-batch is written twice: a naive append to orders_append, and a deduplicating MERGE into orders keyed on order_id. Replaying a batch shows which of the two sinks survives a crash between write and checkpoint commit. """ from pyspark.sql import SparkSession, Window from pyspark.sql import functions as F from pyspark.sql.types import (DoubleType, StringType, StructField, StructType, TimestampType) WAREHOUSE = "file:///tmp/sd_blog/warehouse" CHECKPOINT = "file:///tmp/sd_blog/checkpoints/orders" spark = ( SparkSession.builder.appName("sd-orders-stream") .config("spark.sql.extensions", "org.apache.iceberg.spark.extensions." "IcebergSparkSessionExtensions") .config("spark.serializer", "org.apache.spark.serializer.KryoSerializer") .config("spark.sql.catalog.sd", "org.apache.iceberg.spark.SparkCatalog") .config("spark.sql.catalog.sd.type", "hadoop") .config("spark.sql.catalog.sd.warehouse", WAREHOUSE) .config("spark.sql.shuffle.partitions", "4") .getOrCreate() ) spark.sql("CREATE NAMESPACE IF NOT EXISTS sd.shop") for table in ("orders", "orders_append"): spark.sql(f""" CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS sd.shop.{table} ( order_id STRING, customer_id STRING, amount DOUBLE, status STRING, order_ts TIMESTAMP, updated_ts TIMESTAMP, kafka_partition INT, kafka_offset BIGINT) USING iceberg PARTITIONED BY (days(order_ts))""") schema = StructType([ StructField("event_id", StringType()), StructField("order_id", StringType()), StructField("customer_id", StringType()), StructField("amount", DoubleType()), StructField("status", StringType()), StructField("order_ts", TimestampType()), StructField("updated_ts", TimestampType()), ]) events = ( spark.readStream.format("kafka") .option("kafka.bootstrap.servers", "kafka:29092") .option("subscribe", "sd_blog_orders") .option("startingOffsets", "earliest") .option("maxOffsetsPerTrigger", "400") .load() .select(F.from_json(F.col("value").cast("string"), schema).alias("e"), F.col("partition").alias("kafka_partition"), F.col("offset").alias("kafka_offset")) .select("e.*", "kafka_partition", "kafka_offset") .drop("event_id") ) def write_batch(batch_df, batch_id): batch_df.persist() batch_df.writeTo("sd.shop.orders_append").append() # Keep the newest version of each order inside the batch, so MERGE # never sees two source rows for one target row. latest = Window.partitionBy("order_id").orderBy( F.col("updated_ts").desc(), F.col("kafka_offset").desc()) (batch_df.withColumn("rn", F.row_number().over(latest)) .where("rn = 1").drop("rn") .createOrReplaceTempView("batch_orders")) batch_df.sparkSession.sql(""" MERGE INTO sd.shop.orders t USING batch_orders s ON t.order_id = s.order_id WHEN MATCHED AND s.updated_ts > t.updated_ts THEN UPDATE SET * WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT *""") print(f"batch {batch_id}: {batch_df.count()} events") batch_df.unpersist() query = ( events.writeStream .foreachBatch(write_batch) .option("checkpointLocation", CHECKPOINT) .trigger(availableNow=True) .start() ) query.awaitTermination() for table in ("orders", "orders_append"): # foreachBatch writes through a cloned session with its own catalog # cache; without REFRESH this session still sees the empty table. spark.sql(f"REFRESH TABLE sd.shop.{table}") n = spark.table(f"sd.shop.{table}").count() print(f"{table}: {n} rows") spark.sql("""SELECT status, count(*) AS orders FROM sd.shop.orders GROUP BY status ORDER BY status""").show() spark.stop() Step 4: run, crash, replay Copy both scripts into the container and publish run 1: docker cp produce_orders.py spark-master:/tmp/ docker cp orders_stream.py spark-master:/tmp/ docker exec spark-master bash -c '$SPARK_HOME/bin/spark-submit \ --master "local[2]" \ --conf spark.eventLog.enabled=false --conf spark.ui.enabled=false \ /tmp/produce_orders.py 1' published 1050 events to sd_blog_orders Run the streaming job: docker exec spark-master bash -c '$SPARK_HOME/bin/spark-submit \ --master "local[2]" \ --conf spark.eventLog.enabled=false --conf spark.ui.enabled=false \ --jars $(ls $ICEBERG_HOME/iceberg-spark-runtime*.jar) \ /tmp/orders_stream.py' batch 0: 398 events batch 1: 398 events batch 2: 254 events orders: 1000 rows orders_append: 1050 rows +------+------+ |status|orders| +------+------+ |PLACED| 1000| +------+------+ maxOffsetsPerTrigger = 400 split the 1,050 events into three batches. The append table holds all 1,050 events, including the 50 duplicates. The MERGE table holds 1,000 orders, one per order_id. Now simulate a crash after the sink wrote batch 2 but before Spark recorded the commit. Delete the commit entry (and its checksum file, or the next commit fails with FileAlreadyExistsException ... .2.crc already exists) and run the same job again with no new data: docker exec spark-master rm /tmp/sd_blog/checkpoints/orders/commits/2 \ /tmp/sd_blog/checkpoints/orders/commits/.2.crc docker exec spark-master bash -c '$SPARK_HOME/bin/spark-submit \ --master "local[2]" \ --conf spark.eventLog.enabled=false --conf spark.ui.enabled=false \ --jars $(ls $ICEBERG_HOME/iceberg-spark-runtime*.jar) \ /tmp/orders_stream.py' batch 2: 254 events orders: 1000 rows orders_append: 1304 rows +------+------+ |status|orders| +------+------+ |PLACED| 1000| +------+------+ Spark found offsets/2 without commits/2 and re-ran batch 2 over the same 254 events. The append table grew by exactly 254 rows, to 1,304, while the source still holds 1,050 events. The MERGE table did not change. Finally, publish run 2 and process it: docker exec spark-master bash -c '$SPARK_HOME/bin/spark-submit \ --master "local[2]" \ --conf spark.eventLog.enabled=false --conf spark.ui.enabled=false \ /tmp/produce_orders.py 2' docker exec spark-master bash -c '$SPARK_HOME/bin/spark-submit \ --master "local[2]" \ --conf spark.eventLog.enabled=false --conf spark.ui.enabled=false \ --jars $(ls $ICEBERG_HOME/iceberg-spark-runtime*.jar) \ /tmp/orders_stream.py' batch 3: 399 events batch 4: 141 events orders: 1500 rows orders_append: 1844 rows +-------+------+ | status|orders| +-------+------+ | PLACED| 1470| |SHIPPED| 30| +-------+------+ The 540 new events became batches 3 and 4. The MERGE table now has 1,500 orders: 30 moved to SHIPPED, and the 10 stale PENDING events were rejected by s.updated_ts > t.updated_ts, so no order shows PENDING. The append table holds 1,844 rows for 1,590 published events: the 254-row replay, plus every duplicate and every superseded version. Step 5: why the in-batch dedup matters Remove the window and feed a MERGE two copies of one key, and Spark refuses the whole statement: """Show what MERGE does when one micro-batch carries the same key twice.""" from pyspark.sql import SparkSession spark = ( SparkSession.builder.appName("sd-merge-dup") .config("spark.sql.extensions", "org.apache.iceberg.spark.extensions." "IcebergSparkSessionExtensions") .config("spark.serializer", "org.apache.spark.serializer.KryoSerializer") .config("spark.sql.catalog.sd", "org.apache.iceberg.spark.SparkCatalog") .config("spark.sql.catalog.sd.type", "hadoop") .config("spark.sql.catalog.sd.warehouse", "file:///tmp/sd_blog/warehouse") .getOrCreate() ) spark.sql("CREATE NAMESPACE IF NOT EXISTS sd.shop") spark.sql("DROP TABLE IF EXISTS sd.shop.merge_dup PURGE") spark.sql("CREATE TABLE sd.shop.merge_dup (order_id STRING, status STRING) " "USING iceberg") spark.sql("INSERT INTO sd.shop.merge_dup VALUES ('o00001', 'PLACED')") spark.createDataFrame( [("o00001", "SHIPPED"), ("o00001", "SHIPPED")], "order_id STRING, status STRING", ).createOrReplaceTempView("retried_batch") try: spark.sql(""" MERGE INTO sd.shop.merge_dup t USING retried_batch s ON t.order_id = s.order_id WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET * WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT *""") except Exception as err: # the failure is the point code = "MERGE_CARDINALITY_VIOLATION" print(f"MERGE failed: {code}" if code in str(err) else err) spark.sql("DROP TABLE sd.shop.merge_dup PURGE") spark.stop() MERGE failed: MERGE_CARDINALITY_VIOLATION The full error is SparkRuntimeException: [MERGE_CARDINALITY_VIOLATION] The ON search condition of the MERGE statement matched a single row from the target table with multiple rows of the source table. In a streaming job this fails the batch, and every restart replays the same batch and fails again, so the query is stuck until the code changes. Deduplicate inside each batch before merging. What the demo proves, and a pitfall it found Replay is the engine’s job; idempotency is yours. Spark re-ran batch 2 with identical input, as its checkpoint protocol promises. Only the sink design decided whether that produced duplicates. The catalog cache pitfall. The first version of orders_stream.py counted the tables at the end without REFRESH TABLE and printed 0 rows for both, although the data was there. Structured Streaming runs each query in a cloned SparkSession, and foreachBatch hands you a DataFrame bound to that clone, whose Iceberg catalog has its own table cache. The driver session still held the table it loaded at creation time, before any batch committed. REFRESH TABLE invalidates the cached entry. A monitoring job that reads row counts from a long-lived session can report stale numbers in the same way. Clean up docker exec spark-master rm -rf /tmp/sd_blog docker exec kafka kafka-topics --bootstrap-server kafka:29092 \ --delete --topic sd_blog_orders Demo interview questions 13. Your streaming job writes to a table with foreachBatch. How do you make it exactly-once? foreachBatch gives at-least-once: an uncommitted batch is re-run with the same offsets and the same batch_id. I make the write idempotent. Either I MERGE on the entity key after deduplicating within the batch, so a replay rewrites the same rows, or I use a sink that records the batch id it committed and skips a repeat (Delta Lake supports this with the txnAppId and txnVersion writer options). A plain append inside foreachBatch duplicates the batch on replay. 14. An old event arrives after a newer one for the same order. What protects the table? The event’s own time, not the arrival order. The contract carries updated_ts, and the MERGE updates only WHEN MATCHED AND s.updated_ts > t.updated_ts. Within a batch, a window keeps the newest version per key, with the Kafka offset as a tie-breaker. Without the guard, “latest wins” means “last to arrive wins”, and a retried or delayed event rolls the order back. Real-world scenarios: ten worked designs Each design follows the framework in compressed form: assumptions, an estimate, the flow, the decisions that matter, and the failure modes an interviewer will push on. The numbers are assumptions to state, not facts about any company. Design 1: clickstream analytics for a large website Prompt. Collect page views and clicks from web and mobile, power product dashboards within five minutes, and keep history for analysis. Assumptions and estimate. 10 TB a day of JSON events at about 1 KB each is 10 billion events a day, about 116,000 events a second on average and roughly 350,000 at a 3x peak, around 350 MB/s. web / mobile SDK ──► collector API (stateless, autoscaled, batches events) │ key = session_id or user_id ▼ Kafka clicks.raw ── 7 days ──► stream job: │ parse, validate, enrich │ (geo, user agent), dedup ▼ on event_id bronze (Iceberg, raw JSON + parsed) ──► silver sessions partitioned by event hour (30-min gap) │ │ ▼ ▼ gold: hourly metrics ──────────────► OLAP store (Pinot / per page, funnel, cohort ClickHouse) for 5-minute dashboards Key decisions. The collector batches events and returns quickly; mobile SDKs buffer offline, so expect events hours or days late and partition bronze by event hour while accepting writes to old partitions. Sessionisation is a stateful operation keyed by user with an inactivity gap, typically 30 minutes; run it in the stream with a watermark, or hourly in batch if five-minute freshness only applies to page-level counts. Bot traffic is filtered in silver with a flag, not dropped, so the rule can change later. Failure modes. A viral page makes one key hot if you key by page; key by session instead. A mobile release that floods duplicate events is absorbed by event_id dedup. Identity resolution (anonymous id to logged-in user) changes history, so keep it as a mapping table joined at read time rather than rewriting events. Design 2: CDC from an OLTP database to the lakehouse in under five minutes Prompt. Replicate 300 PostgreSQL tables into the lakehouse with under five minutes of lag, including deletes, for analytics. PostgreSQL ── logical replication slot ──► Debezium (Kafka Connect) │ snapshot first, then WAL changes │ one topic per table │ │ key = primary key ▼ ▼ outbox / heartbeat table Kafka + Schema Registry (Avro) │ ▼ stream job per table group, 1-min trigger bronze: append change events (op, lsn) silver: MERGE on PK, ordered by lsn; op = 'd' ──► DELETE Key decisions. Debezium takes a consistent snapshot, then streams from the replication slot, so the lake starts from a known point. Order changes for a row by the source log position (the LSN for PostgreSQL), not by arrival time. Keep bronze append-only with every change event; silver is the MERGE result. Schema changes go through the registry with backward compatibility, and a column drop at the source becomes a nullable column in the lake rather than a failure. Merge-on-read tables suit high-update tables; compact them on a schedule. Failure modes. If Debezium stops, the replication slot keeps WAL on the primary until the disk fills; cap it with max_slot_wal_keep_size and alert on slot lag. A large table’s initial snapshot can take hours; incremental snapshots let streaming continue during it. Reconcile row counts per table per hour against the source. Design 3: a real-time operations dashboard with a 10-second SLA Prompt. Show orders per minute, revenue and error rates per region with data at most 10 seconds old. Key decisions. Ten seconds rules out lakehouse commits as the serving path, so the stream job aggregates in tumbling or sliding windows and writes the results to a low-latency store: an OLAP engine that ingests from Kafka directly (Pinot, Druid, ClickHouse with a Kafka engine) or a key-value store holding the current window counts with a TTL. The same events still land in the lakehouse for history and for correcting late data. The dashboard reads the fast store; anything older than a day reads gold. Failure modes. Late events update a window already shown; decide whether the dashboard corrects old buckets or rolls forward, and say which. A burst that causes consumer lag makes the dashboard stale silently; show the data’s age on the dashboard itself. Design 4: log aggregation for 10,000 servers Assumptions and estimate. 10,000 servers at 5,000 lines a second each is 50 million lines a second; at 300 bytes a line that is 15 GB/s, about 1.3 PB a day before compression. The estimate is the design: at this volume, sampling and tiering are not optional. agents (Fluent Bit / Vector) ── batch, compress, local buffer on disk │ drop DEBUG at source; sample INFO; keep WARN+ at 100% ▼ Kafka (per-service topics) ──► stream: parse, add metadata, route │ ├─► search cluster: 7 days hot │ └─► object storage: Parquet, zstd, │ partitioned by service/hour, ▼ queried with Trino; 90 days metrics extracted from logs ──► time-series store for alerting Key decisions. Agents buffer to local disk so a Kafka outage does not lose logs or block applications. Filtering and sampling happen at the edge, because shipping and then dropping costs network and broker disk. Hot search holds days, the lake holds months, and retention is set per log level and service. Failure modes. A noisy service floods the pipeline; enforce per-service quotas in Kafka. A parsing change breaks a format; keep the raw line in the lake so it can be re-parsed. Design 5: a fraud feature pipeline with a 100 ms decision Prompt. Score card transactions at 5,000 a second with features such as “transactions for this card in the last 10 minutes” and “distance from the last transaction”. payment API ──► Kafka txns (key = card_id) ──► Flink keyed state per card: counts in sliding windows, last location, amount stats │ upsert features ▼ payment API ── sync call ──► scoring service ──► online feature store (decision < 100 ms) │ model (Redis / DynamoDB, │ single-digit ms reads) ▼ decision event ──► Kafka ──► lakehouse (training data, point-in-time correct) Key decisions. The decision path is synchronous and reads precomputed features; nothing heavy runs inside the 100 ms. Features are computed by a stateful stream keyed by card, so all of one card’s events go to one task. The same feature definitions feed the offline store with point-in-time joins, so training sees what the model would have seen at decision time; mismatched logic between the two is training-serving skew. Failure modes. If the feature store is slow, the scoring service needs a fallback rule set and a timeout, decided with the business: allow, block, or review. Feature freshness lag shows up as missed fraud, so alert on it. Design 6: IoT telemetry from one million devices Assumptions and estimate. One million devices reporting every 5 seconds is 200,000 messages a second; at 200 bytes each, 40 MB/s. Key decisions. Devices speak MQTT to a broker built for many long-lived connections, which bridges to Kafka keyed by device_id. The stream computes per-device rolling statistics and threshold alerts with keyed state (RocksDB for a million keys). Recent raw data goes to a time-series store with downsampling; everything lands in the lakehouse partitioned by date, sorted or clustered by device for per-device queries. Failure modes. Devices reconnect after an outage and send hours of buffered data at once, so the watermark must tolerate it or the late data must go through a batch path. Device clocks drift; record both device time and ingestion time. Design 7: a multi-tenant file ingestion service Prompt. Customers upload CSV files of up to 5 GB; parse, validate, store and report errors back to them. customer ──► pre-signed upload URL ──► s3://landing/<tenant>/<upload_id>/ │ object-created event ▼ queue ──► validation job (per file) │ schema + row rules per tenant ├─► valid rows ──► bronze, tagged │ tenant, upload_id └─► rejected rows ─► errors table + report to tenant status table: upload_id, state (RECEIVED → VALIDATING → LOADED | FAILED) Key decisions. Uploads go straight to object storage through pre-signed URLs, so the API never carries file bytes. Processing is keyed by upload_id, which makes a re-run of the same file a replace, not an append. Each tenant gets quotas and a separate prefix, and tenant id is a column in every table for isolation and deletion. Failure modes. A malformed 5 GB file should fail fast on a sampled header check, not after an hour. One large tenant must not starve others; use per-tenant concurrency limits. Design 8: an e-commerce warehouse for daily reporting Prompt. 2 million orders a day across web and stores; finance, marketing and operations dashboards refreshed daily, with history kept as it was. Key decisions. This is a batch design, and saying so early is a strength: 2 million orders a day is about 23 a second. Ingest with CDC or daily extracts into bronze, build silver with dbt or Spark, and model gold as a star schema: fact_order_line at one row per order line, conformed dim_customer and dim_product with SCD Type 2 history, and a date dimension. Partition the facts by order date. Separate compute for loading and for BI queries so a heavy dashboard does not delay the load. The data modeling guide covers this model in full. Failure modes. Returns and cancellations arrive days later and change past totals; decide whether gold restates history or records adjustments. A fact joined to the current dimension version instead of the version valid at order time rewrites history. Design 9: a data quality platform for 500 tables Key decisions. Checks are declared next to the data, as YAML or dbt tests in version control, owned by the dataset owner. The orchestrator runs them as a stage after each load. Gold checks block publishing; bronze checks warn. Results go to a metrics store with history, so the platform can detect drift (row counts, null rates) against the past instead of fixed thresholds alone. Lineage connects a failed check to downstream consumers, and the catalog shows each table’s health. Failure modes. Alert fatigue: hundreds of low-value checks get ignored. Start with freshness, volume and key uniqueness on the most-used tables, and add checks after incidents. Design 10: GDPR right to erasure across the lake Prompt. Delete a user’s personal data within 30 days of a request, across Kafka, the lakehouse, backups and derived tables. Key decisions. Keep PII in as few tables as possible, keyed by a user id, and refer to users elsewhere by a pseudonymous key. Then erasure is a delete in those tables plus a rewrite of affected files: a table format DELETE writes new files or delete files, and only snapshot expiry and orphan-file cleanup physically remove the old bytes. Old snapshots still contain the data until they expire, so the expiry schedule is part of the compliance window. Kafka retention shorter than the erasure window avoids rewriting topics. An alternative is crypto-shredding: encrypt each user’s PII with a per-user key and delete the key. Failure modes. Time travel and backups resurrect deleted data; document how long each retains it. Derived aggregates that cannot identify a person can stay; derived tables with user-level rows must be included. Production failures: where designs break Symptom Cause Design fix Revenue doubles after a node restart Append sink replayed an uncommitted batch Idempotent MERGE on a key, or a batch-id-aware sink Streaming job fails on every restart MERGE_CARDINALITY_VIOLATION from duplicate keys in one batch Deduplicate within the batch before MERGE An order shows an old status Stale event overwrote a newer one: last to arrive won Version guard on event time or log position Primary database disk fills overnight CDC connector stopped; replication slot retained WAL max_slot_wal_keep_size, slot-lag alert Consumer lag climbs while CPU is idle Rebalance storms: processing exceeds max.poll.interval.ms (default 300000 ms) Smaller polls, faster processing, or more partitions One task runs for hours, others finish Hot key or skewed partition Salting, AQE skew join, a separate path for the outlier Queries slow down week by week Thousands of small files and snapshots Compaction, larger commits, snapshot expiry Backfill makes the live pipeline miss its SLO Shared compute and source Separate pool, throttled backfill, read from the lake Dashboard flat at zero, no alert Job succeeded with zero rows Volume checks against history Monitoring reports stale counts Cached table in a long-lived session REFRESH TABLE, or read through a fresh session Scenario interview questions 15. Design a pipeline that ingests clickstream data and serves 5-minute dashboards. What are the hardest parts? Late and duplicate events, sessionisation state, and keeping two serving paths consistent. Mobile clients send events hours late, so bronze is partitioned by event time and accepts writes to old partitions, and gold numbers for recent hours are marked provisional. Duplicates from SDK retries are removed by event_id at the silver MERGE. Sessions need keyed state with an inactivity gap and a watermark. The dashboards read an OLAP store fed by the stream; history reads gold, and a daily reconciliation compares the two. 16. Your CDC connector was down for six hours. What happens, and how do you recover? On PostgreSQL the replication slot holds WAL since the connector’s last confirmed position, so nothing is lost as long as the primary has disk; that is why slot lag is a P1 alert and max_slot_wal_keep_size is set, accepting that an invalidated slot means a re-snapshot. When the connector restarts it resumes from the slot, Kafka absorbs the burst, and the stream job catches up, bounded by maxOffsetsPerTrigger so batches stay a manageable size. The silver MERGE is ordered by LSN, so replayed changes apply correctly. Then I reconcile counts for the window. 17. How would you handle a request to delete one user's data from the lakehouse? I would have designed for it: PII lives in a few tables keyed by user id, and everything else uses a pseudonymous key. The deletion job runs a table-format DELETE on those tables, which writes new files or delete files. The old bytes remain in earlier snapshots, so snapshot expiry and orphan-file removal must run within the compliance window, and time travel beyond it is not allowed for those tables. Kafka retention is shorter than the window. For data that cannot be rewritten, per-user encryption keys allow crypto-shredding. 18. When would you not use Kafka? When there is one consumer, freshness is hourly or daily, and the source can be re-read. A daily extract or CDC files landed in object storage and loaded in batch are simpler and cheaper. Kafka earns its operating cost when several consumers need the same events, when bursts must be absorbed, or when sub- minute freshness and replay from a log are requirements. Optimisation, tuning knobs and best practices Partitioning and skew Partition storage by the column most queries filter on, usually a date or hour of event time, and keep partitions large enough to hold files of hundreds of megabytes. Over-partitioning (by date and user id, say) creates millions of tiny files. Within partitions, sort or cluster by a second frequent filter so file-level min and max statistics can skip files. For skewed joins, Spark’s adaptive query execution splits oversized shuffle partitions. It is on by default (spark.sql.adaptive.enabled = true, spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.enabled = true). A partition is treated as skewed when it is larger than spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.skewedPartitionFactor (5.0) times the median and larger than spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.skewedPartitionThresholdInBytes (256 MB). When the skew is a known hot key, salting it or handling it in a separate branch is more predictable. The data skew post covers both. Backpressure and rate limits When consumers fall behind, the log absorbs it, and consumer lag is the signal. Act on it in order: scale the bottleneck stage, bound the batch size so a backlog does not create one enormous batch (maxOffsetsPerTrigger for Spark’s Kafka source), and shed or defer low-priority work. A backlog larger than retention is data loss, so alert on lag as time (“40 minutes behind”) against the retention window, not as a message count. Small files and table maintenance Each streaming commit adds files and a snapshot. Schedule maintenance per table: Task Iceberg procedure Why Compact small files CALL sd.system.rewrite_data_files('shop.orders') Fewer, larger files; faster scans Expire snapshots CALL sd.system.expire_snapshots('shop.orders', TIMESTAMP '2026-10-21 00:00:00') Bounds metadata and frees storage Remove orphan files CALL sd.system.remove_orphan_files(table => 'shop.orders') Deletes files left by failed writes Rewrite manifests CALL sd.system.rewrite_manifests('shop.orders') Faster planning on tables with many commits Iceberg’s default snapshot age for expiry is 5 days (history.expire.max-snapshot-age-ms = 432000000), which also bounds how far back time travel works after expiry runs. Cost Name the cost drivers with the design, because the interviewer will ask: Driver Lever Always-on streaming compute Micro-batch on a schedule (availableNow) when freshness allows Log storage Retention sized to the replay need; tiered storage for long retention Object storage Columnar formats with zstd, lifecycle rules to colder tiers Query compute Partition pruning, clustering, pre-aggregated gold tables, auto-suspend Cross-zone and egress traffic Keep producers, brokers and consumers in-region; rack-aware consumers Duplicate copies Fewer layers with clear contracts; views where a copy adds nothing Tuning checklist Area Knob Default Guidance Kafka producer acks all (Kafka 3.0+) Keep all for data you cannot lose Kafka producer enable.idempotence true (Kafka 3.0+) Keep enabled Kafka topic min.insync.replicas 1 2 with replication factor 3 Kafka topic retention.ms 604800000 (7 days) Replay window plus margin Kafka consumer max.poll.interval.ms 300000 Raise only with a reason; prefer smaller polls Spark spark.sql.shuffle.partitions 200 AQE coalesces; set for the largest stage Spark spark.sql.adaptive.advisoryPartitionSizeInBytes 64 MB Target shuffle partition size Spark spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold 10 MB Raise for medium dimensions if memory allows Spark spark.sql.files.maxPartitionBytes 128 MB Input split size for file scans Spark streaming maxOffsetsPerTrigger (Kafka source) None Bound batches during catch-up Spark streaming spark.sql.streaming.stateStore.providerClass HDFS-backed RocksDB provider for large state Iceberg write.target-file-size-bytes 536870912 (512 MB) Keep large; compact streaming tables Iceberg commit.retry.num-retries 4 Raise for many concurrent writers Tuning interview questions 19. Your streaming table has 200,000 small files. How did that happen, and what do you do? Each micro-batch commit writes at least one file per written partition per task, so a short trigger interval, many shuffle partitions and fine-grained partitioning multiply into many small files. I would lengthen the trigger interval if freshness allows, reduce the number of writing tasks or use a hash distribution so each partition gets fewer files, and schedule rewrite_data_files for compaction plus expire_snapshots and orphan-file cleanup. I would also check whether partitioning is too fine for the volume. 20. Consumer lag keeps growing. Walk me through the diagnosis. First, is it all partitions or a few? A few means skew: a hot key or an uneven partition assignment. All partitions means throughput: check whether the job is CPU-bound, waiting on the sink (slow commits, a throttled database), or rebalancing because processing exceeds max.poll.interval.ms. Then act: scale the bottleneck, bound batch sizes, fix the hot key, or add partitions with a plan for the key remapping. Throughout, I compare lag in time with the retention window, because a backlog beyond retention loses data. 21. How would you cut the cost of a 50 TB-a-day platform? Measure first: compute, storage, log retention and data transfer each need a number. Then the usual levers: run streams that only need 15-minute freshness as scheduled micro-batches instead of always-on clusters; use spot or preemptible capacity for batch with retries; store columnar with zstd and lifecycle old partitions to colder tiers; compact and cluster so queries scan less; pre-aggregate the most expensive dashboard queries into gold tables; and keep traffic in one region. Each change gets a before and after number. Key takeaways A data system design answer is judged on what happens after the happy path: the restart, the replay, the late event, the schema change, the bill. The framework puts those questions in the order an interviewer expects. Consumer and decision first, then numbers, then the contract, then the diagram, then recovery, operations and trade-offs. The mental model to carry into the room: The log and the lake are your replay stores. Know how far back each goes, and design every sink so that replaying into it is safe. Delivery is at-least-once; effects are made exactly-once at the sink. The demo showed it: Spark replayed batch 2 with identical input, the append table grew from 1,050 to 1,304 rows, and the MERGE table stayed at 1,000. Event time orders versions; arrival time does not. A version guard in the MERGE rejected all 10 stale events. Commits are the unit of cost in a lakehouse. Batch them, compact them, and expire them. Quality is monitored on data. Freshness, volume, schema, validity and reconciliation, with owners and lineage. Practise each worked design out loud against a 40-minute timer. For each one, say the binding requirement, the estimate, the replay story and one rejected alternative. If you can do that for all ten, the specific prompt matters much less. entry.title: 50 job websites for remote and tech roles, and how to use them well

link.title: 50 job websites for remote and tech roles, and how to use them well

entry.content:
• Why a list of job websites needs notes
  • The 50 sites, grouped by what they are good for
    • Big aggregators
    • Remote-first boards
    • Startups
    • Freelance and contract marketplaces
    • Creative and design
    • Diversity-focused
  • Which groups to use for which goal
  • Finding roles before they reach aggregators
  • Practical lessons
  • Key takeaways

TL;DR

  • Fifty sites sounds like a lot, but they fall into six groups: big aggregators, remote-first boards, startup boards, freelance marketplaces, creative portfolios and diversity-focused boards. Most people need two or three groups, not all six.
  • “Remote” usually means remote within a region. On most global remote boards, the large majority of data and engineering roles are restricted to the US, Europe or LATAM. Filter by country before you read a single description.
  • Many companies post straight to their applicant tracking system (Greenhouse, Lever, Ashby). Searching those domains directly finds roles days before they show up on aggregators.
  • A listing on an aggregator is not proof the job is open. Check the original posting first; a lot of results point at closed roles.
  • Read the screening questions before you start an application. Address, notice period, salary, work-hour overlap and conflict-of-interest questions are common, and having the answers ready turns a 20-minute form into a 3-minute one.

Why a list of job websites needs notes

Lists of job websites are everywhere, and most of them stop at the names. The names are the easy part. What costs time is discovering, site by site, that a board is US-only, that its “remote” filter means “remote in Europe”, that a listing is four months old, or that applying requires an account on yet another platform.

This post groups the 50 sites by what they are good for and adds the notes I wish I had before I started using them, particularly for engineers based in India looking at remote or Bangalore roles.

The 50 sites, grouped by what they are good for

Big aggregators

These index millions of listings, including company career pages. They have the widest coverage and the most noise.

# Site Best for
1 LinkedIn Everything. Easy Apply plus recruiter visibility. Filter by date posted and experience level.
2 Indeed Very broad coverage. Use the country site (for example in.indeed.com) for local roles.
3 SimplyHired US-focused aggregator.
4 Jooble Aggregator with country editions.
5 CareerBuilder US-focused.
6 ZipRecruiter US-focused, strong on alerts.
7 Adzuna Aggregator with salary data and an India edition.
8 Talent.com Aggregator with salary estimates.
9 The Muse Company profiles plus listings, US-heavy.
10 Totaljobs / CWJobs / Technojobs UK market.
11 Hired Reverse marketplace for tech roles; check current availability in your region.

Remote-first boards

Every listing is remote in some form. Read the location line carefully: most are remote within a country or time zone.

# Site Notes
12 We Work Remotely One of the largest remote boards; each listing states the allowed region.
13 Remote OK Large, tag-based, shows salary ranges.
14 Remotive Curated; small but clean.
15 Remote.co Curated remote roles and remote-company profiles.
16 Working Nomads Curated digest, good email alerts.
17 Jobspresso Hand-picked tech, marketing and support roles.
18 JustRemote Remote and partially remote roles.
19 Himalayas Good country filter, company profiles, salary data.
20 NoDesk Curated remote roles and resources.
21 Dynamite Jobs Remote-only, vetted listings.
22 Pangian Global remote community and board.
23 SkipTheDrive US-focused remote roles.
24 Jobicy Remote-only board with salary data and company research.
25 Jobgether Remote roles with location-eligibility matching; many listings are posted on behalf of partner companies.
26 Flexa Flexible and remote roles, UK and Europe heavy.
27 Remote Rocketship Strong country filter (for example India - Remote), sorted by date added.
28 Remote4Me Remote aggregator.
29 Remotees Remote aggregator.
30 RemoteHabits Remote roles plus remote-work guides.
31 DailyRemote Daily-updated remote aggregator.
32 TrulyRemoteWork Roles that are remote without hidden location limits.
33 Europe Remotely Remote roles for Europe-based candidates.
34 FlexJobs Hand-screened remote and flexible roles; paid subscription.

Startups

# Site Notes
35 Wellfound (formerly AngelList Talent) Startup roles with salary and equity shown up front; apply with one profile.
36 Y Combinator: Work at a Startup Roles at YC companies, one profile for all of them.
37 Hacker News: Who is hiring? Monthly thread; many posts are founders hiring directly.
38 Welcome to the Jungle Startup and scale-up roles with rich company pages.
39 Arbeitnow Europe-focused, with a public API and visa-sponsorship filter.

Freelance and contract marketplaces

These are for gig and contract work. You bid on projects or get matched; there is no traditional application.

# Site Notes
40 Upwork The largest general freelance marketplace.
41 Toptal Screened network for senior freelancers.
42 Freelancer Project bidding.
43 Fiverr Productised services (“gigs”).
44 PeoplePerHour Freelance projects, UK and Europe heavy.
45 freelancermap Freelance IT projects with no commission on contracts.
46 Contra Commission-free freelance profiles.
47 Arc Vetted remote developers, freelance and full-time.

Creative and design

# Site Notes
48 Dribbble Design roles; your portfolio is the application.
49 Behance Creative roles tied to Behance portfolios.

Diversity-focused

# Site Notes
50 PowerToFly Roles at companies hiring for diverse teams, with virtual hiring events.

Which groups to use for which goal

  • Full-time engineering role in your own city: LinkedIn and the country edition of Indeed, plus the regional boards your market actually uses. In India that means adding Naukri and Instahyre, which are not in the 50 but carry a large share of senior engineering roles.
  • Full-time remote role from India: Remote Rocketship and Himalayas (country filters), Jobgether, and the ATS search described below. Treat the global remote boards as a bonus, not the main source.
  • Startup role: Wellfound, Work at a Startup and the monthly Hacker News thread.
  • Contract or side income: the freelance marketplaces, chosen by how you want to be paid (bids, gigs or a vetted network).

Finding roles before they reach aggregators

Most companies publish openings on their applicant tracking system first, and aggregators pick them up later. Greenhouse, Lever and Ashby host job pages on predictable domains, so you can search them directly:

"data engineer" remote site:greenhouse.io OR site:jobs.lever.co OR site:ashbyhq.com

Swap in your own title and add a location, for example (India OR Bengaluru). In Google, open Tools, then Any time, and choose Past 24 hours or Past week.

Two caveats from using this:

  • Search engines rate-limit site: queries quickly. Run a few targeted searches rather than dozens of variations.
  • Greenhouse has a public read-only API that tells you whether a posting is still open and lists its required questions, at https://boards-api.greenhouse.io/v1/boards/<company>/jobs/<id>?questions=true. A 404 means the role is closed, which saves opening a form for nothing.

Practical lessons

  1. Filter by eligible location first. On the global remote boards I checked in one week, almost every data engineering role was limited to the US, Europe or LATAM. Country filters (Remote Rocketship, Himalayas) and per-listing region lines (We Work Remotely) save the most time.
  2. Check that the listing is live. Aggregator results often point at postings that were closed weeks ago. Open the original ATS page before you plan your answers.
  3. Read the screening questions up front. The ones that slow people down are full postal address, notice period and earliest start date, current and expected compensation, years with specific tools, willingness to work overlapping hours, and conflict-of-interest declarations. Keep these answers in one document and reuse them.
  4. Expect some applications to need an account. Workday, Dayforce and some other career sites require registering per company. Budget the time, or prioritise roles with a direct form.
  5. Tailor, but do not rewrite from scratch. One strong base resume plus a short, honest “why this company” paragraph covers most applications.
  6. Track everything. A simple sheet with date, site, company, role, link and status prevents duplicate applications and makes follow-ups easy.

Key takeaways

  • Pick the two or three groups of sites that match your goal instead of working through all 50.
  • For remote roles, eligibility is the real filter; use boards that let you filter by country.
  • Search Greenhouse, Lever and Ashby directly to see roles first, and confirm each one is still open.
  • Prepare your screening answers once and reuse them; that is where most application time goes.
